slab = Box(np.diag([10.0, 10.0, 30.0]), pbc=[True, True, False])

positions = np.array([[11.0, -1.0, 5.0], [3.0, 4.0, 25.0]])
wrapped, image = box.wrap(positions)
# wrapped: [[1, 9, 5], [3, 4, 1]]   image: [[1, -1, 0], [0, 0, 2]]
box.minimum_image([[9.0, 0.0, 0.0]])  # [[-1, 0, 0]]

docs.title: Creating a box
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning matrix float64, (3,) float64 or (3, 3) float64 Å A number gives a cube; three numbers an orthogonal box; a (3, 3) array a general box whose rows are the lattice vectors a, b, c. origin (3,) float64 (0, 0, 0) Å Position of the corner from which the lattice vectors start. pbc bool or (3,) bool True Periodicity along a, b and c.

Other constructors:

Constructor Meaning Box.from_lengths_angles(a, b, c, alpha=90, beta=90, gamma=90, origin, pbc) Edge lengths in Å and angles in degrees (alpha between b and c, beta between a and c, gamma between a and b). a lies along x and b in the xy plane. Box.from_lammps(lo, hi, tilt=(0, 0, 0), pbc) LAMMPS bounds (xlo, ylo, zlo), (xhi, yhi, zhi) and tilt factors (xy, xz, yz). Box.enclosing(positions, padding=1.0) Non-periodic orthogonal box around a set of positions, for molecules and clusters.

Lattice vectors that are not finite or are linearly dependent raise InvalidParameter.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Name Type Unit Meaning matrix (3, 3) float64 Å Lattice vectors, one per row. origin (3,) float64 Å Corner of the box. pbc (3,) bool Periodicity. inverse (3, 3) float64 1/Å Inverse of matrix. volume float64 Å³ Volume. lengths (3,) float64 Å Lengths of a, b, c. angles (3,) float64 degree alpha, beta, gamma. thickness (3,) float64 Å Distance between each pair of opposite faces. is_orthogonal bool Whether the lattice vectors lie along +x, +y, +z.

The arrays are read-only. Boxes compare equal with == when all values are identical, and box.allclose(other) compares them within a tolerance.

docs.title: Coordinates
docs.text: Method Returns to_fractional(positions) Coordinates in units of the lattice vectors, relative to origin. to_cartesian(fractional) Positions in Å. wrap(positions) (wrapped, image): positions mapped into the box along periodic directions, and integer image flags. minimum_image(vectors) The shortest periodic image of each displacement vector. to_lammps() The box in LAMMPS restricted triclinic form, with the rotation to apply to positions and other vectors.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
With the lattice vectors as rows of the matrix \(H\), a position \(\mathbf r\) has fractional coordinates \(\mathbf s = (\mathbf r - \mathbf r_0) H^{-1}\), where \(\mathbf r_0\) is the origin.

Wrapping gives image flags \(\mathbf n = \lfloor \mathbf s \rfloor\) along periodic directions, so that the wrapped position has \(0 \le s_i < 1\) and \(\mathbf r = \mathbf r_\text{wrapped} + \mathbf n H\). Shifting a position by whole lattice vectors and wrapping it back returns the original numbers exactly.

Minimum image returns the shortest periodic image of each vector for every box whose tilt factors are within half of the corresponding edge length, the limit LAMMPS uses.

Thickness is the distance between the two faces not crossed by lattice vector \(i\).

LAMMPS form. LAMMPS needs a along +x, b in the xy plane and positive diagonal entries: \(H' = \begin{pmatrix} l_x & 0 & 0\\ xy & l_y & 0\\ xz & yz & l_z \end{pmatrix}\). to_lammps() returns \(H'\) and the rotation \(Q\) with \(H' = HQ\); every vector \(\mathbf v\), positions and velocities included, becomes \(\mathbf v Q\). A box already in this form comes back unchanged, with \(Q\) the identity. Left-handed lattice vectors, which LAMMPS rejects, are made right-handed by swapping b and c, which describes the same lattice.

docs.title: Changing a system
docs.text:
A system never changes. To change something, make a new system with one of the methods below; the old one stays as it was. This page shows the methods, then what a new system shares with the old one and what it copies, and why nothing can change a system in place.

import copy
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(10, 10, 10))
charged = crystal.with_columns(charge=0.0)
moved = crystal.with_columns(positions=crystal["positions"] + [0.5, 0.0, 0.0])
strained = crystal.with_box(crystal.box.matrix * 1.01, scale_positions=True)
labelled = crystal.with_info(energy=-3.54, label="perfect")
"charge" in crystal.table.columns  # False: crystal is as it was

docs.title: The methods
docs.text:
Method Makes a system with with_columns(*exprs, **named) columns added or replaced, the positions too: polars expressions or Series, NumPy arrays, one value for all atoms, or the results of analyses with_box(box, *, scale_positions=False) another box, or other lattice vectors with the same origin and periodicity; with scale_positions=True the atoms keep their fractional coordinates and deform with the box with_info(values, /, **updates) other global information: values replaces all of it, {} clears it; then updates adds or replaces entries, and None removes one with_topology(topology) another topology, or none with None with_table(table) another table of the same atoms in the same order, for operations of polars on the whole table select(*columns), drop(*columns), rename(names) only some columns, in a given order; without some columns; columns renamed filter, gather, sort some of the atoms, or all in another order; see Selecting and ordering atoms

The names and the meaning of with_columns, select, drop, rename, filter and sort are those of polars: the first four work on columns, the last two on rows, that is atoms.

with_columns takes polars expressions too, computed on the table:

doubled = charged.with_columns(
    pl.col("charge") + 1.0, height=pl.col("positions").arr.get(2)
)

and the result of an analysis, whose per-atom values it adds as columns:

from mdapy.identify import CommonNeighborAnalysis

with_structure = crystal.with_columns(CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(crystal))
with_structure.table["cna_structure"].dtype  # Int8

The columns of a result are named by its method and options, such as cna_structure, ptm_rmsd or q6_average_voronoi, so that several analyses stay side by side. Runs of one analysis with different numbers, such as two cutoffs, take names of yours, which become prefixes:

from mdapy.analysis import CoordinationNumber
from mdapy.identify import PolyhedralTemplateMatching

several = crystal.with_columns(
    CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(crystal),
    PolyhedralTemplateMatching().compute(crystal),
    near=CoordinationNumber(cutoff=3.0).compute(crystal),
    far=CoordinationNumber(cutoff=4.0).compute(crystal),
)
several.table.columns  # ..., cna_structure, ptm_structure, near_coordination, far_coordination

Two values for one column in one call are an error. A later call replaces the column, as when the same analysis runs again on a new frame.

with_table is for operations of polars on the whole table that have no method of their own, such as a join with values kept elsewhere:

numbered = crystal.with_columns(id=np.arange(1, len(crystal) + 1))
measured = pl.DataFrame({"id": [2, 1], "stress": [1.5, 0.5]})
joined = numbered.with_table(
    numbered.table.join(measured, on="id", how="left", maintain_order="left")
)
joined["stress"][:3]  # 0.5, 1.5 and NaN for the atoms not measured

It cannot tell whether the atoms of the new table are in the same order: the topology refers to atoms by their row, so to reorder atoms use sort or gather, which renumber the topology, and to remove some use filter.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
select keeps the columns given, in that order, and computes those given as polars expressions; drop removes columns; rename gives columns new names. The positions are always kept: leaving them out, dropping them or renaming them raises an error.

analysed = with_structure.with_columns(charge=0.0, csp=0.0)
written = analysed.select("element", "positions", "cna_structure")  # for a file
lean = analysed.drop("csp", "charge")
standard = analysed.with_columns(q=0.1).drop("charge").rename({"q": "charge"})

A column renamed to a standard name, such as charge or type, is checked as one: type must hold whole numbers from 1.

docs.title: Global information
docs.text:
with_info adds, replaces or removes entries, or, given a mapping, replaces all of them:

labelled.with_info(energy=-3.60)  # energy replaced, label kept
labelled.with_info(label=None)  # label removed
labelled.with_info({})  # nothing left
labelled.with_info({"source": "relaxed"}, step=10)  # source and step only

filter, gather and sort keep the global information as it is. After filter some of it may no longer hold, the energy of the whole system for example; clear or replace it when it does not:

upper = labelled.filter("positions.z > 18").with_info({})

docs.title: What is shared and what is copied
docs.text:
The data of a system lives in its columns. A new system is a new table whose columns are those of the old system, except the ones that change:

  • columns that do not change are shared: both systems point to the same memory, and no data is copied;
  • columns that change are new: only they take new memory;
  • arrays given to a system, by its constructor or by these methods, are copied once, so changing them afterwards does not change the system.
np.shares_memory(charged["positions"], crystal["positions"])  # True: shared
np.shares_memory(moved["positions"], crystal["positions"])  # False: new positions
np.shares_memory(strained["positions"], crystal["positions"])  # False: scaled positions
np.shares_memory(labelled["positions"], crystal["positions"])  # True: only info changed
Operation New memory with_info, with_topology, with_box, select, drop, rename none, but for columns select computes with_box(box, scale_positions=True) the positions with_columns(...) the columns added or replaced filter, gather, sort the rows kept, of every column, since they are no longer a block of the old table system.table, system["positions"] none

So frames made by moving the atoms of one system hold one copy of the elements, the types and every other column that does not change, and a copy of the positions per frame:

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = crystal["positions"]
frames = [
    crystal.with_columns(positions=x + rng.normal(0.0, 0.05, x.shape))
    for _ in range(10)
]

When a new system is made, MDAPY checks only the columns that change: a new box or new global values cost no work on the table, new positions are checked to be finite, and a new type column to be at least 1. A new table given to with_table is checked whole.

docs.title: What del does
docs.text:
del system removes a name, not data. A column stays in memory as long as any system, or any array read from one, uses it, and is freed with the last of them. Systems made from another do not depend on it: each holds its own references to the columns it shares.

crystal2 = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(10, 10, 10))
charged2 = crystal2.with_columns(charge=0.0)  # shares the positions
del crystal2
len(charged2)  # 4000: charged2 is whole, the positions are still in use

The memory of a column is freed when nothing uses it any more: deleting a system frees the columns only it had, and none that a system made from it, or one it was made from, still shares. A neighbor list keeps the system it was built for, and an array from system["name"] keeps the column it views.

docs.title: Shallow or deep copies
docs.text:
A new system is a shallow copy of the old one in memory, since it points to the same columns; but it behaves as a deep copy, since neither system can change those columns. Changing a system always means making a new one, so what is shared is never written to.

There is therefore no copy method. copy.copy and copy.deepcopy return the system itself, as they do for a Python tuple, instead of spending memory on a copy that could never differ:

copy.deepcopy(crystal) is crystal  # True

To change values with NumPy, copy the array, change the copy and make a new system from it:

x = crystal["positions"].copy()  # a writable copy
x[:, 0] += 0.1
shifted = crystal.with_columns(positions=x)

docs.title: Other processes
docs.text:
Systems, boxes, topologies and triangle meshes pickle, so they go to other processes, such as the workers of a ProcessPoolExecutor, and come back as unchangeable as they left:

from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
from mdapy.identify import CommonNeighborAnalysis
from mdapy.io import read_trajectory


def fcc_atoms(system):
    return int((CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(system).structure == 1).sum())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    frames = list(read_trajectory("melt.dump"))
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
        print(list(pool.map(fcc_atoms, frames)))

Pickle is no file format, though: a pickle of one version of MDAPY may not load in another. Save systems with mdapy.io.write.

docs.title: Why nothing changes a system in place
docs.text:
Every way into a system gives something that cannot change it:

  • system["name"] gives read-only NumPy arrays; those of columns and components are views of the table, which cannot be made writable:
try:
    crystal["positions"][0, 0] = 1.0
except ValueError as error:
    print(error)  # assignment destination is read-only
  • table is a copy that shares the columns. polars columns are copy on write: changing a value of a column, or adding, replacing or removing columns of the copy, makes new memory for the copy only.
table = crystal.table
table.insert_column(0, pl.Series("tag", np.zeros(len(crystal))))
"tag" in crystal.table.columns  # False
  • info is a read-only mapping of read-only copies of the values given; the Box and the Topology cannot change either.
  • A system takes no new attributes and lets none be replaced:
try:
    crystal.positions_backup = None
except AttributeError as error:
    print(error)  # a System cannot be changed; ...

The internals of a system have names that start with two underscores and are not part of its interface: code that reaches them on purpose knows what it does, and nothing in MDAPY relies on it.

This is what lets MDAPY share without copying. A neighbor list built for a system serves every system with the same positions and box, such as one that only has more columns; an analysis given a reference configuration, such as atomic strain, keeps it for every configuration it compares; systems can be read from several threads at once. None of this would hold if a system could change after it was made.

docs.title: Expanding a selection
docs.text:
mdapy.neighbor.expand_selection grows a selection of atoms by their neighbors: the atoms within a cutoff of a selected atom, the nearest neighbors of each selected atom, or the atoms bonded to one, as many times as asked, as OVITO's expand selection modifier does.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.neighbor import expand_selection

crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(6, 6, 6))
center = [int(np.argmin(np.linalg.norm(crystal["positions"] - 10.8, axis=1)))]
first = expand_selection(crystal, center, cutoff=3.0)  # the atom and its 12 neighbors
second = expand_selection(crystal, center, cutoff=3.0, iterations=2)  # 55 atoms
nearest = expand_selection(crystal, center, num_neighbors=12)  # the same 13
upper = expand_selection(crystal, crystal["positions"][:, 2] > 15, cutoff=3.0)  # a mask

The two shells about an atom in the middle, cut open:

from mdapy.visualization import render

shell = np.zeros(len(crystal), dtype=np.int32)  # 0: the other atoms
shell[second] = 1
shell[first] = 2
shell[center] = 3
colors = np.array(
    [
        [0.86, 0.86, 0.86],  # others
        [0.55, 0.63, 0.80],  # second shell
        [0.40, 0.76, 0.65],  # first shell
        [0.84, 0.15, 0.16],  # the atom
    ]
)
lower = crystal["positions"][:, 2] < 10.9
render(
    crystal.filter(lower),
    "images/expand-selection.png",
    color=colors[shell[lower]],
    view="top",
    width=900,
    height=600,
    legend=dict(zip(["others", "second shell", "first shell", "the atom"], colors)),
)

The lower half of the crystal seen from above, cut through the atom in the middle.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
expand_selection(system, atoms, *, cutoff=None, num_neighbors=None, bonds=False, iterations=1)

Name Type Default Unit Meaning system System the atoms and the box atoms (N,) bool or indices the atoms selected cutoff float64 Å add the atoms closer than this to a selected atom num_neighbors int32 add the num_neighbors nearest neighbors of each selected atom bonds bool False add the atoms bonded to a selected atom, by the bonds of the topology iterations int32 1 how many times the selection grows, each time by the neighbors of every atom selected so far; 0 leaves it as it is

Give exactly one of cutoff, num_neighbors and bonds. Neighbors are found through the periodic boundaries, with the neighbor lists of MDAPY.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: A boolean mask of one value per atom: the atoms selected and those added. With num_neighbors, an atom joins when it is one of the nearest neighbors of a selected atom, not the other way around, as in OVITO. The selection stops growing early once a step adds nothing.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: expand_selection raises InvalidParameter when not exactly one of cutoff, num_neighbors and bonds is given, when iterations is not an integer or is negative, when atoms is not a mask or indices of the system, and as NeighborList.build for the cutoff and the number of neighbors; MissingProperty with bonds when the system has no bonds.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• OVITO's expand selection.
  • Selecting and ordering atoms.

docs.title: Reading and writing files
docs.text:
mdapy.io.read reads one frame of a file into a System, and mdapy.io.write writes one or more systems to a file. To go through the frames of a file one at a time, see Trajectories. The format is found from the file name, and compressed files are handled transparently.

import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.io import formats, read, write

water = mp.System(
    positions=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.96, 0.0, 0.0], [-0.24, 0.93, 0.0]],
    box=mp.Box(10.0),
    elements=["O", "H", "H"],
    info={"energy": -14.2},
)
write("water.xyz", water)
same = read("water.xyz")
assert same.table.equals(water.table.select(same.table.columns))

write("frames.xyz.gz", [water, water.with_columns(positions=water["positions"] + 1.0)])
last = read("frames.xyz.gz", frame=-1)
formats()  # the formats mdapy can read and write

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
mdapy.io.read(path, format=None, *, frame=0, **options)

Name Type Default Meaning path str or path The file. format str from the name Format name; see Formats. frame int32 0 Frame to read from a file that holds several; negative values count from the end. **options Options of the format, listed on its page.

It returns a System. Compressed files are recognized from their first bytes, whatever their name: gzip, bzip2, xz, and zstd with Python 3.14 or newer.

Reading frame k skips the frames before it without reading their atoms; frame=-1 goes through the whole file. Of an uncompressed file only the parts that are read are loaded; a compressed file is decompressed into memory first.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text:
mdapy.io.write(path, systems, format=None, **options)

Name Type Default Meaning path str or path The file; it is replaced if it exists. systems System or iterable of System One system, or several for a format that holds several frames. format str from the name Format name. **options Options of the format, listed on its page.

An iterator of systems, such as a generator, is written one system at a time, so a long trajectory need not fit in memory. If writing fails, the incomplete file is removed.

docs.title: Compressed files
docs.text:
A name ending in .gz, .bz2, .xz or .zst compresses the file, and reading needs nothing more.

Use .gz. MDAPY compresses it on all threads, and other programs that read compressed files read it. The others compress on one thread, so they take much longer, for a file not much smaller. See Reading and writing files for the times of gzip.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
Name Extensions Read Write Frames Page cif .cif yes no several CIF extxyz .xyz, .extxyz yes yes several Extended XYZ lammps-data .data, .lmp, names data.* yes yes one LAMMPS data lammps-dump .dump, .lammpstrj, names dump.* yes yes several LAMMPS dump outcar .outcar, names OUTCAR* yes no several VASP OUTCAR pdb .pdb, .ent yes no several PDB poscar .vasp, .poscar, names POSCAR*, CONTCAR* yes yes one VASP POSCAR mdapy .mdapy yes yes several MDAPY files

mdapy.io.detect_format(path) returns the format of a file name. It ignores a compression suffix and compares the extension without regard to case; name patterns such as data.* count only when no extension matches. It raises UnsupportedFormat when no format, or more than one, fits the name; pass format= in that case. mdapy.io.formats() returns this table as a polars DataFrame.

docs.title: Numbers in text files
docs.text:
• Reading gives the double closest to the decimal number in the file, exactly as Python's float() does. A decimal point is always ., even if the program has set a locale that uses a comma, as GUI toolkits do.
  • Writing uses the shortest text that reads back to the same double, so a file written by MDAPY reads back to exactly the same numbers.
  • Unit conversions by a power of ten, such as velocities in Å/fs in a file and Å/ps in MDAPY, add no rounding and also round-trip exactly.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Exception When FileFormatError The file does not follow its format. The message starts with file:line:, and the exception has path and line attributes. UnsupportedFormat Unknown format name, a format that cannot be read or written, or zstd before Python 3.14. InvalidParameter The frame does not exist, or a system cannot be written in the format. FileNotFoundError The file does not exist.

docs.title: Neighbor lists
docs.text:
A NeighborList holds pairs of atoms, including periodic images, in any box: every pair closer than a cutoff, the nearest neighbors of each atom, or the atoms that share a face of their Voronoi cells. Analyses and calculators take one with the keyword neighbors=, so a list can be built once and shared: it serves every system with the same positions in the same box, whatever their other columns.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
box = mp.Box([[10.0, 0, 0], [2.0, 9.0, 0], [-1.0, 1.0, 11.0]])
system = mp.System(box.to_cartesian(rng.random((200, 3))), box, elements="Ar")

nl = mp.NeighborList.build(system, cutoff=4.0)
nl.counts  # neighbors of each atom
nl.i, nl.j, nl.shifts  # the pairs
nl.distances, nl.vectors
shorter = nl.within(3.0)  # no new search

twelve = mp.NeighborList.build(system, num_neighbors=12)
twelve.distances.reshape(-1, 12)  # nearest first

faces = mp.NeighborList.build(system, voronoi=True)
faces.areas  # Å², the face that each pair shares

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
NeighborList.build(system, cutoff=None, *, num_neighbors=None, voronoi=False, face_threshold=0, relative_face_threshold=0, edge_threshold=0, progress=None, cancel=None)

Name Type Default Unit Meaning system System the atoms and the box cutoff float64 Å build every pair closer than this, positive num_neighbors int32 build the num_neighbors nearest neighbors of each atom, positive voronoi bool False build the Voronoi neighbors of each atom face_threshold, relative_face_threshold, edge_threshold float64 0 Å², , Å with voronoi, the faces that count, as in the Voronoi analysis progress callable None called as progress(done, total), see Parallelism cancel CancelToken None stops the search

Give exactly one of cutoff, num_neighbors and voronoi.

Any box works: triclinic, left-handed, periodic in some directions only, and thinner than the cutoff or than the distance to the farthest neighbor. An atom then sees several images of the same neighbor, and images of itself, each as its own pair; a single atom in a small periodic cell has a full list.

build raises InvalidParameter when:

  • not exactly one of cutoff, num_neighbors and voronoi is given, or cutoff or num_neighbors is not a positive number (an integer for num_neighbors);
  • a threshold is negative, relative_face_threshold is 1 or more, or a threshold is given without voronoi;
  • with voronoi, two atoms are at the same position;
  • a system without periodic directions has num_neighbors atoms or fewer;
  • a pair is more than 127 boxes away, which comes from positions far outside the box, such as unwrapped coordinates after a long diffusion; wrap them into the box first with Box.wrap;
  • the atoms fill a tiny part of the space they span, so that the search would take too long, such as a million atoms in groups more than a micrometer apart along every direction, or in one group in a periodic box wider than a micrometer. Analyze each group on its own, or use a smaller box.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
Attribute Type Meaning system System the system the list was built for offsets (N + 1,) int64 the pairs of atom i are offsets[i]:offsets[i + 1] j (P,) mdapy.index_dtype the second atom of each pair shifts (P, 3) int8 the periodic image of j: zero along non-periodic directions distances (P,) float64 distance in Å areas (P,) float64 or None in a list of Voronoi neighbors, the area in Å² of the face of each pair; None otherwise cutoff float64 every pair is closer than it, in Å; for nearest and Voronoi neighbors, the largest distance, slightly enlarged num_neighbors int32 or None pairs per atom in a list of nearest neighbors, None otherwise voronoi bool whether the list holds Voronoi neighbors

The arrays are read-only. mdapy.index_dtype is int32, or int64 in MDAPY built with 64-bit atom indices. A list keeps these arrays only, 15 bytes per pair with int32 indices; i and vectors (below) are computed when asked for and not kept. The vector from atom i to the image of atom j is

\[ \mathbf{r}_{ij} = \mathbf{x}_j - \mathbf{x}_i + \mathbf{n}_{ij} \mathbf{H}, \]

with \(\mathbf{n}_{ij}\) the shifts and \(\mathbf{H}\) the box matrix, whose rows are the lattice vectors, for the positions as stored, inside the box or not. Both kinds of list compute a distance the same way, so a pair has the same distance, to the last bit, in either.

In a list within a cutoff every pair appears in both directions. The pairs of an atom come in an order that depends on the positions, the box and the cutoff, never on the number of threads, until an analysis puts the nearest first (below). In a list of nearest neighbors each atom has num_neighbors pairs, nearest first; pairs at the same distance are ordered by j and then by the image, so the equal neighbors of a perfect crystal come in a definite order. There j may be among the nearest of i without i being among the nearest of j.

docs.title: Voronoi neighbors
docs.text:
With voronoi=True, the neighbors of an atom are the atoms across the faces of its Voronoi cell, periodic images included, one pair for each face that counts, with the area of the face in areas. The walls that close a box in a direction that is not periodic are not neighbors. A face counts for each of its two atoms separately: with a relative_face_threshold, which depends on the surface of each cell, a pair may be in the list of one atom only; without it every pair appears in both directions, with the same area. The pairs of an atom come in an order that depends on the positions and the box only.

A list of Voronoi neighbors goes to the analyses that take one, such as the Steinhardt parameters with voronoi=True; the analyses of the neighbors within a cutoff or of the nearest neighbors refuse it, since it holds neither.

docs.title: Lists given to analyses
docs.text:
An analysis given a list with neighbors= reads it where it is, without a copy. An analysis of the neighbors within a cutoff takes a list with that cutoff or a longer one, and leaves out the pairs farther than its own.

An analysis of the k nearest neighbors of each atom takes a list with at least k pairs per atom. From a list within a cutoff, the first such analysis puts the k nearest pairs of each atom first, in the order of a list of nearest neighbors, in the list itself: the pairs of each atom stay the same and change their order, in j, shifts and distances together. The list keeps the number sorted, so a later analysis of as many neighbors or fewer finds them in place, and one of more sorts a few more. Sums of floating-point numbers over the pairs of an atom, such as the Steinhardt parameters within a cutoff, may then differ in their last bits from those of the same list before. A list of nearest neighbors is in that order already. Read the arrays of a list after the analyses, not before.

One kernel at a time reads a list and none while it is sorted, so analyses running in several threads may share one.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Name Returns counts (N,) int64 number of pairs of each atom i (P,) mdapy.index_dtype first atom of each pair, a new array made from offsets on each access vectors (P, 3) float64 vectors \(\mathbf{r}_{ij}\) in Å, a new array computed from the positions and shifts on each access within(cutoff) the pairs closer than a smaller cutoff, in their order, without a new search; the list itself for its own cutoff. From a list of nearest neighbors it gives a list within a cutoff; a list of Voronoi neighbors refuses it. sorted() the same pairs, each atom's sorted by distance, pairs at the same distance by atom and then image, as in a list of nearest neighbors; a list of Voronoi neighbors keeps its areas fits(system) whether the list serves a system: the one it was built for, or any with equal positions in an equal box len(nl) the number of pairs P

The arrays work directly with NumPy, for example to sum over the neighbors of each atom or to look at the pairs of one atom:

weights = np.exp(-nl.distances)
per_atom = np.bincount(nl.i, weights=weights, minlength=len(system))

pairs = slice(nl.offsets[5], nl.offsets[6])
nl.j[pairs], nl.distances[pairs]  # the neighbors of atom 5

ordered = nl.sorted()
nearest = ordered.j[ordered.offsets[:-1][nl.counts > 0]]  # each atom's nearest

The 12 nearest neighbors of atom 5, some of them across the periodic boundaries of the tilted box:

from mdapy.visualization import render

near = twelve.j[twelve.offsets[5] : twelve.offsets[6]]
colors = np.full((len(system), 3), 0.8)
colors[near] = [0.95, 0.6, 0.1]  # the neighbors, orange
colors[5] = [0.85, 0.15, 0.1]  # the atom, red
radius = np.full(len(system), 0.25)
radius[near] = 0.55
radius[5] = 0.8
render(
    system,
    "images/neighbor.png",
    color=colors,
    radius=radius,
    width=800,
    height=600,
    legend={
        "the atom": (0.85, 0.15, 0.1),
        "its neighbors": (0.95, 0.6, 0.1),
        "others": (0.8, 0.8, 0.8),
    },
)

Atom 5 (red) and its 12 nearest neighbors (orange) among the 200 atoms of the triclinic box; a neighbor near the opposite face is one of its periodic images.

docs.title: Overlapping atoms
docs.text:
mdapy.neighbor.find_overlapping selects the atoms closer than a distance to another atom, which are the atoms that clash where structures are put together. By default it selects what to delete: as few atoms as it can, so that no pair that close is left. With keep_one=False it selects every atom that overlaps another, to see where they are.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.neighbor import find_overlapping
from mdapy.transform import affine, combine

crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(12, 12, 1))
center = crystal.box.matrix.sum(axis=0) / 2
inside = np.linalg.norm((crystal["positions"] - center)[:, :2], axis=1) < 14
c, s = np.cos(np.radians(25)), np.sin(np.radians(25))
rotation = np.array([[c, -s, 0], [s, c, 0], [0, 0, 1]])
grain = affine(crystal.filter(inside), rotation, center - rotation @ center, box=False)
merged = combine(crystal.filter(~inside), grain)  # the grain turned by 25°

too_close = find_overlapping(merged, 2.0)  # 16 atoms of the grain
every = find_overlapping(merged, 2.0, keep_one=False)  # 36, of both
cleaned = merged.filter(~too_close)  # no two atoms closer than 2 Å

The atoms of the grain that find_overlapping selects:

from mdapy.visualization import assign_color, render

grain_atoms = np.arange(len(merged)) >= len(merged) - len(grain)
shown = assign_color(merged, "#9ecae1")
shown = assign_color(shown, "#fdae6b", atoms=grain_atoms)
shown = assign_color(shown, "#d62728", atoms=too_close)
render(shown, "images/overlapping.png", view="top", width=600, height=600)

Copper seen along z: the crystal (blue), the grain turned by 25° in it (orange), and the atoms of the grain closer than 2 Å to an atom of the crystal (red).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
find_overlapping(system, distance, *, keep_one=True, molecules=False, atoms=None)

Name Type Default Unit Meaning system System the atoms and the box distance float64 Å two atoms closer than this overlap keep_one bool True select only what to delete, as below; False selects every atom that overlaps another molecules bool False treat the molecules of the molecule column as wholes: atoms of one molecule do not overlap each other, and those of a molecule are selected together; an atom of molecule 0 counts alone atoms (N,) bool or indices all the atoms considered; the others neither overlap nor are selected

Distances are measured through the periodic boundaries, with the neighbor lists of MDAPY; atoms on top of each other overlap.

To delete as few as possible, the atoms that overlap the fewest others are kept first, the lower index before the higher, and each atom kept deletes those it overlaps. Of three atoms in a row where only neighbors overlap, the middle one goes; of an atom that overlaps four others that do not overlap each other, that atom goes. An atom that overlaps its own periodic image goes too. The very fewest is too hard to find for many atoms, and this rule comes close to it.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: A boolean mask of one value per atom. With keep_one, deleting the atoms selected leaves no pair closer than distance, and of each group of atoms that all overlap one another, as the copies of an atom, one is kept: that of the lowest index. Along a chain of atoms each closer than distance to the next only, every second atom is selected and the two ends are kept. OVITO keeps an atom of each group picked at random, so the atoms it selects can differ from these, their number in each group not.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: InvalidParameter when atoms is not a mask or indices of the system, and as NeighborList.build for the distance.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• OVITO's find overlapping particles.
  • Expanding a selection, selecting atoms.

docs.title: Parallelism
docs.text:
MDAPY runs its compiled kernels on a thread pool of its own. This page shows how to choose the number of threads, how to follow and stop long computations, and how MDAPY behaves next to PyTorch and LAMMPS.

import mdapy as mp

mp.get_num_threads()  # default: the logical CPUs this process may use
mp.set_num_threads(8)  # for the rest of the process

with mp.num_threads(2):  # only inside this block
    ...

docs.title: Choosing the number of threads
docs.text:
Name Type Default Meaning set_num_threads(n) function Use n threads from now on. num_threads(n) context manager Use n threads inside a with block, then restore the previous value. get_num_threads() function The current number of threads. MDAPY_NUM_THREADS environment variable logical CPUs this process may use Initial number of threads, read once when MDAPY is imported.

n must be a positive integer; anything else raises InvalidParameter. An invalid MDAPY_NUM_THREADS makes import mdapy fail with the same error, rather than silently falling back to a default.

The setting is global to the process, not to the calling Python thread.

docs.title: Progress and cancellation
docs.text:
Computations that can take long, such as NeighborList.build, accept two keyword-only arguments.

Name Type Default Meaning progress callable or None None Called as progress(done, total) with the number of finished and total work items. cancel CancelToken or None None Stops the computation once token.cancel() is called.

progress is called on the thread that started the computation, which also does a share of the work, between its pieces of work and at most every 50 ms, and once more with done == total when it finishes. done never decreases. If progress raises an exception, the computation stops and that exception propagates to the caller.

A cancelled computation raises Cancelled. The token can be cancelled from any thread, including from inside progress, and can be reused after token.reset().

token = mp.CancelToken()
# in a GUI: connect a "Stop" button to token.cancel
try:
    result = some_analysis.compute(system, progress=report, cancel=token)
except mp.errors.Cancelled:
    ...

Pressing Ctrl-C stops a running kernel and raises KeyboardInterrupt as usual.

docs.title: Reproducible results
docs.text: Results do not depend on the number of threads: the same computation with 1 or 64 threads gives bit-for-bit identical numbers.

docs.title: Working with PyTorch and LAMMPS
docs.text:
MDAPY does not use OpenMP and loads no OpenMP runtime. Two copies of an OpenMP runtime in one process (for example MDAPY's and PyTorch's) is a common cause of crashes such as OMP: Error #15 on macOS; this cannot happen with MDAPY, so no workaround such as KMP_DUPLICATE_LIB_OK is needed.

Other libraries keep their own thread settings:

  • PyTorch: torch.set_num_threads.
  • NumPy (BLAS): the OMP_NUM_THREADS or OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS environment variables.
  • polars: the POLARS_MAX_THREADS environment variable, which must be set before polars is first imported.

When several libraries compute at the same time, keep the total number of threads close to the number of CPU cores. After each piece of parallel work, MDAPY's idle threads keep checking for more for 0.2 ms before they sleep, so that the steps of one computation follow each other without waking them.

docs.title: Calling MDAPY from several threads
docs.text:
Compiled kernels release the Python global interpreter lock (GIL), so other Python threads, for example a GUI event loop, keep running while MDAPY computes.

The pool serves one computation at a time. If a second Python thread starts a computation while the pool is busy, that computation runs on its own thread instead of waiting. It gives the same result, only without parallel speed-up.

docs.title: Many processes
docs.text:
Every process starts as many threads as there are CPUs, so when many processes compute at once, give each of them one thread: ten processes without a limit were six to seven times slower than ten with one thread each. See Screening alloys in many processes.

Start processes with spawn, as multiprocessing.get_context("spawn") gives it, never with fork. MDAPY's own pool works with fork, a forked child creating its own on first use, but this is a limit of polars: once a parent has used its threads, as the functions of MDAPY do, a forked child that needs them hangs without a message. Linux uses fork by default before Python 3.14, so ask for spawn there. MDAPY gives a RuntimeWarning in every process that was forked.

docs.title: Selecting and ordering atoms
docs.text:
Three methods make a system of some of the atoms of another, or of all of them in another order:

Method Keeps Order filter(*conditions, **equal) the atoms that meet every condition as they were gather(atoms) the atoms of the given indices as given sort(*by, descending=False) every atom by the values of columns

The names and their meaning are those of polars: filter keeps rows by a condition, gather takes rows by index, sort orders them. where gives the atoms of the conditions of filter as a mask.

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(6, 6, 6))
crystal = crystal.with_columns(
    element=np.where(np.arange(len(crystal)) % 4 == 0, "Ni", "Cu"),
    id=np.arange(len(crystal), 0, -1),
)

nickel = crystal.filter(element="Ni")
upper = crystal.filter("positions.z > 10")
core = crystal.filter("(positions.x - 10.8)**2 + (positions.y - 10.8)**2 < 25")
first_ten = crystal.gather(np.arange(10))
by_id = crystal.sort("id")

Each returns a new system with the same box and global information; the system it was made from does not change. Bonds, angles and other topology terms follow their atoms: they are renumbered, and a term loses its place when one of its atoms is left out.

docs.title: filter
docs.text:
filter keeps the atoms that meet every condition given, in their order. A condition is one of:

Condition Example a condition written as a Python expression over the columns "positions.z > 10 and element == 'Cu'" a column and the value it must equal, as a keyword element="Ni", type=2 a polars expression pl.col("charge") > 0 a boolean NumPy array of one value per atom system["positions"][:, 2] > 10

Several conditions must all hold:

upper_nickel = crystal.filter("positions.z > 10", element="Ni")
same = crystal.filter("positions.z > 10 and element == 'Ni'")
assert len(upper_nickel) == len(same)

Without a condition, filter keeps every atom. An atom whose value is missing, such as a null in a column read from a file, does not meet a condition.

docs.title: Conditions as text
docs.text:
A condition written as text is a Python expression in which the names are columns. It is read with Python's own parser and turned into a polars expression, so it is as fast as polars, and nothing in it is run as Python code.

Text is needed because a condition such as positions.z > 10 cannot be written directly in Python: Python would compute "z" > 10 before MDAPY sees it.

Columns are written by their names, charge, type, element. A name that is not a Python name, such as one with a space, a bracket or a leading digit, goes in backticks (the key left of 1), as in pandas: `Shear Strain` > 0.1. This is rarely needed: the columns of MDAPY are Python names, columns from OVITO become names in lowercase with underscores, and LAMMPS columns such as c_stress[1] … c_stress[6] become one array column c_stress. Outside an expression no backticks are needed: system["Shear Strain"] reads the column as it is.

Components of array columns are written column.component, by name or by index from 0:

Components Names Example 3 x, y, z positions.z, velocities.x, forces.y, image.z 4 x, y, z, w orientation.w 9 xx, xy, xz, yx, yy, yz, zx, zy, zz, a 3 × 3 tensor by rows atomic_virials.xy any number 0, 1, … positions.2, group.1

Columns of 6 components have no names, only indices: their order depends on where they come from (LAMMPS writes per-atom stresses as xx, yy, zz, xy, xz, yz; the Voigt order is xx, yy, zz, yz, xz, xy). MDAPY itself keeps per-atom tensors as 9 components.

Values: numbers, True and False, and text in quotes, 'Cu' or "Cu". Elements compare as their symbols.

Operators and functions:

Kind Written Example comparisons ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=; chained as in Python 0 < positions.z < 10 logic and, or, not type == 1 or not charge > 0 membership in, not in a list element in ['Cu', 'Ni'] arithmetic +, -, *, /, //, %, ** (power) positions.x**2 + positions.y**2 < 25 functions abs, sqrt, exp, log, log10, sin, cos, tan, arcsin, arccos, arctan, floor, ceil, round abs(velocities.z) > 2

&, | and ~ also mean and, or and not, as in pandas, but they bind tighter than comparisons, so each comparison needs parentheses: (type == 1) | (charge > 0).

The same expressions give values: system["positions.x**2 + positions.y**2"] is the value of each atom, see Values by name.

More examples:

sphere = crystal.filter(
    "sqrt((positions.x - 10.8)**2 + (positions.y - 10.8)**2 + (positions.z - 10.8)**2) < 6"
)
slab = crystal.filter("4 <= positions.z < 8")
fast = crystal.with_columns(
    velocities=np.random.default_rng(0).normal(0, 1, (len(crystal), 3))
).filter("velocities.x**2 + velocities.y**2 + velocities.z**2 > 4")
corners = crystal.filter("floor(positions.x / 3.615) % 2 == 0", element="Cu")

Four of these selections, each in the box of the whole crystal:

from mdapy.visualization import render, write_png

size = {"width": 400, "height": 400}
pictures = [render(part, legend=True, **size) for part in (nickel, core, sphere, slab)]
write_png("images/selecting.png", np.hstack(pictures))

From the left: the nickel atoms, every fourth atom of the crystal; the cylinder core of radius 5 Å along z; the sphere of radius 6 Å; the slab between z = 4 and 8 Å.

docs.title: Masks and polars expressions
docs.text:
A boolean mask computed with NumPy serves when a condition needs more than one atom at a time, such as distances to other atoms:

center = crystal["positions"].mean(axis=0)
distance = np.linalg.norm(crystal["positions"] - center, axis=1)
middle = crystal.filter(distance < 5.0)

A polars expression reaches everything polars does, for example the components of a vector with arr.get:

upper = crystal.filter(pl.col("positions").arr.get(2) > 10)

docs.title: Masks
docs.text:
where takes the same conditions as filter and gives the atoms that meet them as a boolean mask, without making a new system. A mask is how analyses, render and reduce take some of the atoms (their atoms argument), and masks combine with &, | and ~:

nickel_mask = crystal.where(element="Ni")  # (N,) bool
upper_mask = crystal.where("positions.z > 10")
both = nickel_mask & upper_mask
others = ~both
assert (crystal.filter(both)["positions"] == crystal["positions"][both]).all()

where() without conditions is true for every atom.

docs.title: gather
docs.text:
gather takes the atoms of the given indices, in that order. Indices count from 0; negative ones count from the end; each atom may be given once.

last = crystal.gather([-1])
order = np.random.default_rng(1).permutation(len(crystal))
shuffled = crystal.gather(order)
back = shuffled.gather(np.argsort(order))  # the original order again
assert back.table.equals(crystal.table)

A boolean mask belongs to filter, which gather reminds when given one.

docs.title: sort
docs.text:
sort orders all atoms by the values of columns:

Name Type Default Meaning *by column names, column.component, or polars expressions the keys: atoms equal in the first are ordered by the second, and so on descending bool or one bool per key False sort from the largest 
by_id = crystal.sort("id")
by_height = crystal.sort("positions.z")
layers = crystal.sort("positions.z", "positions.x", descending=[True, False])
by_element = crystal.sort("element")  # by atomic number: Ni (28) first, then Cu (29)

Atoms with equal keys keep their order, so sorting is repeatable. Elements sort by atomic number, not alphabetically.

docs.title: After selecting or reordering
docs.text:
A per-atom result of an analysis, and a neighbor list, hold one entry per atom in the order of the system they were computed for.

Attach a result with with_columns before selecting or reordering, and it follows its atoms:

from mdapy.identify import CommonNeighborAnalysis

structure = CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(crystal)
labelled = crystal.with_columns(structure).sort("id")
labelled.table["cna_structure"]  # in the new order

A neighbor list fits only the atoms it was built for. After filter, gather or sort, nl.fits(new) is false and an analysis given that list raises InvalidParameter; build a new list for the new system. Analyses that are not given a list find the neighbors themselves and are not affected.

nl = mp.NeighborList.build(crystal, 3.0)
nl.fits(crystal)  # True
nl.fits(crystal.sort("id"))  # False: the atoms are in another order

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
The three methods raise InvalidParameter with what went wrong:

Cause Message an unknown column no column 'charge'; the columns are positions, element, id an array column without a component positions has 3 components; write one of positions.0, positions.1, positions.2, positions.x, positions.y, positions.z an unknown component stress has no component 'xx'; write one of stress.0, … text that is not a Python expression cannot read the condition 'type >': invalid syntax something conditions do not support Subscript is not supported in the condition 'positions[0] > 0' a condition that does not give true or false 'type + 1' does not give true or false for each atom a mask of the wrong length or type a mask must hold 864 booleans, got int64 of shape (864,) indices out of range, repeated, or not integers atom index out of range for 864 atoms, atom indices must not repeat sort without a key give a column to sort by

docs.title: Systems
docs.text:
A System is one atomic configuration: a table with one row per atom, a simulation box, global information such as the energy, and for molecules an optional topology of bonds, angles, dihedrals and impropers. Every analysis, builder, reader and calculator of MDAPY takes and returns systems.

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import mdapy as mp

water = mp.System(
    positions=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.96, 0.0, 0.0], [-0.24, 0.93, 0.0]],
    box=mp.Box(10.0),
    elements=["O", "H", "H"],
    info={"energy": -14.2},
)
print(water)
# System: 3 atoms (H2 O)
#   box:      10 × 10 × 10 Å, orthogonal, periodic x y z
#   columns:  positions (3), element
#   info:     energy = -14.2
water["positions"]  # (3, 3) NumPy array of the positions, read-only
water.table  # the per-atom table, a polars DataFrame

A system never changes. Methods such as with_columns, filter and sort return a new system and leave the old one as it is; see Changing a system and Selecting and ordering atoms.

docs.title: Creating a system
Columns
docs.text:
The table holds one row per atom and any number of columns. Columns with a standard name have a fixed type. They are converted to it whenever they are set, when a system is made and by with_columns and with_table, so the rest of MDAPY can rely on it:

Column Type Unit Meaning positions (3,) float64 Å positions, required velocities (3,) float64 Å/ps velocities forces (3,) float64 eV/Å forces element element chemical symbol type int32 atom type, from 1 id int64 atom identifier molecule int64 molecule identifier mass float64 amu mass charge float64 e charge image (3,) int32 periodic image flags movable (3,) bool whether the atom may move along x, y and z

A conversion that would change a value raises an error. Small int64 image flags become int32, and 1.0 becomes type 1, but 1.5 as a type, 2**40 as an image flag, or 2 in movable do not fit, and neither does the wrong number of values per atom. Standard columns must not have missing values, positions, velocities, forces, masses and charges must be finite, masses positive and types at least 1. Every other column is kept as it is: numbers, booleans, text, and arrays of numbers such as the ptm_orientation of polyhedral template matching. The Glossary lists the columns that MDAPY itself writes.

The element column holds chemical symbols; underneath they are atomic numbers, so elements compare as text and sort by atomic number:

water.table["element"].to_list()  # ['O', 'H', 'H']
water.table["element"].to_physical().to_list()  # [8, 1, 1]

docs.title: Reading data
docs.text: Name Meaning system["name"] The values of a column, a component or an expression, one per atom, as a read-only NumPy array; system["positions"] are the (N, 3) positions in Å, without a copy. table The per-atom table as a polars DataFrame. box The Box. info Global information, a read-only mapping. topology The Topology, or None. len(system) The number of atoms.

docs.title: Values by name
docs.text:
system["name"] gives the values of each atom as a NumPy array. The name is a column, a component of an array column written column.component, or an expression over the columns, written as in the conditions of filter:

from mdapy.build import build_crystal

alloy = build_crystal("fcc", 3.6, elements="Cu", repeat=(3, 3, 3))
alloy = alloy.with_columns(
    element=np.where(np.arange(len(alloy)) % 4 == 0, "Ni", "Cu"),
    charge=np.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, len(alloy)),
)
alloy["charge"]  # (108,) float64
alloy["positions.z"].max()  # the largest z
alloy["positions"]  # (108, 3)
alloy["sqrt(positions.x**2 + positions.y**2)"]  # distance from the z axis
alloy["element"]  # ['Ni', 'Cu', 'Cu', ...]
Name Example Gives a column "charge", "element", "positions" its values, (N,) or (N, k) for an array column a component "positions.z", "velocities.x", "group.1" one component, (N,) an expression "positions.x**2 + positions.y**2", "charge > 0" the value of each atom, (N,)

Components are named as in conditions: x, y, z for 3 values, x, y, z, w for 4, xx to zz by rows for 9, and the index from 0 for any number. A column or a component is read where it is, without a copy, for numbers without missing values; an expression is computed. The arrays are read-only, so they cannot change the system.

Every column is read this way, the positions too: a system has no attribute for a column, so that each is read and changed the same way, by system["name"] and with_columns. A system is indexed only by names: atoms are chosen with filter, gather and sort, and a system is not a sequence of atoms to loop over.

docs.title: The table
docs.text:
Everything else is read from the table, a polars DataFrame on which every polars operation works, for example counts and averages by element:

alloy.table.group_by("element").agg(pl.len(), pl.col("charge").mean())
alloy.table["positions"].arr.get(2).max()  # the largest z, as polars writes it

The table is a copy of the system's own: changing it does not change the system. To make a changed system, see Changing a system.

docs.title: Printing a system
docs.text:
print(system) gives a summary of a few lines:

System: 108 atoms (Cu81 Ni27)
  box:      10.8 × 10.8 × 10.8 Å, orthogonal, periodic x y z
  columns:  positions (3), element, charge
  info:     energy = -3.54, timestep = 1000
  topology: 2 bonds, 1 angle
  • the number of atoms and the elements, the most frequent first;
  • the box: its lengths for an orthogonal box, with its origin when that is not zero, or for a triclinic box the lengths of a, b, c and the angles between them; and its periodic directions;
  • the columns, with the number of components of array columns in parentheses;
  • the global information, if any: numbers and short text with their values, arrays with their shape;
  • the topology, if any: the number of terms of each kind.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for inconsistent input: neither or both of positions and table, positions not of shape (N, 3) or not finite, unknown chemical symbols, types below 1, missing values in standard columns, values that do not fit the type of a standard column, or topology indices beyond the number of atoms.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
A Topology holds the bonds, angles, dihedrals and impropers of a molecular system. A system has one or none; it comes from LAMMPS data files and other formats that store bonds, or is given when a system is made.

import polars as pl
import mdapy as mp

water = mp.System(
    positions=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.96, 0.0, 0.0], [-0.24, 0.93, 0.0]],
    box=mp.Box(10.0),
    elements=["O", "H", "H"],
    topology=mp.Topology(bonds=[[0, 1], [0, 2]], angles=[[1, 0, 2]]),
)
water.topology.bonds  # a polars DataFrame of two bonds
len(water.topology)  # 3 terms in all

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
A topology has four tables, bonds, angles, dihedrals and impropers, with 2, 3, 4 and 4 atoms per term. Each is given as an (M, k) array of atom indices, all of type 1, or as a polars DataFrame with the columns:

Column Type Meaning atoms (k,) int64 Atom indices: rows of the system's table, from 0. type int32 Type of the term, from 1; 1 when not given. type_label str, optional Name of the type, for example "O-H".

Other columns are kept. Atom order follows LAMMPS: the central atom of an angle is the second one, dihedral atoms follow the chain, and the meaning of the improper order depends on the improper style.

labelled = mp.Topology(
    bonds=pl.DataFrame(
        {"atoms": [[0, 1], [0, 2]], "type": [1, 1], "type_label": ["O-H", "O-H"]}
    ),
    angles=[[1, 0, 2]],
)
labelled.bonds["type_label"].to_list()  # ['O-H', 'O-H']
Name Meaning bonds, angles, dihedrals, impropers each table, a copy that shares its columns tables() the four tables by kind len(topology) the number of terms of every kind max_atom_index() the largest atom index of any term, or -1 remap(mapping) a topology with atoms renumbered: mapping[old] is the new index, or -1 for an atom removed

docs.title: Topology follows the atoms
docs.text:
A topology refers to atoms by their row in the table, so it changes with them. filter, gather and sort renumber the terms whose atoms are all kept, and drop the terms that lose an atom:

oxygen = water.filter(element="O")
len(oxygen.topology)  # 0: both bonds and the angle lost a hydrogen
reordered = water.gather([2, 1, 0])
reordered.topology.bonds["atoms"].to_list()  # [[2, 1], [2, 0]]

Like a system, a topology never changes: remap and the methods of systems return new ones.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Topology raises InvalidParameter for a table of the wrong shape or types, negative atom indices, a term that repeats an atom, missing values, or a type below 1; a system raises it for a topology that refers to atoms it does not have.

docs.title: Trajectories
docs.text:
mdapy.io.read_trajectory opens the frames of a file without reading them. A frame is read when it is used, so a long trajectory never has to fit in memory, and iterating over it starts at once.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.io import read_trajectory, write

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
system = mp.System(rng.random((10, 3)) * 5, mp.Box(5.0), elements="Ar")
frames = (
    system.with_columns(positions=system["positions"] + 0.01 * k).with_info(step=k)
    for k in range(100)
)
write("run.xyz", frames)

with read_trajectory("run.xyz") as trajectory:
    first = trajectory[0]  # reads one frame
    every_tenth = trajectory[::10]  # a trajectory of 10 frames, nothing read
    steps = [frame.info["step"] for frame in every_tenth]
    count = len(trajectory)  # 100
    write("every_tenth.mdapy", every_tenth)  # writes the selected frames

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
mdapy.io.read_trajectory(path, format=None, *, topology=None, **options) takes the same arguments as mdapy.io.read, without frame; the options of the format apply to every frame. path may also name several files, and topology a system whose atoms the frames move. It returns a Trajectory:

Operation Result trajectory[i] the frame i, read from the file; negative indices count from the end trajectory[a:b:c] a Trajectory of the selected frames, sharing the open file trajectory.file_of(i) the path of the file that holds frame i, without reading the frame for frame in trajectory the frames in order, one at a time len(trajectory) the number of frames trajectory.path, trajectory.format the file, or the pattern or first file of several, and the format of the first file trajectory.close(), with ... releases the files trajectory.map(function) the frames through a function, below

Any format works; a format that holds one frame gives a trajectory of one frame. A trajectory is an iterable of systems, so mdapy.io.write writes it, or a slice of it, to any format that holds several frames.

docs.title: Reading frames
docs.text:
A frame is read when it is used, and opening a trajectory reads nothing else: iteration starts at once even for a file of many gigabytes. len, negative indices and slices read through the whole file once, without keeping its atoms.

A compressed file is decompressed into memory when the trajectory is opened; an uncompressed one is not. The file is released by close(), at the end of a with block, or once no trajectory of it is used any more.

If the file ends in the middle of a frame, the frames before it are read normally and the incomplete frame raises FileFormatError when it is reached.

docs.title: Frames through a function
docs.text:
trajectory.map(function) gives the frames through a function of a frame, such as a pipeline of analyses that adds their columns, each computed when it is used. It is a sequence as the trajectory is: indices, slices (mapped as well), len and iteration, which reads the frames one after the other; its map adds another function. The analyses of trajectories, such as TimeAverage or TimeSeries, and remove_drift or smooth_trajectory take it as they take the trajectory.

from mdapy.analysis import TimeSeries


def with_height(frame):
    """The frame with the height of each atom above the middle of the box."""
    return frame.with_columns(height=frame["positions.z"] - 2.5)


with read_trajectory("run.xyz") as trajectory:
    analyzed = trajectory.map(with_height)
    mean = TimeSeries("height", "mean").compute(analyzed)  # one value a frame
    last = analyzed[-1]  # the last frame, with its height when it is read

docs.title: Several files
docs.text:
A pattern with * stands for the files it matches, in the order of the numbers in their names, so that dump.10.lammpstrj follows dump.9.lammpstrj; a list gives the files in its order. The frames of each file follow those of the file before, and files of one frame and of many mix:

for k in range(3):
    write(f"part.{k * 50}.xyz", [system.with_info(step=k)] * 2)

parts = read_trajectory("part.*.xyz")  # part.0, part.50, part.100: 6 frames
chosen = read_trajectory(["part.100.xyz", "part.0.xyz"])  # 4 frames

Each file has the format of its name, so formats mix, or that of the first file when a name tells nothing; format= gives one format to all. At most two files are open at a time, so a pattern may match thousands of files.

docs.title: A topology for the frames
docs.text:
LAMMPS dumps hold positions, data files the bonds, angles, charges and molecules. With topology, each frame takes the atoms of a system, such as one read from a data file, with all of these:

from mdapy.io import read

oxygens = rng.random((4, 3)) * 12 + 1
positions = np.stack(
    [oxygens, oxygens + [0.96, 0, 0], oxygens + [-0.24, 0.93, 0]], axis=1
).reshape(-1, 3)
water = mp.System(
    positions,
    mp.Box(15.0),
    elements=["O", "H", "H"] * 4,
    topology=mp.Topology(
        bonds=[[3 * k, 3 * k + i] for k in range(4) for i in (1, 2)],
        angles=[[3 * k + 1, 3 * k, 3 * k + 2] for k in range(4)],
    ),
).with_columns(
    charge=[-0.8476, 0.4238, 0.4238] * 4, molecule=np.repeat([1, 2, 3, 4], 3)
)
write("water.data", water, atom_style="full")
data = read("water.data")  # ids 1 to 12

# dumps of the positions only, the atoms in any order
for step in range(3):
    shuffled = data.gather(rng.permutation(12)).select("id", "type", "positions")
    write(f"water.{step}.dump", shuffled.with_info(timestep=step))

for frame in read_trajectory("water.*.dump", topology=data):
    frame.topology.bonds  # the eight bonds of the data file
    frame["charge"]  # its charges, in its order

Each frame, much as OVITO's load trajectory makes it:

  • has the atoms of the topology in their order, matched by id, with the columns of the frame and those of the topology the frame lacks;
  • leaves out the atoms a frame lacks, with their bonds, angles, dihedrals and impropers, the others renumbered; frames with every atom share the Topology object of the system;
  • has the box of the frame, periodic along the directions its file tells (LAMMPS dumps, extended XYZ and MDAPY files), or along those of the topology for files periodic by convention, such as POSCAR; the information of both, that of the frame first; and loses the image flags of the topology when the frame has none.

A LAMMPS data file cannot tell the boundaries of the simulation, while its dumps do: a slab read with its dumps stays a slab. OVITO keeps the periodicity of the topology.

Without ids, a frame must have as many atoms as the topology, taken in order, and the ids of the topology, if any, must be 1 to N in order. Reading a frame raises InvalidParameter when it has atoms the topology lacks (OVITO adds them), when ids repeat, or when without ids the numbers of atoms differ.

docs.title: Columnar grains on a hexagonal pattern
docs.text: A columnar polycrystal has grains that all span one axis of the box, so its boundaries are planes parallel to that axis: a quasi two-dimensional polycrystal, thin and quick to simulate. With the seeds on a triangular lattice, the grains are regular hexagons. This page builds such a polycrystal of copper with its columns along [111], turns the grains so that every boundary is of high angle, and relaxes it.

docs.title: The unit along the columns
docs.text:
The columns run along z, so the unit has z along [111]; about [111], fcc looks the same after a turn of 60°.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.build import build_crystal, build_polycrystal

a = 3.615
unit = build_crystal(
    "fcc", a, elements="Cu", orientation=[(1, 1, -2), (-1, 1, 0), (1, 1, 1)]
)
unit.box.matrix[2, 2]  # 6.26 Å, three (111) planes

docs.title: Seeds on a triangular lattice
docs.text:
A rectangle of \(d \times d\sqrt{3}\) holds two points of a triangular lattice of spacing \(d\). Repeat it 3 × 2 times for twelve grains 40 Å across:

d = 40.0
cells = (3, 2)
pair = np.array([[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [d / 2, d * np.sqrt(3) / 2, 0.0]])
seeds = np.vstack(
    [
        pair + [i * d, j * d * np.sqrt(3), 0.0]
        for i in range(cells[0])
        for j in range(cells[1])
    ]
)
len(seeds)  # 12

docs.title: Turns about the column axis
docs.text:
Each grain turns about z by its own angle. About [111], fcc looks the same after 60°, so two grains differ by at most 30°, and below about 15° their boundary is a row of separate dislocations, which a relaxation can all but remove. Points of a triangular lattice can take three families so that neighbors never share one: with families 20° apart, and a little of its own for each grain, every boundary is of high angle.

from mdapy.build import rotations_about

family = [
    (i - k) % 3 for i in range(cells[0]) for j in range(cells[1]) for k in range(2)
]
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
angles = 20.0 * np.array(family) + rng.uniform(-2.0, 2.0, len(seeds))
rotations = rotations_about("z", angles)

The box is no longer than the unit along z, so the polycrystal is columnar: the box takes the length of the unit there, and every grain spans it.

box = mp.Box([cells[0] * d, cells[1] * d * np.sqrt(3), 1.0])
columns = build_polycrystal(unit, box, seeds, orientations=rotations)
len(columns), columns.box.matrix[2, 2]  # 8531 atoms, 6.26 Å

docs.title: Relax
docs.text:
Relax the positions with the EAM potential of copper of Zhou et al.:

from mdapy.calculators import EAM
from mdapy.simulation import minimize

result = minimize(columns, EAM.zhou(["Cu"]), max_force=0.05)
relaxed = result.system
result.converged  # True

docs.title: Every boundary is of high angle
docs.text:
Two grains meet where an atom of one has a neighbor in the other. Their misorientation is the difference of their angles, modulo the 60° of the [111] axis:

grain = relaxed.table["grain"].to_numpy()
nl = mp.NeighborList.build(relaxed, 3.0)
across = grain[nl.i] < grain[nl.j]
pairs = np.stack([grain[nl.i][across], grain[nl.j][across]], axis=1)
pairs = np.unique(pairs, axis=0)  # each pair of grains that meet, once
turn = np.abs(angles[pairs[:, 0]] - angles[pairs[:, 1]]) % 60.0
misorientation = np.minimum(turn, 60.0 - turn)
len(pairs)  # 36: each grain meets six others
misorientation.min(), misorientation.max()  # 17.2 and 22.6 degrees

docs.title: A picture
docs.text:
Look down the columns, colored by structure and by grain:

from mdapy.identify import CommonNeighborAnalysis
from mdapy.visualization import render

cna = CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(relaxed)
cna.counts()  # mostly fcc; boundaries "other"
render(
    relaxed,
    "images/columns.png",
    color=cna,
    view="top",
    width=1200,
    height=900,
    legend=True,
)
render(
    relaxed,
    "images/grains.png",
    color="grain",
    colormap="labels",
    view="top",
    width=1200,
    height=900,
    legend=True,
)
By structure: fcc green, others white By grain

Every boundary stays after the relaxation, as a continuous line of white atoms.

docs.title: A machine-learned potential for CrCoNi
docs.text:
A machine-learned potential is checked against the first-principles calculations it learned from, and against measurements. This page takes the NEP model for CrCoNi alloys of Wu et al. (2026) and computes the phonon dispersions of bcc Cr, hcp Co and fcc Ni, drawn over the DFT dispersions (VASP and phonopy) of the same paper, and the elastic constants of the CrCoNi alloy from 0 to 1000 K, against measured ones. See Phonons, Quasi-harmonic approximation and Elastic constants at finite temperature for the functions themselves.

Cite the model and the data

The NEP model and the DFT dispersions come from Wu et al. (2026). Cite that paper when you use them.

Download the model nep.txt (a copy of the one in the NEP-CrCoNi repository, which also holds the training data) and the DFT dispersions Cr.band.dat, Co.band.dat and Ni.band.dat, and SQS.xyz, a special quasirandom structure of equiatomic CrCoNi with 108 atoms, into the working directory.

docs.title: Phonons of Cr, Co and Ni
The crystals
docs.text:
Relax the conventional cell of each metal at zero pressure with the model, and reduce it to its primitive cell:

import numpy as np
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.calculators import NEP
from mdapy.lattice_dynamics import phonons, primitive_cell
from mdapy.simulation import minimize

nep = NEP("nep.txt")


def relaxed(element, structure, a):
    """The conventional cell of a metal, relaxed at zero pressure."""
    start = build_crystal(structure, a, elements=element)
    return minimize(start, nep, cell="full", max_force=1e-6, max_stress=1e-5).system


conventional = {
    "Cr": relaxed("Cr", "bcc", 2.84),
    "Co": relaxed("Co", "hcp", 2.49),
    "Ni": relaxed("Ni", "fcc", 3.52),
}
primitive = {element: primitive_cell(cell) for element, cell in conventional.items()}
for element, cell in conventional.items():
    print(element, np.round(np.linalg.norm(cell.box.matrix, axis=1), 4))

Cr [2.843 2.843 2.843]
Co [2.494  2.494  4.0174]
Ni [3.5164 3.5164 3.5164]

docs.title: Phonons
docs.text:
The force constants come from displacements of the atoms in a supercell, by default the most nearly cubic one at least twice the cutoff of the model across:

results = {element: phonons(cell, nep) for element, cell in primitive.items()}
for element, result in results.items():
    print(element, result)

Cr Phonons(1 atom, supercell of 250 cells)
Co Phonons(2 atoms, supercell of 90 cells)
Ni Phonons(1 atom, supercell of 256 cells)

docs.title: Along the paths of the DFT calculations
docs.text:
The DFT dispersions follow the paths below. Their special points are given in units of the reciprocal vectors of the conventional cells; a matrix takes them to those of the primitive cells. The DFT path of Ni goes from U to K, two equivalent points of the Brillouin zone, as a line of its own; here the path breaks at U and starts again at K.

paths = {
    "Cr": [[("N", [0.5, 0.5, 0]), ("Γ", [0, 0, 0]), ("H", [0, 1, 0]),
            ("P", [0.5, 0.5, 0.5]), ("Γ", [0, 0, 0])]],
    "Co": [[("Γ", [0, 0, 0]), ("K", [1 / 3, 1 / 3, 0]), ("M", [0.5, 0, 0]),
            ("Γ", [0, 0, 0]), ("A", [0, 0, 0.5])]],
    "Ni": [[("Γ", [0, 0, 0]), ("X", [0, 1, 0]), ("U", [0.25, 1, 0.25])],
           [("K", [0.75, 0.75, 0]), ("Γ", [0, 0, 0]), ("L", [0.5, 0.5, 0.5])]],
}  # fmt: skip

sections, bands = {}, {}
for element, path in paths.items():
    to_primitive = primitive[element].box.matrix @ np.linalg.inv(
        conventional[element].box.matrix
    )
    sections[element] = [[(name, to_primitive @ q) for name, q in s] for s in path]
    bands[element] = results[element].band_structure(sections[element], points=101)

docs.title: Against DFT
docs.text:
read_band_structure reads the band.dat files of phonopy. Each line between two special points has 101 wave vectors in both, so the frequencies compare point by point; the DFT lines are stretched onto the lines of the model, whose lattice constants differ a little.

from mdapy.lattice_dynamics import read_band_structure

dft = {element: read_band_structure(f"{element}.band.dat") for element in paths}


def lines(bands):
    """The distances and frequencies of each line between two special points."""
    n = len(bands.distances) // 101
    return list(zip(np.split(bands.distances, n), np.split(bands.frequencies, n)))


on_path = {}
for element in paths:
    theirs = lines(dft[element])
    if element == "Ni":
        del theirs[2]  # the line from U to K
    on_path[element] = [
        (np.interp(d, d[[0, -1]], x[[0, -1]]), frequencies)
        for (x, _), (d, frequencies) in zip(lines(bands[element]), theirs)
    ]
    difference = np.concatenate(
        [f - g for (_, f), (_, g) in zip(lines(bands[element]), on_path[element])]
    )
    print(f"{element}: {np.sqrt(np.mean(difference**2)):.2f} THz root mean square")

Cr: 0.36 THz root mean square
Co: 0.34 THz root mean square
Ni: 0.17 THz root mean square

from mdapy.visualization import plot

with plot.style():
    fig, axes = plot.figure("double", ncols=3)
    for ax, element, title in zip(axes, paths, ("bcc Cr", "hcp Co", "fcc Ni")):
        plot.band_structure(bands[element], ax=ax, color="#2a78d6")
        for x, frequencies in on_path[element]:
            ax.plot(x, frequencies, color="#eb6834", lw=0.8, ls="--")
        ax.set_title(title)
        ax.set_ylim(0, None)
    axes[0].plot([], [], color="#2a78d6", label="NEP")
    axes[0].plot([], [], color="#eb6834", lw=0.8, ls="--", label="DFT")
    axes[0].legend(frameon=False)
    plot.save(fig, "images/crconi-phonons", formats=("png",))

docs.title: Converged with the supercell?
docs.text:
Force constants beyond the supercell are left out. Check the dispersion of Ni in a supercell of 6 × 6 × 6 conventional cells, given as a matrix of primitive cells:

matrix = 6 * conventional["Ni"].box.matrix @ np.linalg.inv(primitive["Ni"].box.matrix)
larger = phonons(primitive["Ni"], nep, supercell=np.rint(matrix).astype(int))
again = larger.band_structure(sections["Ni"], points=101)
change = np.abs(again.frequencies - bands["Ni"].frequencies).max()
print(larger, f"{change:.3f} THz")

Phonons(1 atom, supercell of 864 cells) 0.018 THz

The default supercell is converged to some hundredths of a THz, well below the differences from DFT; the largest of those, the highest optical branch of Co at Γ, is the model's own.

docs.title: At 0 K
docs.text:
Relax the special quasirandom structure at zero pressure, and compute its elastic constants from the stress under small strains, the atoms relaxed under each. The cell is cubic on average; average the constants over the three equivalent directions:

from mdapy.io import read
from mdapy.lattice_dynamics import ElasticResult, elastic_constants

start = read("SQS.xyz")
sqs = minimize(
    start, nep, cell="full", max_force=1e-6, max_stress=1e-5, max_steps=20000
).system


def cubic(c):
    """C11, C12 and C44 averaged over the equivalent directions."""
    return (
        np.mean(np.diag(c)[:3]),
        np.mean(c[[0, 0, 1], [1, 2, 2]]),
        np.mean(np.diag(c)[3:]),
    )


static = elastic_constants(sqs, nep, max_force=1e-6)
print("C11 %.1f, C12 %.1f, C44 %.1f GPa" % cubic(static.constants))

C11 288.6, C12 183.7, C44 143.8 GPa

docs.title: From 0 to 1000 K
docs.text:
The quasi-harmonic approximation gives the volume of the crystal at each temperature from the free energy of its vibrations, and thermal_elastic_constants the elastic constants there, from the second derivatives of the static energy and of the free energy of the vibrations under strain. The structure, 10.6 Å across, is taken as its own supercell to keep this affordable; it takes about 10 minutes on ten cores.

from mdapy.lattice_dynamics import quasi_harmonic, thermal_elastic_constants

temperatures = np.arange(0, 1001, 100.0)
qha = quasi_harmonic(sqs, nep, temperatures, supercell=1, mesh=4)
thermal = thermal_elastic_constants(qha, nep, supercell=1, mesh=4)
print("0 K: C11 %.1f, C12 %.1f, C44 %.1f GPa" % cubic(thermal.isothermal[0]))
print(
    f"{qha.volume[0] * len(sqs) / sqs.box.volume - 1:.2%} larger than the static cell"
)

0 K: C11 283.2, C12 181.1, C44 140.1 GPa
0.52% larger than the static cell

At 0 K the two methods differ by 2 to 3 % on the same structure: the vibrations of the atoms at zero point expand the crystal by 0.5 %, which softens it, while the strains of elastic_constants act on the static crystal. At the same volume, the second derivatives of the energy and the stresses under strain give the same constants to 0.1 GPa.

docs.title: From molecular dynamics
docs.text:
The quasi-harmonic approximation takes the anharmonic vibrations in only through the volume. md_elastic_constants takes them all, from the mean stress of molecular dynamics under small strains. Here it runs in LAMMPS with the NEP of KOKKOS, pair_style nep/kk, on a GPU, in 4 × 4 × 4 copies of the structure, 6912 atoms, for 120 ps under each of the 12 strains; each temperature takes about 10 minutes on one GPU:

from mdapy.calculators import LAMMPS
from mdapy.lattice_dynamics import md_elastic_constants
from mdapy.transform import replicate

gpu = LAMMPS(
    "pair_style nep/kk\npair_coeff * * nep.txt Cr Co Ni",
    ["Cr", "Co", "Ni"],
    cmdargs=["-k", "on", "g", "1", "-sf", "kk", "-pk", "kokkos", "newton", "on", "neigh", "half"],
)  # fmt: skip
crystal = replicate(sqs, (4, 4, 4))
hot = np.arange(300, 1001, 100.0)
md = [
    md_elastic_constants(
        crystal, gpu, t, timestep=0.002, equilibration=10000, production=50000
    )
    for t in hot
]
for t, result in zip(hot[::3], md[::3]):
    print("%.0f K: C11 %.1f, C12 %.1f, C44 %.1f GPa" % (t, *cubic(result.constants)))

300 K: C11 268.6, C12 173.7, C44 131.8 GPa
600 K: C11 247.7, C12 163.5, C44 119.9 GPa
900 K: C11 225.2, C12 152.7, C44 107.4 GPa

Against the isothermal constants of the quasi-harmonic approximation:

quasi = np.array([cubic(c) for c in thermal.isothermal])
dynamic = np.array([cubic(result.constants) for result in md])
spread = np.array([cubic(result.errors) for result in md])
with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    for k, name in enumerate(("C$_{11}$", "C$_{12}$", "C$_{44}$")):
        (line,) = ax.plot(temperatures, quasi[:, k], label=f"{name}, quasi-harmonic")
        ax.errorbar(hot, dynamic[:, k], spread[:, k], fmt="o", color=line.get_color(),
                    capsize=2, label=f"{name}, MD")  # fmt: skip
    ax.set_xlabel("temperature (K)")
    ax.set_ylabel("elastic constants (GPa)")
    ax.legend(ncol=2)
    plot.save(fig, "images/crconi-md", formats=("png",))

The isothermal constants of CrCoNi with the NEP model: lines from the quasi-harmonic approximation, points from molecular dynamics, with their standard errors, smaller than the points. At 300 K the two agree to 1 GPa. Above, the constants of molecular dynamics soften more slowly: at 1000 K C11 is 217 against 213 GPa, C12 149 against 142 GPa and C44 104 against 100 GPa: the quasi-harmonic approximation, which takes the anharmonic vibrations in only through the volume, softens the crystal faster.
