plot.figure gives several panels with nrows and ncols, and the plots of MDAPY draw on any of them: here the partial radial distribution functions of a CuNi alloy, the structures of the shaken copper by common neighbor analysis, and the number of neighbors of the atoms of a nanoparticle against their distance from its center.

from mdapy.analysis import CoordinationNumber
from mdapy.build import random_alloy
from mdapy.identify import CommonNeighborAnalysis


def shake(system, amount):
    moved = system["positions"] + rng.normal(0, amount, (len(system), 3))
    return system.with_columns(positions=moved)


alloy = random_alloy(
    build_crystal("fcc", 3.6, repeat=(6, 6, 6)), {"Cu": 1, "Ni": 1}, seed=1
)
partial = RadialDistributionFunction(cutoff=6.0, bins=120).compute(shake(alloy, 0.1))
structures = CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(shaken)
center = crystal.box.matrix.sum(axis=0) / 2
distance = np.linalg.norm(crystal["positions"] - center, axis=1)
particle = shake(crystal.filter(distance < 14), 0.1)
particle = particle.with_columns(
    **CoordinationNumber(cutoff=3.0).compute(particle).columns(),
    distance=np.linalg.norm(particle["positions"] - center, axis=1),
)

with plot.style():
    fig, (left, middle, right) = plot.figure("double", 55, nrows=1, ncols=3)
    plot.rdf(partial, ax=left, partial=True)
    plot.structure_counts(structures, ax=middle)
    plot.scatter(particle, "distance", "coordination", ax=right)
    right.set_xlabel("distance from the center (Å)")
    for ax, label in zip((left, middle, right), "abc"):
        plot.panel_label(ax, label)
    plot.save(fig, "images/plotting-panels", formats=("png",))

a: the partial functions of CuNi. b: the shaken copper is fcc but for the atoms shaken most. c: 12 neighbors inside the nanoparticle, fewer at its surface.

sharex=True or sharey=True in plot.figure gives the panels one axis, and plot.panel_label a bold letter at the top left of each. Each plot of MDAPY sets its labels and returns its axes, so a line of one's own can go on top, as in the other figures.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
plot.save(fig, "figure") writes figure.pdf, figure.svg and figure.png: PDF and SVG keep the text as text, which Illustrator or Inkscape can change, and the fonts embedded as TrueType, as journals ask; PNG has 300 dots per inch. formats chooses some of them, and fig.savefig("figure.tiff", dpi=600) writes any other format.

In a notebook a figure shows when its with plot.style(): ends, as the style holds only inside it: make the figure, change it and save it inside the with.

docs.title: A polycrystal of fcc and bcc grains
docs.text: build_polycrystal fills every grain with the same crystal. For grains of two phases, build the polycrystal twice with the same seeds and orientations, once from each crystal: both then have the same grains, and each grain can be taken from either. This page builds a nanocomposite of copper (fcc) and tantalum (bcc) grains, removes the atoms that come too close where the phases meet, and checks each grain with common neighbor analysis.

docs.title: The same grains twice
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.build import build_crystal, build_polycrystal, random_rotations

box = mp.Box(100.0)
grains = 8
seeds = np.random.default_rng(7).random((grains, 3)) * 100.0
rotations = random_rotations(grains, seed=8)

copper = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu")
tantalum = build_crystal("bcc", 3.303, elements="Ta")
fcc = build_polycrystal(copper, box, seeds, orientations=rotations)
bcc = build_polycrystal(tantalum, box, seeds, orientations=rotations)

Both have a grain column, numbered as the seeds. Take grains 0 to 3 from the copper polycrystal and the others from the tantalum one, and join the two tables:

in_copper = [0, 1, 2, 3]
table = pl.concat(
    [
        fcc.table.filter(pl.col("grain").is_in(in_copper)),
        bcc.table.filter(~pl.col("grain").is_in(in_copper)),
    ]
)
composite = mp.System(table=table, box=fcc.box)

docs.title: Atoms too close
docs.text:
Inside one polycrystal, build_polycrystal already removed the atoms of neighboring grains that came too close. Where a copper grain meets a tantalum grain the two crystals were built separately, so atoms of the two can overlap. Remove as few as possible, so that no two stay closer than 0.7 times the nearest distance of copper, with find_overlapping, as build_polycrystal does:

from mdapy.neighbor import find_overlapping

too_close = find_overlapping(composite, 0.7 * 3.615 / np.sqrt(2))
composite = composite.filter(~too_close)
too_close.sum(), len(composite)  # 672 atoms removed, 66 678 left

docs.title: The structure of each grain
docs.text:
Common neighbor analysis tells fcc from bcc. Attach the result as a column and count the structures in each grain with polars:

from mdapy.identify import CommonNeighborAnalysis

cna = CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(composite)
labelled = composite.with_columns(cna)
counts = (
    labelled.table.group_by("grain", "element")
    .agg(
        atoms=pl.len(),
        fcc=(pl.col("cna_structure") == 1).mean(),
        bcc=(pl.col("cna_structure") == 3).mean(),
    )
    .sort("grain")
)
print(counts)

The copper grains come out about 70 % fcc and the tantalum grains about 70 % bcc; the rest are atoms at the boundaries, whose neighbors fit neither structure.

docs.title: A picture
docs.text:
Color the atoms by structure and cut the box in half to see inside:

from mdapy.visualization import render

front = composite["positions"][:, 0] < 50.0
render(
    composite,
    "images/composite.png",
    atoms=front,
    color=cna,
    width=1200,
    height=900,
    legend=True,
)
render(
    composite,
    "images/composite-elements.png",
    atoms=front,
    width=1200,
    height=900,
    legend=True,
)
By structure: fcc green, bcc blue, others white By element

Before a simulation, relax the composite with a potential made for both elements (see Energy minimization): the boundaries between the phases rearrange, and how much depends strongly on the potential.

docs.title: From MDAPY 1.x
docs.text: MDAPY 2.0 is written anew, and code written for 1.x does not run with it unchanged. This page gives the 2.0 way of each common 1.x call. MDAPY 1.x stays on PyPI for code that needs it, pip install "mdapy<2" (see Compatibility).

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
• A system never changes. Each change returns a new system, such as system.with_columns(...) or system.with_box(...). The 1.x system.cal_* methods, which wrote columns into system.data, are now analysis classes: result = Analysis(parameters).compute(system), then system = system.with_columns(result) adds the result's columns.
  • Positions are one column, positions, of (N, 3) float64, and so are velocities and forces; 1.x had x, y, z, vx, ... system.table is the polars DataFrame of the atoms (1.x system.data).
  • Everything has a module: mdapy.io, mdapy.build, mdapy.transform, mdapy.identify (structure analyses), mdapy.analysis, mdapy.calculators, mdapy.simulation, mdapy.lattice_dynamics, mdapy.mlip, mdapy.visualization and mdapy.interop. The top level holds only the foundations: System, Box, Topology, NeighborList and the threads.
  • Neighbor lists are objects, built once and given to the analyses that share them, compute(system, neighbors=nl), not a state of the system.
  • Potentials are given to what uses them, as minimize(system, potential), not attached as system.calc.
  • Results have named attributes, and figures are drawn by mdapy.visualization.plot, not by plot() methods of the results.

The units are LAMMPS's metal units, Å, eV and ps, as in 1.x; stress and pressure are in GPa (see Units).

docs.title: One script in both
docs.text:
In MDAPY 1.x:

import mdapy as mp

system = mp.build_crystal("Cu", "fcc", 3.615, nx=10, ny=10, nz=10)
system.cal_common_neighbor_analysis()
system.cal_centro_symmetry_parameter(12)
rdf = system.cal_radial_distribution_function(rc=5.0, nbin=100)
rdf.plot()
system.write_dump("copper.dump")

In MDAPY 2.0:

from mdapy.analysis import RadialDistributionFunction
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.identify import CentroSymmetryParameter, CommonNeighborAnalysis
from mdapy.io import write
from mdapy.visualization import plot

system = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(10, 10, 10))
system = system.with_columns(
    CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(system),  # the column cna_structure
    CentroSymmetryParameter(12).compute(system),  # the column csp
)
rdf = RadialDistributionFunction(5.0, bins=100).compute(system)
with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure()
    plot.rdf(rdf, ax=ax)
write("copper.dump", system)

docs.text:

docs.title: Neighbors
docs.text:
MDAPY 1.x MDAPY 2.0 system.build_neighbor(rc, max_neigh) nl = mp.NeighborList.build(system, rc), then compute(system, neighbors=nl); no max_neigh system.build_nearest_neighbor(k) mp.NeighborList.build(system, num_neighbors=k) system.build_voronoi_neighbor() mp.NeighborList.build(system, voronoi=True) system.create_bonds(rc) create_bonds(system, rc), from mdapy.transform: the bonds in the topology

docs.text:
From mdapy.identify; system.with_columns(result) adds the columns.

MDAPY 1.x MDAPY 2.0 Column cal_common_neighbor_analysis(rc=None) CommonNeighborAnalysis(cutoff=None) cna_structure cal_polyhedral_template_matching(structure) PolyhedralTemplateMatching(structures=("fcc", "hcp", "bcc")) ptm_structure, ptm_rmsd, ... cal_ackland_jones_analysis() AcklandJonesAnalysis() ackland_jones_structure cal_identify_diamond_structure() DiamondStructure() diamond_structure cal_centro_symmetry_parameter(N) CentroSymmetryParameter(N) csp cal_common_neighbor_parameter(rc) CommonNeighborParameter(rc) cnp cal_chill_plus(cutoff) ChillPlus(cutoff) chill_plus_structure identify_fcc_planar_faults=True PlanarFaults() planar_fault

docs.text:
MDAPY 1.x MDAPY 2.0 TachyonRender(...).render_system(system, output_figure="a.png") render(system, "a.png"), from mdapy.visualization; device="gpu" on the graphics card colors=..., radii=... color= (a column, colors or a structure result), radius= View(system) in a notebook show_image(render(system)) mp.set_figure(), mp.save_figure(fig, name) with plot.style(): fig, ax = plot.figure(), plot.save(fig, name) rdf.plot() and the other plot() methods plot.rdf(rdf), plot.structure_factor, plot.msd, plot.warren_cowley, plot.band_structure and others

See Rendering and Plots.

docs.title: What 2.0 does otherwise
docs.text:
No max_neigh. A neighbor list holds any number of neighbors for each atom, as one list of pairs. Nothing has to be guessed before the search, no atom loses neighbors to a limit set too low, a dense region and a gas share one list, and the memory follows the pairs there are. The same holds for every analysis, which takes no such limit either.

split_xyz: a trajectory is read frame by frame, and each frame written to a file of its own:

from mdapy.io import read_trajectory

write("frames.xyz", [system, system])  # two frames in one file
with read_trajectory("frames.xyz") as trajectory:
    for k, frame in enumerate(trajectory):
        write(f"frame_{k}.xyz", frame)

average_by_neighbor: a neighbor list gives it in a few lines of NumPy, here the mean of csp over each atom and its neighbors:

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp

nl = mp.NeighborList.build(system, 3.0)
csp = system["csp"]
total = csp + np.bincount(nl.i, weights=csp[nl.j], minlength=len(system))
system = system.with_columns(csp_average=total / (nl.counts + 1))

The notebook viewer View is left out to keep MDAPY lean: render makes the picture and show_image(render(system)) shows it in a notebook. A graphical application with fuller features is developed separately.

Since 2.1: orthogonal_cell is mdapy.transform.orthogonal_cell (see Orthogonal cells), and Spline is mdapy.fitting.Spline (see Interpolation).

Coming in a later 2.x release: set_pka and BondStiffness. They will be additions, so code written for 2.0 keeps working (see Compatibility).

Threads: MDAPY_NUM_THREADS sets the number of threads as in 1.x, and mp.set_num_threads(n) changes it while running (see Parallelism).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: MDAPY needs Python 3.11 or newer, and on macOS, macOS 14 or newer. Its only required dependencies are NumPy 2.3.1 or newer and polars 2.

docs.title: From PyPI
docs.text:
pip install mdapy

This is the usual way. PyPI holds built packages for Linux on x86-64 and on ARM, macOS on Apple silicon and Windows on x86-64, so nothing has to be compiled. Elsewhere, pip builds MDAPY from its source archive, which needs the tools below.

These systems are the ones officially supported. On others, such as macOS on an Intel processor, MDAPY built from source should work as well, but no package is built for them and no test runs on them.

docs.title: From a source archive
docs.text:
Build the source archive on PyPI, instead of taking a built package:

pip install --no-binary mdapy mdapy

or a source archive you have downloaded:

pip install mdapy-*.tar.gz

docs.title: From git
docs.text:
For the newest code, directly:

pip install "git+https://github.com/mushroomfire/mdapy.git"

or from a clone, which also has the tests and the documentation:

git clone https://github.com/mushroomfire/mdapy.git
cd mdapy
pip install .

docs.title: What a build needs
docs.text:
Installing from a source archive or from git compiles MDAPY, which needs:

Needed Version How to get it A C++ compiler C++17: GCC, Clang or MSVC Debian, Ubuntu: sudo apt install g++; Fedora, RHEL: sudo dnf install gcc-c++; macOS: xcode-select --install; Windows: Visual Studio with "Desktop development with C++" CMake 3.18 or newer pip install cmake, or the package of your system scikit-build-core, nanobind 0.10 or newer, 2.4 or newer pip fetches them for the build NumPy, polars 2.3.1 or newer, 2 or newer pip installs them with MDAPY

No OpenMP library and no other third-party code is needed.

docs.title: An old Linux
docs.text:
The built packages on PyPI need glibc 2.27 or newer, about as those of NumPy do: Ubuntu 18.04, RHEL 8 or newer. mdapy.show_versions() or ldd --version tells which glibc a machine has.

On an older system pip finds no built package that fits, and builds MDAPY and NumPy from their source archives, which takes the tools above. A message such as GLIBC_2.27 not found means a package built for a newer system. On a cluster, a newer compiler usually comes from a module, such as module load gcc. In a conda environment, get a compiler and NumPy that run on the old system first, and pip then builds MDAPY alone:

conda install -c conda-forge compilers numpy polars
pip install mdapy

docs.title: Pictures on the GPU
docs.text: Pictures are traced on the GPU with Metal on macOS and Direct3D 12 on Windows, in every build, and with Vulkan on Linux when the build finds Vulkan's headers: install them before MDAPY, as libvulkan-dev on Debian and Ubuntu or vulkan-headers on Fedora and RHEL. MDAPY opens the Vulkan loader, libvulkan.so.1, only for a picture on the GPU; the loader and the driver come with the graphics drivers. Without the headers, or without a GPU, pictures are traced on the processor.

docs.title: 64-bit atom indices
docs.text:
Atom indices in results such as neighbor lists are 32-bit integers, enough for 2,147,483,647 atoms and half the memory of 64-bit ones. For larger systems, build MDAPY with 64-bit indices:

pip install . -Ccmake.define.MDAPY_INDEX64=ON

mdapy.index_dtype tells which build is installed:

python -c "import mdapy; print(mdapy.index_dtype)"   # int64

The table of a System holds a row per atom, and the default runtime of polars at most 4,294,967,295 rows. Beyond that, install the 64-bit runtime of polars too, which polars then takes by itself:

pip install "polars[rt64]"
python -c "import polars; print(polars.get_index_type())"   # UInt64

docs.title: Optional dependencies
docs.text:
MDAPY needs only NumPy and polars. Other packages, when installed, switch on the parts of MDAPY that use them; without them the rest works, and these parts raise an error that names the package to install.

Package Install For matplotlib pip install "mdapy[plot]" the plots of mdapy.visualization.plot spglib, seekpath pip install "mdapy[symmetry]" the space group; phonons and elastic constants from fewer computations; band_structure("auto") ASE pip install "mdapy[ase]" to_ase, from_ase, and calculators between ASE and MDAPY freud pip install "mdapy[freud]" to_freud, from_freud pymatgen pip install "mdapy[pymatgen]" to_pymatgen, from_pymatgen OVITO pip install ovito to_ovito, from_ovito LAMMPS its Python module, built with LAMMPS the LAMMPS calculator, molecular dynamics and elastic constants from molecular dynamics

Extras combine: pip install "mdapy[plot,symmetry,ase]". OVITO's package from PyPI warns in a conda environment, where conda's own is preferred, so it is not an extra; nor is LAMMPS, whose Python module comes with a build of LAMMPS with the packages of styles each user needs.

docs.title: Tests and documentation
docs.text:
Extra Installs For dev pytest, pytest-cov, pytest-xdist, coverage, ruff, matplotlib, ASE, spglib running the tests and the linter docs MkDocs Material, mkdocstrings building this site

The tests that compare MDAPY with other programs run where these are installed and are skipped otherwise; continuous integration installs them all:

Package Version Compared OVITO 3.17.1 structure identification and analyses, atom by atom freud 3.6.1 analyses that freud implements LAMMPS stable 30 Sep 2026, with MANYBODY, MOLECULE, EXTRA-COMPUTE and VORONOI calculators, analyses, molecular dynamics; the dynamical matrix where PHONON is built in phonopy 4.8.6 force constants, frequencies, densities of states, thermal properties seekpath 2.2.2 the paths of band_structure("auto") pymatgen pymatgen-core conversions

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
An editable install rebuilds nothing on import; rerun the install after changing C++ code.

pip install -e ".[dev,docs]"
pytest                      # run the test suite
pytest --cov                # with coverage (fails below 90 % in total)
ruff check . && ruff format --check .
mkdocs serve                # preview the documentation

The test suite and the coverage rules are described in Contributing.

docs.title: Quick tour
docs.text: This page builds a small copper crystal, writes and reads it, finds its neighbors, computes its energy with a potential, relaxes it and writes the result. Every block runs as shown, in order. To learn step by step instead, start with the lessons.

docs.title: A system
docs.text:
A System holds the atoms, as a table of columns, and the simulation box.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

a = 3.615  # Å
system = build_crystal("fcc", a, elements="Cu", repeat=(3, 3, 3))
len(system), system.box.volume  # 108 atoms, Å^3

See Systems, Topology and Simulation box.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
from mdapy.io import read, write

write("copper.xyz", system)
back = read("copper.xyz")
np.abs(back["positions"] - system["positions"]).max()  # 0.0

See Reading and writing files and, for a whole trajectory, Trajectories.

docs.title: Neighbors
docs.text:
nl = mp.NeighborList.build(system, 3.0)
nl.counts  # 12 neighbors for every atom of fcc
nl.distances.min()  # a / sqrt(2)

See Neighbor lists.

docs.title: Energy and forces
docs.text:
from mdapy.calculators import EAM

potential = EAM.zhou(["Cu"])
result = potential.compute(system, ("energy", "forces", "virial"))
result.energy / len(system)  # eV per atom
result.stress  # (3, 3) GPa

See Calculators and EAM.

docs.title: Relaxation
docs.text:
The atoms are displaced at random, then the positions and the box relax to the nearest minimum of the energy.

from mdapy.simulation import minimize

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
rattled = system.with_columns(
    positions=system["positions"] + rng.normal(scale=0.05, size=(108, 3))
)
relaxed = minimize(rattled, potential, cell="full")
relaxed.converged, relaxed.energy, relaxed.stress
write("relaxed.xyz", relaxed.system)  # with forces, energy and stress

See Energy minimization.

docs.title: Analysis and pictures
docs.text:
A polycrystal, its grain boundaries found by common neighbor analysis and drawn by the ray tracer:

from mdapy.build import build_polycrystal
from mdapy.identify import CommonNeighborAnalysis
from mdapy.visualization import render

grains = build_polycrystal(
    build_crystal("fcc", a, elements="Cu"), mp.Box(60.0), 6, seed=4
)
structures = CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(grains)
structures.counts()  # fcc, and other at the boundaries
render(
    grains,
    "images/quick-tour.png",
    atoms=grains["positions"][:, 0] < 30,  # the half at x < 30 Å
    color=structures,
    style="matte",
    width=900,
    height=600,
    legend=True,
)

Six grains of copper cut in half: fcc atoms green, grain boundaries white, in the matte style.

See Building structures, Common neighbor analysis and Rendering.

docs.title: 2. Asking the atoms questions
docs.text: Here is the third idea: every analysis is used the same way. Learn it once and you can use all of them. This lesson asks of a copper nanoparticle: how many of its atoms are on the surface, and which are still in the crystal?

docs.title: A nanoparticle
docs.text:
Cut a sphere out of a crystal. A new column holds the distance from the center, and filter keeps the atoms within 18 Å:

import numpy as np
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(12, 12, 12))
center = crystal["positions"].mean(axis=0)
crystal = crystal.with_columns(
    distance=np.linalg.norm(crystal["positions"] - center, axis=1)
)
particle = crystal.filter("distance < 18")
print(particle)

System: 2112 atoms (Cu2112)
  box:      43.38 × 43.38 × 43.38 Å, orthogonal, periodic x y z
  columns:  positions (3), element, distance

The box is still periodic, but it is 7 Å wider than the particle, more than any cutoff below, so the particle does not meet its own images.

docs.title: The pattern
docs.text:
Count the neighbors of each atom:

from mdapy.analysis import CoordinationNumber

analysis = CoordinationNumber(cutoff=3.0)  # 1. the parameters
result = analysis.compute(particle)  # 2. the computation
particle = particle.with_columns(result)  # 3. the answer, as a column
print(particle)

System: 2112 atoms (Cu2112)
  box:      43.38 × 43.38 × 43.38 Å, orthogonal, periodic x y z
  columns:  positions (3), element, distance, coordination, coordination_Cu

These three steps are the same for every analysis in MDAPY. A wrong parameter fails at step 1, before anything is computed. The new column is like any other, so everything from the last lesson works on it:

surface = particle.filter("coordination < 12")
print(f"{len(surface)} of {len(particle)} atoms are on the surface")
print(particle.table.group_by("coordination").len().sort("coordination"))

724 of 2112 atoms are on the surface
shape: (7, 2)
┌──────────────┬──────┐
│ coordination ┆ len  │
│ ---          ┆ ---  │
│ i64          ┆ u32  │
╞══════════════╪══════╡
│ 6            ┆ 168  │
│ 7            ┆ 108  │
│ 8            ┆ 84   │
│ 9            ┆ 172  │
│ 10           ┆ 72   │
│ 11           ┆ 120  │
│ 12           ┆ 1388 │
└──────────────┴──────┘

A column can color a picture, by its name:

from mdapy.visualization import render

render(
    particle,
    "images/coordination.png",
    atoms=particle["positions.x"] < center[0],
    color="coordination",
    colormap="labels",
    box=False,
    width=800,
    height=600,
    legend=True,
)

Inside, every atom has 12 neighbors. The surface has fewer, and fewest at the edges and corners.

docs.title: Another question, the same pattern
docs.text:
Which atoms are in the crystal? Common neighbor analysis looks at how the neighbors of each atom are bonded:

from mdapy.identify import CommonNeighborAnalysis

structures = CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(particle)
print(structures.counts())
particle = particle.with_columns(structures)

{'other': 724, 'fcc': 1388, 'hcp': 0, 'bcc': 0, 'ico': 0}

The result of a structure analysis also knows its colors, so it can be passed to render directly:

render(
    particle,
    "images/structures.png",
    atoms=particle["positions.x"] < center[0],
    color=structures,
    box=False,
    width=800,
    height=600,
    legend=True,
)

Green for fcc atoms, white for the rest: the surface, as common neighbor analysis needs a full shell of neighbors.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Replace CommonNeighborAnalysis() with PolyhedralTemplateMatching(), also from mdapy.identify. Does it find the same fcc atoms?
  2. Add the column of CentroSymmetryParameter(12) to the particle, and color by "csp".
An answer 
from mdapy.identify import CentroSymmetryParameter, PolyhedralTemplateMatching

print(PolyhedralTemplateMatching().compute(particle).counts())
centro = particle.with_columns(CentroSymmetryParameter(12).compute(particle))
render(centro, "images/csp.png", color="csp")

Next: from numbers to figures. All the analyses are listed in the overview of analyses.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text:
The lessons on one page. Everything here assumes:

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp

and the imports in the table at the end.

docs.title: Get a system
docs.text: I want Write a file system = read("file.data") a crystal build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(8, 8, 8)) a polycrystal build_polycrystal(crystal, mp.Box(100.0), 8, seed=1) atoms of my own mp.System(positions, mp.Box(20.0), elements="Cu") to know what I have print(system)

docs.title: Read it
docs.text: I want Write a column system["positions"], system["element"] a component system["positions.z"] an expression system["positions.x**2 + positions.y**2"] the number of atoms len(system) the box system.box.matrix, system.box.volume, system.box.pbc global values system.info["timestep"] anything else system.table, a polars DataFrame

docs.title: Change it
docs.text:
A system never changes: each of these returns a new one.

I want Write a new or changed column system.with_columns(charge=values) the columns of an analysis system.with_columns(result), named after it, as cna_structure the columns of two runs of one analysis system.with_columns(near=first, far=second) to move atoms system.with_columns(positions=new_positions) another box system.with_box(matrix, scale_positions=True) global values system.with_info(energy=-3.54) some atoms, by condition system.filter("positions.z > 10", element="Cu") some atoms, by index system.gather(indices) the atoms in another order system.sort("id") to drop columns system.drop("velocities")

docs.title: Ask it
docs.text:
Every analysis has the same three steps:

result = Analysis(parameters).compute(system)
system = system.with_columns(result)  # per-atom values, as columns
I want Write the structure of each atom CommonNeighborAnalysis(), PolyhedralTemplateMatching() their numbers result.counts() the number of neighbors CoordinationNumber(cutoff=3.0) the radial distribution RadialDistributionFunction(cutoff=8.0), then result.r, result.g one list for several analyses nl = mp.NeighborList.build(system, 5.0), then compute(system, neighbors=nl)

docs.title: Compute energies
docs.text: I want Write a potential EAM.zhou(["Cu"]) or EAM("Cu.eam.alloy") energy and forces potential.compute(system, ("energy", "forces")) to relax the atoms minimize(system, potential), then result.system to relax the box as well minimize(system, potential, cell="full")

docs.title: Follow a trajectory
docs.text: I want Write to open a file with read_trajectory("dump.*.lammpstrj") as trajectory: a frame, or some frames trajectory[0], trajectory[::10] the frames through a function trajectory.map(function) one number per frame TimeSeries(function).compute(trajectory) to write them write("out.xyz", trajectory.map(function))

docs.title: Show and save it
docs.text: I want Write a file write("out.xyz", system) a picture render(system, "picture.png") colors by a column render(system, "picture.png", color="coordination") colors by structure render(system, "picture.png", color=result) what the colors mean render(system, "picture.png", color=result, legend=True) some atoms only render(system, "picture.png", atoms=system["positions.x"] < 20) on the graphics card render(system, "picture.png", device="gpu") a figure with plot.style(): fig, ax = plot.figure("single") to save a figure plot.save(fig, "figure")

docs.title: Where each thing is imported from
docs.text: Module Holds mdapy System, Box, Topology, NeighborList, set_num_threads mdapy.io read, write, read_trajectory mdapy.build build_crystal, build_polycrystal, random_alloy and others mdapy.transform replicate, wrap, combine, slice and others mdapy.identify the structure analyses mdapy.analysis every other analysis mdapy.calculators EAM, NEP, LAMMPS, VASP mdapy.simulation minimize, MolecularDynamics, defect energies, free energies, melting points mdapy.lattice_dynamics elastic_constants, phonons, quasi_harmonic and others mdapy.mlip descriptors, choosing frames, errors of a model mdapy.visualization render, plot, write_movie mdapy.interop to_ase, from_ase, to_ovito, from_ovito and others

docs.title: 4. Energies and relaxation
docs.text: So far the atoms stayed where they were put. With an interatomic potential they have an energy and forces, and can relax. This lesson computes a real number, the energy it takes to form a vacancy in copper, in a few lines.

docs.title: A potential
docs.text:
A calculator takes a system and computes what you ask of it. EAM.zhou makes the embedded atom potential of Zhou et al., with no file to download:

import numpy as np
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.calculators import EAM

potential = EAM.zhou(["Cu"])
crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(5, 5, 5))

result = potential.compute(crystal, ("energy", "forces", "virial"))
print(f"{result.energy / len(crystal):.3f} eV per atom")
print(f"largest force {np.abs(result.forces).max():.1e} eV/Å")

-3.540 eV per atom
largest force 8.3e-15 eV/Å

A perfect crystal has no forces, as every atom is pulled alike from all sides.

docs.title: Take out one atom
docs.text:
gather picks atoms by index, so all the indices but the first remove one atom. The atoms around the hole now feel a force:

vacancy = crystal.gather(np.arange(1, len(crystal)))
forces = potential.compute(vacancy, ("forces",)).forces
print(f"largest force {np.abs(forces).max():.3f} eV/Å")

largest force 0.251 eV/Å

docs.title: Relax it
docs.text:
minimize moves the atoms until the forces vanish. It returns the relaxed system, its energy, and whether it converged:

from mdapy.simulation import minimize

relaxed = minimize(vacancy, potential)
print(relaxed.converged, relaxed.steps)
print(f"largest force {relaxed.max_force:.5f} eV/Å")

True 67
largest force 0.00080 eV/Å

docs.title: The energy of a vacancy
docs.text:
Forming a vacancy moves one atom from inside the crystal to its surface, so it costs the energy of the relaxed system less that of N − 1 atoms of the perfect crystal:

perfect = result.energy / len(crystal)
formation = relaxed.energy - (len(crystal) - 1) * perfect
print(f"{formation:.3f} eV")

1.273 eV

Experiments give about 1.28 eV. A system this size has converged, as the tutorial on defect energies shows.

docs.title: Energy per atom
docs.text:
The relaxed system has new columns, as anything that computes per-atom values does. Here is the energy of each atom against that of the crystal, in a nanoparticle:

from mdapy.visualization import render

large = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(10, 10, 10))
center = large["positions"].mean(axis=0)
particle = large.filter(np.linalg.norm(large["positions"] - center, axis=1) < 14)
relaxed = minimize(particle, potential)
particle = relaxed.system.with_columns(
    excess=relaxed.system["atomic_energies"] - perfect
)
print(particle)

render(
    particle,
    "images/excess.png",
    atoms=particle["positions.x"] < center[0],
    color="excess",
    box=False,
    width=800,
    height=600,
    legend="excess energy (eV)",
)

System: 952 atoms (Cu952)
  box:      36.15 × 36.15 × 36.15 Å, orthogonal, periodic x y z
  columns:  positions (3), element, forces (3), atomic_energies, atomic_virials (3),
            excess
  info:     energy = -3099.06, virial (3, 3), stress (3, 3)

The atoms of the surface are bound less strongly, most of all at the corners. This is why a small particle melts below the bulk, as the next lesson shows.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Compute the formation energy in a smaller crystal, repeat=(3, 3, 3). How far is it from 1.273 eV?
  2. Use minimize(vacancy, potential, cell="full"), which also relaxes the box. What changes?
An answer 
small = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(3, 3, 3))
hole = minimize(small.gather(np.arange(1, len(small))), potential)
print(hole.energy - (len(small) - 1) * perfect)  # 1.279 eV: 6 meV more

Next: a nanoparticle melts. See also Calculators, Energy minimization and Defect energies.

docs.title: 3. From numbers to figures
docs.text: Some analyses give one value per atom, as in the last lesson. Others describe the whole system. Their results are plain NumPy arrays, ready for a figure. This lesson shows how heat looks in the radial distribution function of copper.

docs.title: A crystal and a shaken crystal
docs.text:
Atoms at a finite temperature move about their sites. Random displacements give a rough picture of that. Remember that with_columns also replaces columns, the positions too:

import numpy as np
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(12, 12, 12))
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
shaken = crystal.with_columns(
    positions=crystal["positions"] + rng.normal(0, 0.15, (len(crystal), 3))
)

docs.title: A result of the whole system
docs.text:
The pattern is the one you know: parameters, then compute. There is no column to add, as there is one curve for all the atoms:

from mdapy.analysis import RadialDistributionFunction

analysis = RadialDistributionFunction(cutoff=8.0, bins=200)
cold = analysis.compute(crystal)
hot = analysis.compute(shaken)
print(cold.r.shape, cold.g.shape)
print(f"first peak at {hot.r[hot.g.argmax()]:.2f} Å")

(200,) (200,)
first peak at 2.58 Å

The first peak sits close to the nearest-neighbor distance of fcc, a/√2 = 2.556 Å.

docs.title: A figure
docs.text:
hot.r and hot.g are NumPy arrays, so any plotting library will do. mdapy.visualization.plot sets matplotlib up for journals, and plot.save writes the file:

from mdapy.visualization import plot

with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    ax.plot(hot.r, hot.g, label="shaken by 0.15 Å")
    ax.set_xlabel("r (Å)")
    ax.set_ylabel("g(r)")
    ax.legend()
    plot.save(fig, "images/rdf", formats=("png",))

Peaks at the distances between sites of fcc, broadened by the displacements.

docs.title: The ready-made plots
docs.text:
Common results have a plot of their own, with the labels set. A figure can have several panels:

from mdapy.identify import CommonNeighborAnalysis

structures = CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(shaken)

with plot.style():
    fig, (left, right) = plot.figure("double", nrows=1, ncols=2)
    plot.rdf(hot, ax=left)
    plot.structure_counts(structures, ax=right)
    plot.panel_label(left, "a")
    plot.panel_label(right, "b")
    plot.save(fig, "images/panels", formats=("png",))

a: g(r) of the shaken crystal. b: its atoms by structure.

docs.title: Values of the atoms
docs.text:
Histogram gives the distribution of a column. Here, the distance of each atom from its site, computed with the arrays of the two systems:

from mdapy.analysis import Histogram

moved = shaken.with_columns(
    moved=np.linalg.norm(shaken["positions"] - crystal["positions"], axis=1)
)
histogram = Histogram("moved", bins=40).compute(moved)

with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    ax.plot(histogram.center, histogram.counts)
    ax.set_xlabel("Distance moved (Å)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Atoms")
    plot.save(fig, "images/moved", formats=("png",))

The distribution of the length of a three-dimensional Gaussian step.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Shake the crystal by 0.3 Å and draw both curves in one figure. What happens to the height of the first peak?
  2. Save the curve to a text file with np.savetxt("rdf.txt", np.c_[hot.r, hot.g]).
An answer 
harder = crystal.with_columns(
    positions=crystal["positions"] + rng.normal(0, 0.3, (len(crystal), 3))
)
hotter = analysis.compute(harder)
with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    ax.plot(hot.r, hot.g, label="0.15 Å")
    ax.plot(hotter.r, hotter.g, label="0.3 Å")
    ax.legend()
    plot.save(fig, "images/two", formats=("png",))

The peak drops to about half and widens by about twice: its area, the number of neighbors, stays.

Next: energies and relaxation. Figures with MDAPY shows how to change the size of the text, the lines and the colors. See also Plots, Radial distribution function and Histograms.

docs.title: 1. A crystal is a table
docs.text:
Six short lessons teach the Python side of MDAPY. Each runs on its own, needs no input files, and ends with something to try. Three ideas carry you through all of them, and this lesson teaches the first two:

  1. A system is a table of atoms and a box.
  2. A system never changes. Every change makes a new one.
  3. Every analysis is used the same way (lesson 2).

docs.title: Build something and print it
docs.text:
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(8, 8, 8))
print(crystal)

System: 2048 atoms (Cu2048)
  box:      28.92 × 28.92 × 28.92 Å, orthogonal, periodic x y z
  columns:  positions (3), element

This is the first thing to do with any system: printing it tells you the atoms, the box and the columns you have.

docs.title: Read a column by its name
docs.text:
Everything about the atoms is a column, and every column is read the same way. You get a NumPy array, one row per atom:

crystal["positions"]  # (2048, 3), in Å
crystal["positions.z"]  # one component, (2048,)
crystal["element"]  # ['Cu', 'Cu', ...]
crystal["positions.x**2 + positions.y**2"]  # an expression over the columns
crystal.box.volume  # in Å³

docs.title: Change it: you get a new system
docs.text:
Give some atoms another element with with_columns. The arrays can be any NumPy array with one value per atom:

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
alloy = crystal.with_columns(element=rng.choice(["Cu", "Ni"], len(crystal)))
print(alloy)

System: 2048 atoms (Ni1066 Cu982)
  box:      28.92 × 28.92 × 28.92 Å, orthogonal, periodic x y z
  columns:  positions (3), element

crystal is still pure copper. Since nothing changes behind your back, you can keep the systems of every step and compare them.

docs.title: Select atoms
docs.text:
filter keeps the atoms that meet a condition, written as you would say it:

top = alloy.filter("positions.z > 20")
nickel = alloy.filter(element="Ni")
top_nickel = alloy.filter("positions.z > 20", element="Ni")
print(len(top), len(nickel), len(top_nickel))

docs.text:
render draws a system. atoms chooses which atoms to show, so a mask of the atoms with small x cuts the crystal open:

from mdapy.visualization import render

render(
    alloy,
    "images/alloy.png",

Copper and nickel at random on an fcc lattice, the half with x below 15 Å.

mdapy.io.write and mdapy.io.read take any common format, chosen by the name of the file:

from mdapy.io import read, write

write("alloy.xyz", alloy)
back = read("alloy.xyz")
print(len(back))

2048

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Build bcc tantalum with a lattice constant of 3.303 Å.
  2. Add a column layer with the integer part of z divided by 3.303, and color the picture by it with color="layer" and the discrete colormap="labels".
An answer 
tantalum = build_crystal("bcc", 3.303, elements="Ta", repeat=(10, 10, 10))
layered = tantalum.with_columns(layer=(tantalum["positions.z"] // 3.303).astype(int))
render(layered, "images/layers.png", color="layer", colormap="labels")

Next: asking the atoms questions. The reference pages for this lesson are Systems, Changing a system, Selecting and ordering atoms and Rendering.

docs.title: 5. A nanoparticle melts
docs.text: Everything so far has been one configuration. Over time you get a trajectory, a sequence of systems. This lesson heats a copper nanoparticle until it melts and watches it happen. The molecular dynamics runs in LAMMPS, through its Python module; about half a minute on a laptop.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
The particle sits in the middle of a box that is not periodic. MDAPY writes the potential file, so there is nothing to download:

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.calculators import EAM, LAMMPS

crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(12, 12, 12))
center = crystal["positions"].mean(axis=0)
inside = crystal.filter(np.linalg.norm(crystal["positions"] - center, axis=1) < 16)
particle = mp.System(
    inside["positions"] - center + 60.0, mp.Box(120.0, pbc=False), elements="Cu"
)

EAM.zhou(["Cu"]).write("Cu.eam.alloy")
potential = LAMMPS(
    "pair_style eam/alloy\npair_coeff * * Cu.eam.alloy Cu", elements=["Cu"]
)
print(len(particle))

1436

docs.title: Heat it
docs.text:
Give the atoms velocities, let them settle at 300 K, then raise the temperature to 1500 K over 60 ps. save_every=500 keeps the atoms every 500 steps:

from mdapy.simulation import MolecularDynamics

with MolecularDynamics(particle, potential, timestep=0.002) as md:
    md.velocities(600, seed=1)
    md.run(2500, ensemble="nvt", temperature=300)
    md.run(30000, ensemble="nvt", temperature=(300, 1500), save_every=500)
    frames, thermo = md.frames, md.thermo
print(len(frames), frames[0])

61 System: 1436 atoms (Cu1436)
  box:      120 × 120 × 120 Å, orthogonal, not periodic
  columns:  element, positions (3), velocities (3), image (3)
  info:     timestep = 2500, time = 5

frames is a tuple of ordinary systems, so all you learned applies to each. A trajectory analysis takes the whole sequence. thermo is a polars table of the temperature, the energies and so on along the run.

docs.title: One number per frame
docs.text:
TimeSeries gives one number per frame, here from a function of your own. A function of a frame can use anything from the last lessons:

from mdapy.analysis import TimeSeries
from mdapy.identify import CommonNeighborAnalysis


def fcc_fraction(frame):
    """The share of the atoms still in an fcc crystal."""
    return CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(frame).counts()["fcc"] / len(frame)


series = TimeSeries(fcc_fraction).compute(frames)
temperature = np.interp(series.timestep, thermo["step"], thermo["temperature"])
energy = np.interp(series.timestep, thermo["step"], thermo["potential_energy"])

docs.title: The melting curve
docs.text:
from mdapy.visualization import plot

with plot.style():
    fig, (top, bottom) = plot.figure("single", 100, nrows=2, sharex=True)
    top.plot(temperature, series.values)
    top.set_ylabel("Share of fcc atoms")
    bottom.plot(temperature, energy / len(particle))
    bottom.set_ylabel("Energy (eV/atom)")
    bottom.set_xlabel("Temperature (K)")
    plot.save(fig, "images/melting", formats=("png",))

By about 1100 K no fcc atoms remain, and on the way there the energy rises faster: the heat of melting. Bulk copper melts at 1358 K. A particle of 3 nm melts sooner, as its many surface atoms are bound less strongly.

docs.title: Look at it
docs.text:
Pick three frames: the start, the middle and the end. Coloring by structure shows the surface melting first, while a crystal remains inside:

from mdapy.visualization import render

for name, frame in (("start", frames[0]), ("middle", frames[35]), ("end", frames[-1])):
    half = frame["positions.x"] < frame["positions.x"].mean()
    render(
        frame,
        f"images/melt-{name}.png",
        atoms=half,
        color=CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(frame),
        box=False,
        width=500,
        height=500,
        legend=True,
    )

Cut in half, at about 300 K, 1000 K and 1500 K.

docs.title: Keep it in a file, and read it back
docs.text:
mdapy.io.write takes the whole sequence, and read_trajectory opens it without reading the frames. A frame is read when you use it, so a trajectory of many gigabytes opens at once:

from mdapy.io import read_trajectory, write

write("melt.xyz", frames)

with read_trajectory("melt.xyz") as trajectory:
    print(len(trajectory))
    every_tenth = trajectory[::10]  # nothing is read yet
    again = TimeSeries(fcc_fraction).compute(every_tenth)
    print(np.round(again.values, 2))

The melting differs a little from one computer to another, so your numbers may too:

61
[0.61 0.6  0.49 0.3  0.03 0.   0.  ]

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Compute the Lindemann index over the last 20 frames and over the first 20: LindemannIndex().compute(frames[-20:]).
  2. Make the particle larger, with a radius of 25 Å. Does it melt later?
An answer 
from mdapy.analysis import LindemannIndex

print(LindemannIndex().compute(frames[:20]).index)  # solid: about 0.01
print(LindemannIndex().compute(frames[-20:]).index)  # liquid: about 0.13

Next: your own files. See also Molecular dynamics, Trajectories and Time series.

docs.title: 6. Your own files
docs.text:
Now use what you learned on your own simulations. The usual job is: a folder of LAMMPS dumps, an analysis of every frame, and the result in a file for OVITO or a figure. This page makes a few dumps first, so that it runs anywhere; replace them with yours.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.io import write

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(10, 10, 10))
crystal = crystal.with_columns(id=np.arange(1, len(crystal) + 1))
for step in (0, 1000, 2000, 10000):
    shaken = crystal.with_columns(
        positions=crystal["positions"]
        + rng.normal(0, 0.1 + step / 25000, (len(crystal), 3))
    )
    write(f"dump.{step}.lammpstrj", shaken.with_info(timestep=step))

docs.title: One frame
docs.text:
mdapy.io.read finds the format from the name of the file. Print what you got, and you know the columns you have:

from mdapy.io import read

frame = read("dump.1000.lammpstrj")
print(frame)

System: 4000 atoms (Cu4000)
  box:      36.15 × 36.15 × 36.15 Å, orthogonal, periodic x y z
  columns:  id, type, element, positions (3)
  info:     timestep = 1000

If a dump names no elements, its atoms have types. Name them with with_columns, or read a data file for the topology.

docs.title: All the frames
docs.text:
A pattern with * takes the files in the order of the numbers in their names, so dump.10000 comes after dump.2000. Write the analysis of one frame as a function, and map runs it on each frame when that frame is used:

from mdapy.identify import CommonNeighborAnalysis
from mdapy.io import read_trajectory


def analyzed(frame):
    """The frame with the structure of each atom."""
    return frame.with_columns(CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(frame))


with read_trajectory("dump.*.lammpstrj") as trajectory:
    print(len(trajectory))
    for frame in trajectory.map(analyzed):
        print(frame.info["timestep"], (frame["cna_structure"] == 1).mean())

4
0 0.99875
1000 0.904
2000 0.5
10000 0.0

The column cna_structure holds an index into the names of the analysis, and 1 is fcc. Only one frame is in memory at a time, however long the trajectory.

docs.title: Write the result
docs.text:
The same function, with mdapy.io.write. OVITO opens the file with the column cna_structure in it:

with read_trajectory("dump.*.lammpstrj") as trajectory:
    write("analyzed.xyz", trajectory.map(analyzed))

docs.title: A table of the results
docs.text:
To collect a number from each frame, build a list and make a polars table, which writes CSV or anything else:

import polars as pl

rows = []
with read_trajectory("dump.*.lammpstrj") as trajectory:
    for frame in trajectory.map(analyzed):
        rows.append(
            {
                "timestep": frame.info["timestep"],
                "fcc": int((frame["cna_structure"] == 1).sum()),
                "z_max": frame["positions.z"].max(),
            }
        )
table = pl.DataFrame(rows)
table.write_csv("results.csv")
print(table)

docs.title: Large systems
docs.text:
Three things help with millions of atoms:

  • mdapy.set_num_threads(8) chooses the number of threads. MDAPY uses all of them by default, which is rarely what you want on a shared machine.
  • Analyses that need the same neighbors can share one list, which saves most of the search: Sharing neighbor lists.
  • render(..., device="gpu") draws on the graphics card, usually ten times faster: Rendering.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text: You have now seen the whole shape of MDAPY. The cheat sheet sums it up, and the rest of this site is reference: pick the tab of what you need, and the tutorials work through real studies.

docs.title: Building structures
docs.text: MDAPY and Atomsk build fcc copper as a single crystal and as a polycrystal of 20 grains, and write it as a LAMMPS data file, from 4 000 to nearly 10 million atoms. A program is timed only where it builds the structure MDAPY builds.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A node of the Triton cluster of Aalto University, alone for the run: two Intel Xeon Gold 6148 (40 cores, two NUMA nodes), 191 GB, Linux. Python 3.13, MDAPY 2.0.0 built with GCC 12.3, and Atomsk Beta 0.13.1, a statically linked build of its release. The analyses ran on another node, with Intel Xeon Gold 6230, so their times do not compare with these.

How many times faster MDAPY is: a row for each case, the largest gain on top, and a point for each size, larger and darker for more atoms; the number on the right is the speed-up at the largest size.

docs.title: What they show
docs.text:
• Single crystal: MDAPY builds and writes it 30 to 75 times faster than Atomsk, 0.34 s against 25.5 s at nearly 10 million atoms; building it is a repetition of the cell, and most of the time is writing the file.
  • Polycrystal: MDAPY is 44 to 101 times faster, 0.48 s against 48.3 s at nearly 10 million atoms; most of the time is writing the file here too.

docs.title: Times and memory
docs.text: Every case at every size: the shortest of three times, and the memory each build took, the peak resident memory of the process minus its peak before the timings; that of Atomsk, a process of its own, is not counted.

docs.title: Cases
docs.text:
Case MDAPY Atomsk Single crystal mdapy.io.write(path, build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(n, n, n))) atomsk --create fcc 3.615 Cu -duplicate n n n path.lmp Polycrystal mdapy.io.write(path, build_polycrystal(unit, box, seeds, orientations=rotations, min_distance=0.01)) atomsk --polycrystal unit.xsf parameters.txt path.lmp

Atomsk writes every structure it builds to a file, so both programs are timed building the structure and writing it as a LAMMPS data file.

The polycrystal fills a cubic periodic box with 20 grains, the Voronoi cells of 20 seeds at random places, each of fcc copper in a random orientation. Both programs have the same seeds and orientations: Atomsk as a node line with three angles of rotation, about x, then y, then z, and MDAPY as the rotation matrices of those angles. Atomsk removes no atom where grains meet, so MDAPY is asked to remove only atoms at the same place (min_distance 0.01 Å) rather than those closer than 0.7 times the nearest distance, as it does by default.

docs.title: How it is measured
docs.text:
• MDAPY runs in a process of its own with 40 threads. Atomsk runs as a command from that process, with OMP_NUM_THREADS 40; the time of a build by Atomsk includes starting the program.
  • Before the timings, a separate process builds the structure with both programs and reads both files with MDAPY. Single crystal: the same box and the same atoms, in any order, within 1e-9 Å (Atomsk writes 12 decimals). Polycrystal: the same box, as many atoms within 0.5 %, and in each grain the same lattice. The atoms differ: each program places the lattice of a grain in its own way, MDAPY with a lattice site at the seed, Atomsk with the center of a block of lattice at a center of the cell, so that in a grain the atoms of Atomsk are those of MDAPY moved by one vector, a different one for each grain. The check finds that vector the same for every atom of a grain away from its faces, within 1e-6 Å.
  • The times of MDAPY were measured after those of Atomsk, on another node of the same kind.
  • Each process first builds a structure of 500 atoms, then three times the structure; the shortest time counts.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
The comparison is benchmarks/comparison.py in the source repository, the group builders of its cases. It runs the command atomsk, or the program the environment variable ATOMSK names.

ATOMSK=/path/to/atomsk python benchmarks/comparison.py run --group builders \
    --sizes 4000 32000 256000 2048000 9841500 --threads 40 --memory 170 --timeout 1800 \
    --output builders.json   # as above
python benchmarks/comparison.py table builders.json
python benchmarks/comparison.py plot builders.json builders.png

docs.title: MDAPY, OVITO and freud
docs.text: The analyses that MDAPY shares with OVITO and freud, computed on the same systems with the same parameters, from 4 000 to 2 million atoms. A program is timed only where it gives the result of MDAPY, atom by atom.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A node of the Triton cluster of Aalto University, alone for the run: two Intel Xeon Gold 6230 (40 cores, two hardware threads each, two NUMA nodes), 191 GB, Linux. Python 3.13, MDAPY 2.0.0 built with GCC 12.3, OVITO 3.17.1 and freud 3.6.1 from pip, each with 40 threads. Reading and writing files and building structures ran on another node, with Intel Xeon Gold 6148, so their times do not compare with these.

How many times faster MDAPY is: a row for each case, the largest gain on top, and a point for each size, larger and darker for more atoms; the number on the right is the speed-up at the largest size. Left of 1×, the other program is faster.

docs.title: What they show
docs.text:
• OVITO: at 2 million atoms MDAPY is faster in every analysis they share. It builds neighbor lists 6.4 times faster in a quarter of the memory, Voronoi cells 20 to 21 times faster, computes Steinhardt parameters over Voronoi faces 472 times faster (1.5 s against 11 minutes) and finds clusters 5.8 times faster; the other analyses take 1.3 to 3.5 times less time. From 32 000 atoms on, only atomic strain is not faster: OVITO is faster below some 250 000 atoms (3 times at 4 000 and 2 times at 32 000), the two are on par at 256 000, and MDAPY is 1.3 times faster at 2 million.
  • freud: from 256 000 atoms on, MDAPY is faster in every analysis: neighbor lists 20 to 23 times, in a seventh of the memory; the 12 nearest neighbors 6 to 8 times; Voronoi cells 28 to 34 times; Steinhardt parameters over Voronoi faces 37 times; Steinhardt parameters and the radial distribution function 3.2 to 5.5 times; cluster analysis 1.8 to 2.6 times. At 32 000 atoms the two are on par in cluster analysis.
  • One neighbor search for several analyses: the six analyses of copper from one list take 0.89 s at 2 million atoms, against 1.55 s for the six cases timed apart (0.12 s against 0.23 s at 256 000; the radial distribution function apart reaches 6 Å instead of 5 Å). OVITO's pipeline of the six takes about the sum of its cases (3.15 s against 3.32 s).
  • Voronoi faces on demand: the volumes and coordination of 2 million cells take MDAPY 1.10 s and 205 MB; with every face, its neighbor, area and edges, 1.27 s and 1.7 GB.
  • A trajectory: the mean squared displacement of 20 frames read from a dump, most of the time spent reading, takes 1.6 to 1.7 times less time than with OVITO from 32 000 atoms on.
  • 4 000 atoms take a few milliseconds; MDAPY is faster there in every analysis but cluster analysis, Wigner–Seitz occupancies and atomic strain against OVITO, and cluster analysis against freud (0.006 s against 0.001 s).

The fcc copper has its atoms displaced at random by 0.1 Å along each axis, as at room temperature; the silicon by 0.05 Å. The random points have the density of copper and, with a cutoff of 2 Å, are close to percolation, so that clusters of every size form; points with a neighbor within 1e-4 Å of 2 Å are left out, so that single precision gives the same bonds. OVITO's coordination analysis also counts the neighbors of each atom along with the radial distribution function.

docs.title: How it is measured
docs.text:
• Each program runs in a process of its own, with the same number of threads (MDAPY_NUM_THREADS, OVITO_THREAD_COUNT and freud.parallel.set_num_threads).
  • Before the timings, a separate process computes the case with MDAPY and with the other program and compares the results. With OVITO, which computes in double precision as MDAPY does: the same structure types, cluster sizes, occupancies and bins, floating-point values within 1e-10 (1e-8 for Steinhardt parameters weighted by Voronoi faces, whose areas come from two tessellations), for neighbor lists the same number of neighbors of each atom and the same sum of their distances, and for Voronoi cells the same volumes and numbers of faces, and with the faces as many of OVITO's bonds at each atom, but for faces of no area that one tessellation of millions of atoms finds and the other not (at most one atom in 100 000). freud computes in single precision, which rounds positions in a box of 600 Å by some 3e-5 Å: values agree within 1e-4; the numbers of neighbors and the bins of the radial distribution function within the pairs closer than 1e-4 Å to a cutoff or the edge of a bin; Steinhardt parameters of the 12 nearest agree with those MDAPY computes from the positions freud has, within 3e-4, for the atoms whose 12th and 13th neighbors are farther apart than 1e-4 Å, nearly all (freud's harmonics in single precision differ by 2e-5 for all but a few atoms in a million, by up to 2e-4 for those); every Voronoi face of freud above 0.01 Å² is one of MDAPY, and the faces freud leaves out, of distant neighbors, are all below 0.02 Å², so its Steinhardt parameters over Voronoi faces agree within 1e-3. The mean squared displacements agree within 1e-10. A program that differs is not timed.
  • Each process first computes the case for 500 atoms, so that loading libraries and starting threads are not timed, then three times for the system; the shortest time counts.
  • The time runs from the call to the result, with every neighbor search. Making the system and converting it into OVITO's data collection or freud's box and points are not timed. OVITO computes a new pipeline each time, so nothing is cached.
  • A process that grows beyond 170 GB or runs for more than 15 minutes is stopped (80 minutes for Steinhardt parameters over Voronoi faces at 2 million atoms, which take OVITO 11 minutes each time), and a size is skipped where the previous one predicts more memory.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
The comparison is benchmarks/comparison.py in the source repository. It needs OVITO (pip install ovito), freud (pip install freud-analysis) and, for the figure, matplotlib.

python benchmarks/comparison.py run                     # every case
python benchmarks/comparison.py run cna voronoi --sizes 4000 32000 --threads 1
python benchmarks/comparison.py run --sizes 4000 32000 256000 2048000 \
    --threads 40 --memory 170 --timeout 900                # as above
python benchmarks/comparison.py table results.json      # Markdown tables
python benchmarks/comparison.py plot results.json ratio.png

run appends one line of JSON per case and size to results.json (the option --output): the machine, the versions, the agreement of each program, and the times and peak memory of each. A new case is a Case in _cases(): how to make its system, the MDAPY call, and for each other program its call and how to compare its result with that of MDAPY.

docs.title: Reading and writing files
docs.text: MDAPY, OVITO and ASE read and write LAMMPS dumps, LAMMPS data files and extended XYZ of the same systems, plain and gzipped, from 4 000 to nearly 10 million atoms. A program is timed only where it reads the positions that MDAPY wrote, or writes a file that MDAPY reads back as the system.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A node of the Triton cluster of Aalto University, alone for the run: two Intel Xeon Gold 6148 (40 cores, two NUMA nodes), 191 GB, Linux. Python 3.13, MDAPY 2.0.0 built with GCC 12.3, OVITO 3.17.1 and ASE 3.29.0 from pip. The analyses ran on another node, with Intel Xeon Gold 6230, so their times do not compare with these.

How many times faster MDAPY is: a row for each case, the largest gain on top, and a point for each size, larger and darker for more atoms; the number on the right is the speed-up at the largest size.

docs.title: What they show
docs.text:
• OVITO: from 32 000 atoms on, MDAPY reads the three formats 4.7 to 24 times faster and writes them 8.2 to 24 times faster. At 4 000 atoms MDAPY reads 1.0 to 1.3 times faster and writes 2.0 to 3.6 times faster.
  • ASE: from 32 000 atoms on, MDAPY reads 27 to 308 times faster and writes 43 to 130 times faster; at 4 000 atoms, 4.9 to 12 and 9.4 to 13 times. ASE reads a data file of nearly 10 million atoms in 45 s and 18 GB of memory.
  • Gzip: MDAPY compresses on all threads. From 256 000 atoms on it writes gzipped files 14 to 35 times faster than OVITO and 48 to 185 times faster than ASE. It reads them 1.1 to 2.0 times faster than OVITO and 3.8 to 14 times faster than ASE: most of that time is decompressing.
  • Nearly 10 million atoms take MDAPY 0.12 to 0.15 s to read in each format, and 0.26 to 0.35 s to write with every digit; gzipped, 3.2 to 3.7 s to read and 1.8 to 2.0 s to write.
