1 1 2 1 3

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Name Type Default Meaning atom_style str from the file Reading: atom style of the Atoms section, when the file does not name it. Writing: the atom style to write. units str from the file "metal" or "real". Reading: overrides the units named in the first line (units = ..., written by write_data), metal if it names none. Writing: the units to write, otherwise those the file was read in (info["lammps"]["units"]), otherwise metal. elements list of str Reading: the element of each atom type, in type order. Writing: the order of the elements as atom types, for a system without a type column. triclinic str "auto" Writing only: how to write the box, see Box.

docs.title: Atoms
docs.text:
Each atom style has these columns, which become the columns of the same name:

Atom style Atoms line atomic id type x y z charge id type charge x y z bond, angle, molecular id molecule type x y z full id molecule type charge x y z

Three integers at the end of every line are the image flags, the image column. The atom type may be a number or a type label of the Atom Type Labels section; the type column holds the number and, when the file has labels, type_label holds the label.

The atom style is taken from the comment of the section keyword, as in Atoms # full. Without it, lines of 5 values are atomic (8 with image flags) and lines of 7 values full (10). Lines of 6 values fit both charge and molecular: they are read as molecular if the header declares bonds, angles, dihedrals or impropers, and otherwise need atom_style=.

Other atom styles, such as sphere or ellipsoid, and the sections of finite-size particles (Ellipsoids, Lines, Triangles, Bodies) raise UnsupportedFormat.

When writing, the style is atom_style=, otherwise the style the file was read with (info["lammps"]["atom_style"]), otherwise the simplest style that holds the system: full with a topology or molecule column and a charge column, molecular with only the first, charge with only the second, and atomic otherwise. A missing molecule column is written as molecule ID 0, which LAMMPS reads as "not in a molecule". IDs are the id column, or 1 to N.

docs.title: Types, masses and elements
docs.text:
Data files have no elements. When reading, every atom type gets an element from the first of these that names one for every type that has atoms:

  1. the elements= option;
  2. the comment after each mass in the Masses section, as in 1 63.546 # Cu;
  3. the atom type labels, when they are element symbols, with the same case;
  4. the masses, each matching exactly one stable element within 0.01 amu.

Otherwise the system has no element column. The masses of the Masses section become the mass column.

When writing, atom types are the type column. Without it, each element is a type, in the order of elements= or else in the order of first appearance. The Masses section takes, for each type, the mass column, otherwise the masses read from a file (info["lammps"]["masses"]), otherwise the standard atomic weight of the element; a type whose atoms are all one element gets the comment # symbol. Types without atoms keep the masses and labels read from the file.

docs.title: Box
docs.text:
A data file has no periodicity: the box is periodic in all directions. A box given by xlo xhi, ylo yhi, zlo zhi and xy xz yz becomes a box with rows (xhi − xlo, 0, 0), (xy, yhi − ylo, 0), (xz, yz, zhi − zlo) and origin (xlo, ylo, zlo). A general triclinic box, given by avec, bvec, cvec and abc origin, keeps its edge vectors and origin unchanged. Missing bounds are −0.5 and 0.5, as in LAMMPS.

When writing, triclinic selects the form:

triclinic Box written "auto" Bounds and tilt factors when a lies along x and b in the xy plane; otherwise the general form. Positions are never rotated. "general" Always the general form, avec bvec cvec abc origin. "restricted" Always bounds and tilt factors; the box, positions and velocities are rotated as by Box.to_lammps.

LAMMPS needs right-handed edge vectors, so for a left-handed box b and c, and the second and third image flags, are swapped; the lattice and the positions are unchanged.

docs.title: Topology, labels and coefficients
docs.text:
Bonds, Angles, Dihedrals and Impropers become the topology, with atom IDs turned into rows; type labels of the Bond, Angle, Dihedral and Improper Type Labels sections become type_label columns of its tables. Bond IDs are not kept: written terms are numbered from 1.

The other sections and header values are kept in info["lammps"] and are written back unchanged:

Key Content atom_style, units as read atom_types, bond_types, ... the type counts of the header masses mass of every atom type type_labels labels of every type, by kind: atom, bond, ... coeffs each coefficient section (Pair Coeffs, PairIJ Coeffs, Bond Coeffs, the class2 sections, ...), as its style comment and its lines extra the extra ... per atom header values

The timestep of the first line becomes info["timestep"]. Coefficients are not converted between units, so a file read in one unit system cannot be written with coefficients in the other.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
units Velocities in the file Everything else metal Å/ps as in MDAPY real Å/fs, converted to and from Å/ps as in MDAPY (g/mol equals amu; coefficients are not converted)

The conversion moves the decimal point, so it adds no rounding. Other unit systems raise UnsupportedFormat; units="metal" reads such a file with its numbers unchanged.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: • LAMMPS documentation of read_data and write_data: https://docs.lammps.org/read_data.html, https://docs.lammps.org/write_data.html

docs.title: LAMMPS dump
docs.text:
The format lammps-dump reads and writes the text dump files of the LAMMPS dump atom and dump custom commands, following LAMMPS stable_30Sep2026, with any number of frames. Files with extension .dump or .lammpstrj, or names starting with dump., are recognized.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.io import read, write

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
system = mp.System(
    positions=rng.random((4, 3)) * 5,
    box=mp.Box(5.0),
    elements=["Cu", "Cu", "Zr", "Zr"],
).with_columns(velocities=rng.standard_normal((4, 3)))
frames = (
    system.with_columns(positions=system["positions"] + 0.1 * k).with_info(
        timestep=100 * k
    )
    for k in range(3)
)
write("run.dump", frames)
last = read("run.dump", frame=-1)
last.info["timestep"]  # 200

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Name Type Default Meaning units str from the file, else "metal" "metal" or "real". Reading: overrides ITEM: UNITS. Writing: the units of the file. elements list of str Reading: the element of each atom type, in type order, for dumps without an element column. Writing: the order of the elements as atom types, for a system without a type column; without it, the order in which the elements first appear over the frames, so that an element keeps its type in every frame. triclinic str "auto" Writing only: "auto", "general" or "restricted", as for LAMMPS data. columns list of str all columns Writing only: the columns to write besides id, type, element, type_label and the positions.

docs.title: Frames
docs.text:
Each frame has these items, as LAMMPS writes them:

Item Meaning In MDAPY ITEM: UNITS unit system; LAMMPS writes it only in the first frame, and it applies to all ITEM: TIME elapsed time, in ps (metal) or fs (real) info["time"], ps ITEM: TIMESTEP timestep info["timestep"] ITEM: NUMBER OF ATOMS number of rows ITEM: BOX BOUNDS the box and its boundary flags box ITEM: ATOMS the names of the columns the columns

A boundary flag pp makes a direction periodic; f, s and m flags do not. A triclinic box (xy xz yz) is written by LAMMPS as its bounding box, from which the box is recovered as described in the LAMMPS documentation of triclinic boxes; a general triclinic box (abc origin) keeps its edge vectors and origin. The same forms are written. Dumps of other styles (local, cfg, yaml, xyz) and binary dumps raise UnsupportedFormat; xyz dumps can be read as extended XYZ.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
Dump columns MDAPY column Conversion id id type type element element typelabel type_label mol molecule q charge mass mass x y z, else xs ys zs, else xu yu zu, else xsu ysu zsu positions scaled coordinates become Cartesian ix iy iz image vx vy vz velocities real: Å/fs to Å/ps, in decimal fx fy fz forces real: kcal/mol/Å to eV/Å name[1] ... name[k] name, an array column

Vectors need all three components. Other columns, including the coordinate sets not used for the positions, keep their names and values; they are read as int64 when their name starts with i_ and as float64 otherwise. Rows keep the order of the file.

When writing, id (or 1 to N), type (from the type column, or from the elements as for LAMMPS data), element and typelabel if present, and x y z come first, followed by mol, q, mass, ix iy iz, vx vy vz and fx fy fz for the columns that exist, and then every other numeric column under its own name, array columns as name[1] to name[k]. Booleans are written as 0 and 1. The first frame starts with ITEM: UNITS; ITEM: TIME is written when info has time. Other info values are not written.

  • Triclinic boxes in LAMMPS: https://docs.lammps.org/Howto_triclinic.html

docs.title: MDAPY files
docs.text:
The format mdapy (extension .mdapy) stores one or more systems exactly as they are in memory: every column with its type, the box, the information and the topology. It is a ZIP archive of Parquet tables, so its contents can also be read with any Parquet reader, without MDAPY.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.io import read, write

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
system = mp.System(
    positions=rng.random((4, 3)) * 5,
    box=mp.Box(5.0),
    elements=["Cu", "Cu", "Zr", "Zr"],
)
frames = [system.with_info(energy=-3.5 - 0.1 * k, step=k) for k in range(3)]
write("run.mdapy", frames)
last = read("run.mdapy", frame=-1)
assert last.table.equals(frames[-1].table)

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
Member Content manifest.json format ("mdapy"), version (1), the MDAPY version that wrote it, the time, the number of frames and the units. frames.parquet One row per frame: frame, atoms (number of atoms), member (its table of atoms), topology (its topology, or null), box_matrix, box_origin, box_pbc, info (all information, as JSON), and typed columns info.<key>. atoms/00000000.parquet, ... The table of each frame. Its Parquet metadata also holds the box, the information and the topology of the frame. topology/00000000/bonds.parquet, ... The bonds, angles, dihedrals and impropers of a topology, written once for consecutive frames that share it.

The typed columns info.<key> repeat the information that every frame has with the same simple type: a number, boolean or text, or a numeric array of one shape. They make quantities of a whole trajectory readable without its atoms:

import io
import zipfile
import polars as pl

with zipfile.ZipFile("run.mdapy") as archive:
    frames_table = pl.read_parquet(io.BytesIO(archive.read("frames.parquet")))
frames_table["info.energy"].to_list()  # [-3.5, -3.6, -3.7]

The members are stored without further compression; the Parquet tables are compressed with zstd. Members have a fixed date, so writing the same systems gives the same members.

docs.title: What is kept
docs.text:
• Columns: every column with its type, including the element type, arrays of any shape, every width of integers and reals such as int8 and float32, and text.
  • Information: numbers, booleans, text, None, NumPy arrays with their type and shape (including 0-dimensional and empty arrays), nested mappings and sequences, and NaN and infinities. NumPy scalars become Python numbers. Other values raise InvalidParameter.
  • Box and topology, with the type labels and extra columns of its tables.

docs.title: Files that were not closed
docs.text:
The archive is completed when writing ends. If the writing program stops earlier, for example when a simulation is killed, the archive has no directory, frames.parquet or manifest. MDAPY then reads the complete members of atoms in order and takes each frame's box, information and topology from their metadata, so every frame written completely is read. This works for uncompressed files.

A file written by a newer MDAPY with a higher version raises UnsupportedFormat.

docs.title: VASP OUTCAR
docs.text:
The format outcar reads the OUTCAR files of VASP, one frame per ionic step of a single point, a relaxation or molecular dynamics, with the forces, the energy and the virial of each. Files named OUTCAR*, or with extension .outcar, are recognized. MDAPY reads OUTCAR files but does not write them.

from mdapy.io import read, read_trajectory

steps = read_trajectory("OUTCAR")  # one frame per ionic step
last = read("OUTCAR", frame=-1)
last["forces"]  # (N, 3) eV/Å
last.info["energy"]  # eV, the free energy TOTEN
last.info["virial"]  # (3, 3) eV
last.info["converged"]  # whether the electronic loop reached EDIFF

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
In the OUTCAR In MDAPY POTCAR: lines, each written twice, and ions per type element; a type of no ions is allowed direct lattice vectors, the last before the positions of a step box.matrix; periodic in all directions POSITION ... TOTAL-FORCE (eV/Angst) positions (Å) and forces (eV/Å) Total of FORCE on cell =-STRESS (eV), when VASP computed the stress (ISIF ≥ 1) info["virial"], (3, 3) free energy TOTEN info["energy"] (eV), the free energy, of which the forces are the slope aborting loop because EDIFF is reached in the step info["converged"]

Every ionic step is read, whether its electronic loop converged or not, so that a single point that did not converge still gives its atoms; info["converged"] tells which steps reached EDIFF, and a training set keeps those (see Training sets from VASP).

A step ends at its line FREE ENERGIE OF THE ION-ELECTRON SYSTEM; the lines of the machine-learned force field of VASP 6, which start with ML, are not steps. A step cut short at the end of the file is left out. Numbers that VASP writes without a space between them, as -10293.69148-10013.02274, are read apart.

The stress in GPa is -virial / volume (see Units and conventions), the same as that of ASE, which takes it from the line in kB. ASE's get_potential_energy() gives the energy extrapolated to zero smearing, and get_potential_energy(force_consistent=True) the free energy TOTEN that MDAPY reads.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: FileFormatError at the line of the fault for: no line of ions per type before the first step, one that cannot be read, POTCAR lines that do not match the ions per type, an unknown element, a step without lattice vectors, positions and forces or free energy, and a line with fewer numbers than it should have.

docs.text:

  • VASP and the VASP calculator

docs.title: PDB
docs.text:
The format pdb reads the files of the Protein Data Bank: the atoms of each model, their names and residues, the cell and the bonds of the CONECT records. Files with extension .pdb or .ent are recognized. MDAPY reads PDB files but does not write them.

from mdapy.io import read
from mdapy.visualization import render

text = """\
HETATM    1  C1  ETH A   1       1.168  -0.400   0.000  1.00  0.00           C
HETATM    2  C2  ETH A   1       0.000   0.559   0.000  1.00  0.00           C
HETATM    3  O1  ETH A   1      -1.190  -0.228   0.000  1.00  0.00           O
HETATM    4  H1  ETH A   1      -1.947   0.382   0.000  1.00  0.00           H
HETATM    5  H2  ETH A   1       0.043   1.208   0.887  1.00  0.00           H
HETATM    6  H3  ETH A   1       0.043   1.208  -0.887  1.00  0.00           H
HETATM    7  H4  ETH A   1       2.116   0.145   0.000  1.00  0.00           H
HETATM    8  H5  ETH A   1       1.129  -1.037   0.886  1.00  0.00           H
HETATM    9  H6  ETH A   1       1.129  -1.037  -0.886  1.00  0.00           H
CONECT    1    2    7    8    9
CONECT    2    1    3    5    6
CONECT    3    2    4
END
"""
with open("ethanol.pdb", "w") as f:
    f.write(text)

ethanol = read("ethanol.pdb")
ethanol["atom_name"]  # C1, C2, O1, H1, ...
ethanol.topology.bonds  # the eight bonds of CONECT
render(
    ethanol,
    "images/ethanol.png",
    representation="ball_and_stick",
    box=False,  # the box about a molecule
    view=(0.3, 0.5, -1.0),
    width=500,
    height=400,
    legend=True,
)

Ethanol read from the PDB text above: carbon (gray), oxygen (red) and hydrogen (white).

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
Record Columns In MDAPY CRYST1 a, b, c in 7–33, α, β, γ in 34–54 box.matrix: a along x, b in the xy plane; periodic in all directions ATOM, HETATM serial 7–11 id; the number of the atom where the serial is not a number atom name 13–16 atom_name residue name 18–20, residue number 23–26 residue, residue_number x, y, z 31–54 positions element 77–78 element; without one, the element of the atom name: its second column when the first is blank or a digit (CA is carbon, 1HB hydrogen), else its first two letters if they are an element (CL1 is chlorine), else its first MODEL, ENDMDL one frame per model; a file without MODEL is one frame CONECT serials 7–31 bonds of the Topology, each pair once, by id END the end of the frame

The CRYST1 record before the first atom or model gives the cell of every model, unless a model has its own. Without a CRYST1 record, or with one of 1 Å, as some programs write for molecules, the box encloses the atoms and is not periodic. Other records, and the alternate locations, chains, occupancies and temperature factors of atoms, are left out.

The bonds are those of CONECT only; OVITO also bonds atoms close enough, as covalent_bonds does.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: FileFormatError at the line of the fault for: a cell parameter or coordinate that is not a number, an atom record that ends before its coordinates, an atom whose element cannot be told, a CONECT record with a word that is not a serial, and a bond to an atom the model lacks.

docs.title: VASP POSCAR
docs.text:
The format poscar reads and writes the POSCAR and CONTCAR files of VASP, one structure per file. Files named POSCAR* or CONTCAR*, or with extension .vasp or .poscar, are recognized.

import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.io import read, write

si = mp.System(
    positions=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [1.3575, 1.3575, 1.3575]],
    box=mp.Box([[0.0, 2.715, 2.715], [2.715, 0.0, 2.715], [2.715, 2.715, 0.0]]),
    elements=["Si", "Si"],
).with_columns(movable=[[False, False, False], [True, True, True]])
write("POSCAR", si)
same = read("POSCAR")

writes

written by MDAPY
1.0
0.0 2.715 2.715
2.715 0.0 2.715
2.715 2.715 0.0
Si
2
Selective dynamics
Direct
0 0 0 F F F
0.24999999999999997 0.25 0.25 T T T

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Name Type Default Meaning elements list of str Reading only: the elements of the species, for files without a line of element symbols (VASP 4). direct bool True Writing only: write fractional (Direct) coordinates; False writes Cartesian coordinates.

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
Line Meaning In MDAPY 1 comment info["comment"] 2 scaling factor: one number, a negative number giving the cell volume in Å3, or three numbers scaling x, y and z applied to the box and Cartesian coordinates 3–5 lattice vectors box.matrix; the box is periodic in all directions 6 element symbols; POTCAR labels such as Na_pv or Na_pv/6a2f546d name the element before _ element 7 number of atoms of each element 8 optional Selective dynamics (first letter S) next Direct, or Cartesian (first letter C or K) N lines coordinates, and with selective dynamics three flags T (may move) or F positions, movable

Words after the coordinates and flags, such as site labels, and text after ! are ignored. A VASP 4 file, which has no line of element symbols, needs elements=.

A CONTCAR may continue with velocities: the line after the coordinates gives their coordinates (Direct if it starts with D, Cartesian otherwise; VASP leaves it blank and ASE writes Cartesian), followed by one line per atom in Å/fs, which become velocities in Å/ps. The lattice velocities and vectors of a variable-cell run (a line starting with L) and the predictor-corrector block of molecular dynamics are skipped.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text: VASP needs the atoms of each element together. Atoms are grouped by element in the order of first appearance, keeping their order within an element, so a system whose elements are already grouped keeps its order. A POSCAR has no box origin: coordinates are written relative to the origin of the box, and the box read back has its origin at zero. Fractional coordinates are computed from the Cartesian positions, so they can differ from round numbers in the last digit, as in the example above. The comment line is info["comment"] or "written by MDAPY". The scaling factor is 1. With a movable column (three booleans per atom) the file has selective dynamics, and with velocities a velocity block in Å/fs after a blank line, as VASP writes it.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• POSCAR in the VASP wiki: https://www.vasp.at/wiki/index.php/POSCAR
  • CONTCAR in the VASP wiki: https://www.vasp.at/wiki/index.php/CONTCAR

docs.title: Ackland–Jones analysis
docs.text:
AcklandJonesAnalysis gives each atom the crystal structure of its neighborhood, fcc, hcp, bcc, icosahedral or other, from the distribution of the angles between the bonds to its neighbors.

import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.identify import AcklandJonesAnalysis

# bcc iron of 5 x 5 x 5 cubic cells
system = build_crystal("bcc", 2.866, elements="Fe", repeat=(5, 5, 5))

result = AcklandJonesAnalysis().compute(system)
result.counts()  # {'other': 0, 'fcc': 0, 'hcp': 0, 'bcc': 250, 'ico': 0}

In a relaxed polycrystal of iron:

from mdapy.build import build_crystal, build_polycrystal
from mdapy.calculators import EAM
from mdapy.simulation import minimize
from mdapy.visualization import render

grains = build_polycrystal(
    build_crystal("bcc", 2.866, elements="Fe"),
    mp.Box(50.0),
    5,
    seed=4,
    min_distance=1.6,
)
grains = minimize(grains, EAM.zhou(["Fe"]), max_force=0.05, max_steps=300).system
structures = AcklandJonesAnalysis().compute(grains)
render(
    grains,
    "images/ackland-jones.png",
    color=structures,
    width=800,
    height=600,
    legend=True,
)

Five grains of bcc iron (blue) after a short relaxation. The atoms of the boundaries take any type, mostly other (white) but also fcc (green), hcp (red) and ico (yellow): the analysis looks at the angles between bonds and knows nothing of grains.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: AcklandJonesAnalysis() has no parameters. compute(system, *, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis. A given neighbor list must hold the 14 nearest neighbors of every atom.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: A StructureResult with the types of common neighbor analysis: other, fcc, hcp, bcc and ico.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: compute raises InvalidParameter for a neighbor list that does not hold the 14 nearest neighbors.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The analysis takes the 14 nearest neighbors of an atom. With \(r_0^2\) the mean squared distance of the 6 nearest, \(n_0\) and \(n_1\) count the neighbors closer than \(\sqrt{1.45}\, r_0\) and \(\sqrt{1.55}\, r_0\). The cosines of the angles between every two of the \(n_0\) bonds fall into eight bins with the bounds −1, −0.945, −0.915, −0.755, −0.195, 0.195, 0.245, 0.795 and 1, which count \(\chi_0, \dots, \chi_7\). The deviations from the ideal structures are

\[ \begin{aligned} \delta_\mathrm{bcc} &= \frac{0.35\, \chi_4}{\chi_5 + \chi_6 - \chi_4}, \\ \delta_\mathrm{cp} &= \Big|1 - \frac{\chi_6}{24}\Big|, \\ \delta_\mathrm{fcc} &= \frac{0.61}{6} \big(|\chi_0 + \chi_1 - 6| + \chi_2\big), \\ \delta_\mathrm{hcp} &= \frac{1}{12} \big(|\chi_0 - 3| + |\chi_0 + \chi_1 + \chi_2 + \chi_3 - 9|\big), \end{aligned} \]

with \(\delta_\mathrm{bcc} = 0\) when \(\chi_0 = 7\), \(\delta_\mathrm{fcc} = 0\) when \(\chi_0 = 6\), \(\delta_\mathrm{hcp} = 0\) when \(\chi_0 \le 3\), and no bcc when \(\chi_5 + \chi_6 = \chi_4\). The atom is then, checked from the top down:

Condition Type \(\chi_7 > 0\) other \(\chi_4 < 3\) ico when \(11 \le n_1 \le 13\), else other \(\delta_\mathrm{bcc} \le \delta_\mathrm{cp}\) bcc when \(n_1 \ge 11\), else other \(11 \le n_1 \le 12\) fcc when \(\delta_\mathrm{fcc} < \delta_\mathrm{hcp}\), else hcp otherwise other

These are the rules of the original implementation, which LAMMPS runs with legacy yes. An atom with fewer than 6 neighbors, as in a system without periodic directions of fewer than 7 atoms, is other.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• LAMMPS compute ackland/atom.

Please cite

Ackland and Jones (2006).

docs.title: Atomic strain
docs.text:
AtomicStrain measures the local deformation of each atom between a reference configuration and the current one: the von Mises shear and volumetric strains and, when asked for, the strain tensor and the non-affine displacement \(D^2_\text{min}\).

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.analysis import AtomicStrain
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

a = 3.615
reference = build_crystal("fcc", a, elements="Cu", repeat=(4, 4, 4))

# the crystal sheared by 2 % with its box
shear = np.array([[1, 0.02, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]])
current = reference.with_box(
    mp.Box(reference.box.matrix @ shear.T), scale_positions=True
)

strain = AtomicStrain(reference, cutoff=3.0)
result = strain.compute(current)
result.shear  # von Mises shear strain, the same for every atom here
current = current.with_columns(result)  # shear_strain, volumetric_strain

# also the strain tensor and the non-affine displacement
result = AtomicStrain(reference, 3.0, strain_tensor=True, d2min=True).compute(current)
result.strain_tensor[0]  # (3, 3) of the first atom

# many frames against one reference: find its neighbors once
neighbors = mp.NeighborList.build(reference, 3.0)
strain = AtomicStrain(reference, cutoff=3.0, neighbors=neighbors)

A rod of copper twisted about its axis shears more the farther from the axis:

from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.visualization import render

crystal = build_crystal("fcc", a, elements="Cu", repeat=(10, 10, 20))
center = crystal.box.matrix.diagonal() / 2
p = crystal["positions"] - center
rod = crystal.filter(np.hypot(p[:, 0], p[:, 1]) < 15)
rod = rod.with_box(mp.Box(crystal.box.matrix, pbc=False))

p = rod["positions"] - center
angle = 0.004 * p[:, 2]  # radians, growing along the axis
twisted = rod.with_columns(positions=center + np.column_stack([
    p[:, 0] * np.cos(angle) - p[:, 1] * np.sin(angle),
    p[:, 0] * np.sin(angle) + p[:, 1] * np.cos(angle),
    p[:, 2],
]))  # fmt: skip
shear = AtomicStrain(rod, cutoff=3.0).compute(twisted).shear
render(twisted, "images/atomic-strain.png", atoms=p[:, 1] < 0, color=shear, colormap="plasma",
       box=False, view=(0.5, -1, -0.3), width=900, height=600, legend="shear strain")  # fmt: skip

The rod cut along its axis: the von Mises shear strain grows from zero on the axis (dark) to about 0.03 at the surface (yellow), half the twist of 0.004 rad/Å times the distance from the axis.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning reference System the reference configuration, with the same atoms as the systems to compare: matched by the id column where both have one, else in the same order cutoff float64 Å the neighbors closer than it in the reference define the neighbor vectors affine bool False measure the current vectors in the reference box, which removes the homogeneous deformation of the box strain_tensor bool False also give the strain tensor of each atom d2min bool False also compute the non-affine squared displacement of each atom neighbors NeighborList None neighbors of the reference within at least cutoff, used for every configuration; without, compute finds them as it goes each time

compute(system, *, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the current configuration: the atoms of the reference, each moved by less than half the box. Positions may be wrapped back into the box.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A StrainResult:

Attribute Type Unit Meaning shear (N,) float64 the von Mises shear strain \(\eta_\text{s}\), NaN where the reference neighbors do not span three dimensions; its column shear_strain volumetric (N,) float64 the volumetric strain \(\operatorname{tr}\eta / 3\); its column volumetric_strain strain_tensor (N, 3, 3) float64 the Green–Lagrange strain \(\eta\), with strain_tensor, else None d2min (N,) float64 Å² the non-affine squared displacement \(D^2_\text{min}\), with d2min, else None; its column d2min

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for a cutoff that is not positive; compute raises it for a system with another number of atoms or other periodic directions than the reference, or repeated ids; MissingProperty for an atom whose id the reference does not have.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The neighbors of atom \(i\) are the atoms closer than the cutoff in the reference, periodic images included, at the vectors \(\mathbf d^0_j\). Their current vectors \(\mathbf d_j\) follow from each atom's displacement, taken by the nearest periodic image in fractional coordinates, in the current box or, with affine, in the reference box. The deformation gradient minimizes \(\sum_j |\mathbf d_j - F \mathbf d^0_j|^2\):

\[ F = \Big(\sum_j \mathbf d_j \mathbf d^{0\,T}_j\Big)\Big(\sum_j \mathbf d^0_j \mathbf d^{0\,T}_j\Big)^{-1}, \qquad \eta = \tfrac{1}{2}(F^T F - I), \] \[ \eta_\text{s} = \sqrt{\eta_{xy}^2 + \eta_{xz}^2 + \eta_{yz}^2 + \tfrac{1}{6}\big[(\eta_{xx}-\eta_{yy})^2 + (\eta_{yy}-\eta_{zz})^2 + (\eta_{xx}-\eta_{zz})^2\big]}, \qquad D^2_\text{min} = \sum_j |\mathbf d_j - F\mathbf d^0_j|^2 . \]

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• OVITO Atomic strain.

Please cite

Shimizu et al. (2007); for \(D^2_\text{min}\), Falk and Langer (1998).

docs.title: Bond angle distribution
docs.text:
BondAngleDistribution counts the angles between the bonds of each atom, in total and for each triplet of elements.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import BondAngleDistribution
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

# fcc copper of 3 x 3 x 3 cubic cells
system = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(3, 3, 3))

angles = BondAngleDistribution(cutoff=3.0, bins=180).compute(system)
# per atom, 24, 12, 24 and 6 angles at 60, 90, 120 and 180 degrees
angles.angle, angles.counts
angles.triplet("Cu", "Cu", "Cu")  # the angles at Cu between two Cu neighbors

The three close-packed and body-centered lattices, each shaken by 0.05 Å:

from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.visualization import plot

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
crystals = {
    "fcc": (build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(5, 5, 5)), 3.0),
    "bcc": (build_crystal("bcc", 2.87, elements="Fe", repeat=(6, 6, 6)), 2.7),
    "hcp": (build_crystal("hcp", 3.21, elements="Mg", repeat=(6, 6, 4)), 3.6),
}
with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    for name, (crystal, cutoff) in crystals.items():
        shaken = crystal.with_columns(
            positions=crystal["positions"] + rng.normal(0, 0.05, (len(crystal), 3))
        )
        result = BondAngleDistribution(cutoff=cutoff, bins=180).compute(shaken)
        ax.plot(result.angle, result.density, label=name)
    ax.set_xlabel("Bond angle (°)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Density (1/°)")
    ax.legend(frameon=False)
    plot.save(fig, "images/bond-angles", formats=("png",))

fcc and hcp share their angles at 60°, 90°, 120° and 180° and differ by those near 109° and 146° that only hcp has; bcc, with its 8 nearest neighbors, has 70.5°, 109.5° and 180°.

For water, BondAngleDistribution(cutoffs={("O", "H"): 1.2}) keeps only the O–H bonds and triplet("O", "H", "H") gives the H–O–H angles.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning cutoff float64 None Å bonds are shorter than it bins int32 180 number of bins of equal width from 0 to 180 degrees cutoffs dict of (str, str) to float64 None Å instead of cutoff, a bond length for each pair of elements (a, b), in either order; pairs not given are never bonded

compute(system, *, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis. A given neighbor list must reach the largest cutoff; without one, the bonds are found and used at once, never stored. Partial counts and cutoffs need an element column.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A BondAngleResult:

docs.text: Every two bonds \(ij\) and \(ik\) of an atom \(i\) give the angle \(\theta_{jik}\) between the vectors to \(j\) and \(k\), counted in the bin \(\lfloor \theta / \Delta\theta \rfloor\); an atom with \(n\) bonds gives \(n(n - 1)/2\) angles. Bonds join atoms closer than the cutoff of their pair of elements, also across periodic boundaries.

docs.title: Bond length distribution
docs.text:
BondLengthDistribution counts the lengths of the bonds of a topology, in total and for each pair of elements, as OVITO's bond length distribution. The bonds come from a file, such as a LAMMPS data file, or from create_bonds.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import BondLengthDistribution
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.transform import create_bonds

# a silicon-germanium alloy on the diamond lattice, its atoms shaken by 0.05 Å
alloy = build_crystal("diamond", 5.53, elements="Si", repeat=(4, 4, 4))
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
alloy = alloy.with_columns(
    element=rng.choice(["Si", "Ge"], size=len(alloy)),
    positions=alloy["positions"] + rng.normal(0, 0.05, (len(alloy), 3)),
)
bonded = create_bonds(alloy, 2.8)

lengths = BondLengthDistribution(cutoff=2.8, bins=60).compute(bonded)
lengths.length, lengths.counts  # bin centers in Å, bonds in each bin
lengths.bond_lengths  # the length of each bond
lengths.pair("Si", "Ge")  # the Si-Ge bonds

The total distribution and its three pairs:

from mdapy.visualization import plot

with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    ax.plot(lengths.length, lengths.counts, color="black", label="all")
    for a, b in [("Si", "Si"), ("Si", "Ge"), ("Ge", "Ge")]:
        ax.plot(lengths.length, lengths.pair(a, b), label=f"{a}–{b}")
    ax.set_xlim(2.0, 2.8)
    ax.set_xlabel("Bond length (Å)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Bonds")
    ax.legend(frameon=False)
    plot.save(fig, "images/bond-lengths", formats=("png",))

The bonds of 2.39 Å on the common lattice, spread by the shaking; the random alloy has twice as many Si–Ge bonds as Si–Si or Ge–Ge bonds.

docs.title: CHILL+
docs.text:
ChillPlus tells hexagonal ice, cubic ice, clathrate hydrates and their interfaces from liquid water, by the correlation of the bond order of neighboring molecules.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.identify import ChillPlus

# the oxygen atoms of hexagonal ice, one per molecule, the upper half
# disordered like liquid water
ice = build_crystal("lonsdaleite", 4.52, c=7.36, elements="O", repeat=(8, 8, 6))
upper = ice["positions"][:, 2] > 22.0
shake = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(0, 0.5, (len(ice), 3))
water = ice.with_columns(positions=ice["positions"] + shake * upper[:, None])

result = ChillPlus(cutoff=3.5).compute(water)
result.counts()  # {'other': 719, 'hexagonal_ice': 698, ...}
water = water.with_columns(result)  # the column 'chill_plus_structure'

For water of more than oxygen, water.filter(element="O") keeps one atom per molecule. Each molecule in the color of its structure:

from mdapy.visualization import render

side = [0, -1, 0.15]  # seen from the side, slightly from above
render(
    water,
    "images/chill-plus.png",
    color=result,
    view=side,
    width=800,
    height=600,
    legend=True,
)

Hexagonal ice (light blue) under its disordered half (white, other). The molecules at the two interfaces, the lower one across the periodic boundary, are interfacial ice (purple); a few disordered molecules happen to have the bonds of a hydrate (green).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning cutoff float64 3.5 Å neighbors are the molecules closer than it; 3.5 Å for the oxygen atoms of water

compute(system, *, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis; the system holds one atom per molecule, for water its oxygen atoms. A given neighbor list must reach the cutoff.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: A StructureResult with the types below.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for a cutoff that is not positive; compute raises it for a neighbor list that does not fit.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Each molecule \(i\) gets the bond order \(q_{3m}(i) = \sum_j Y_{3m}(\hat{\mathbf r}_{ij})\) over its neighbors \(j\), with the spherical harmonics \(Y_{3m}\) of degree 3, and each bond the correlation

\[ c(i, j) = \frac{\operatorname{Re} \sum_m q_{3m}(i)\, q_{3m}(j)^*}{|q_3(i)|\, |q_3(j)|}. \]

A bond is staggered when \(c < -0.8\) and eclipsed when \(-0.35 < c < 0.25\). A molecule with four neighbors is, checked from the top of the table down:

Index Name Default color Bonds 1 hexagonal_ice light blue 3 staggered and 1 eclipsed 2 cubic_ice orange 4 staggered 3 interfacial_ice purple 3 staggered and no eclipsed, or 2 staggered 4 hydrate green 4 eclipsed 5 interfacial_hydrate yellow-green 3 eclipsed 0 other light grey any other molecule

Please cite

Nguyen and Molinero (2015).

docs.title: Cluster analysis
docs.text:
ClusterAnalysis finds the groups of atoms joined by bonds, also across periodic boundaries, and, when asked for, the positions that keep each group unbroken by the boundaries and the centers of mass and gyration.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.analysis import ClusterAnalysis

# two groups of atoms far apart in a 30 Å box
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
positions = np.vstack([rng.random((20, 3)) * 4, rng.random((10, 3)) * 4 + 15])
system = mp.System(positions, mp.Box(30.0), elements="Cu")

result = ClusterAnalysis(cutoff=3.0).compute(system)
result.sizes  # atoms in each cluster, largest first
system = system.with_columns(result)  # the column 'cluster'

clusters = ClusterAnalysis(cutoff=3.0, unwrap=True, center_of_mass=True, gyration=True)
result = clusters.compute(system)
result.center_of_mass, result.radius_of_gyration  # Å, of each cluster
whole = system.with_columns(
    positions=result.unwrapped
)  # no cluster cut by the boundaries

Copper particles, some of them touching, each cluster in its own color:

from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.visualization import render

crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(22, 22, 22))
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
centers, radii = rng.uniform(15, 65, (9, 3)), rng.uniform(5, 10, 9)
distance = np.linalg.norm(crystal["positions"][:, None] - centers, axis=2)
particles = crystal.filter((distance < radii).any(axis=1))

found = ClusterAnalysis(cutoff=3.0).compute(particles)
found.sizes  # [396, 364, 322, 220, 79, 60, 48]: nine spheres, seven clusters
render(particles, "images/clusters.png", color=found.cluster, colormap="labels",
       box=False, width=800, height=600, legend="cluster")  # fmt: skip

Nine spheres cut from a crystal make seven clusters: the spheres that overlap or touch within the cutoff of 3 Å join into one.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning cutoff float64 None Å atoms closer than it are bonded cutoffs dict of (str, str) to float64 None Å instead of cutoff, a bond length for each pair of elements (a, b), in either order; pairs not given are never bonded unwrap bool False also give the positions with no cluster cut by the periodic boundaries center_of_mass bool False also compute the mass and the center of mass of each cluster gyration bool False also compute the gyration tensor and the radius of gyration of each cluster

compute(system, *, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis. A given neighbor list must reach the largest cutoff; without one, the bonds are found and used at once, never stored. cutoffs need an element column. The masses are the mass column, else those of the elements, else 1 for every atom.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A ClusterResult:

Attribute Type Meaning cluster (N,) int64 the cluster of each atom, numbered from 0 by decreasing size, equal sizes in the order of their first atom; its column cluster sizes (clusters,) int64 the number of atoms of each cluster spanning (clusters,) bool whether the cluster joins a periodic image of itself, spanning the box unwrapped (N, 3) float64 positions in Å with no cluster cut by the periodic boundaries, the first atom of each cluster at its own position; with unwrap, else None masses (clusters,) float64 the mass of each cluster in amu, or its number of atoms without masses; with center_of_mass, else None center_of_mass (clusters, 3) float64 the center of mass of each cluster in Å; with center_of_mass, else None radius_of_gyration (clusters,) float64 the radius of gyration \(R_g\) of each cluster in Å; with gyration, else None gyration_tensor (clusters, 3, 3) float64 the gyration tensor \(G\) of each cluster in Å²; with gyration, else None

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter without exactly one of cutoff and cutoffs, for a cutoff that is not positive or an unknown element; compute raises it for a neighbor list that does not fit, and MissingProperty for cutoffs without an element column.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Two atoms are bonded when closer than the cutoff of their pair of elements; a cluster is a largest set of atoms connected by bonds. An atom without bonds is a cluster of its own.

The unwrapped positions keep the first atom of each cluster where it is and place every other atom at the periodic image next to the atoms it is bonded to. With these positions \(\mathbf u_i\) and the masses \(m_i\) of the atoms of a cluster of mass \(M\),

\[ \mathbf c = \frac{1}{M} \sum_i m_i \mathbf u_i , \qquad G = \frac{1}{M} \sum_i m_i (\mathbf u_i - \mathbf c)(\mathbf u_i - \mathbf c)^T , \qquad R_g = \sqrt{\operatorname{tr} G} . \]

A cluster that joins a periodic image of itself, such as a percolating network or a layer through the box, has no unbroken position: its unwrapped positions, center of mass and gyration depend on the order in which its bonds are taken, and spanning marks it.

docs.title: Common neighbor analysis
docs.text:
CommonNeighborAnalysis gives each atom the crystal structure of its neighborhood: fcc, hcp, bcc, icosahedral or other.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.identify import CommonNeighborAnalysis

# fcc copper of 4 x 4 x 4 cubic cells
a = 3.615
system = build_crystal("fcc", a, elements="Cu", repeat=(4, 4, 4))

result = CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(system)  # adaptive
result.counts()  # {'other': 0, 'fcc': 256, 'hcp': 0, 'bcc': 0, 'ico': 0}
system = system.with_columns(result)  # the column cna_structure

fixed = CommonNeighborAnalysis(cutoff=0.854 * a).compute(system)  # conventional

In a polycrystal the atoms that are not fcc mark the grain boundaries:

from mdapy.build import build_crystal, build_polycrystal
from mdapy.visualization import render, write_png

copper = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu")
grains = build_polycrystal(copper, mp.Box(60.0), 6, seed=4)
structures = CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(grains)
whole = render(grains, color=structures, width=600, height=600, legend=True)
fcc = structures.structure == 1
boundaries = render(
    grains, atoms=~fcc, color=structures, width=600, height=600, legend=True
)
write_png("images/cna.png", np.hstack([whole, boundaries]))

A copper polycrystal of six grains as built, colored by structure: fcc green, other white. Right: the same without the fcc atoms, which leaves the network of grain boundaries.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning cutoff float64 None Å cutoff of the neighbors and of the bonds between them; without it, each atom has its own cutoff (adaptive analysis)

compute(system, *, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis. A given neighbor list must reach the cutoff or, without a cutoff, hold the 14 nearest neighbors of every atom.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A StructureResult with the types

Index Name Default color 0 other light grey 1 fcc green 2 hcp red 3 bcc blue 4 ico yellow

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for a cutoff that is not positive; compute raises it for a neighbor list that does not fit.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Each bond from an atom to one of its neighbors gets a signature of three numbers: the number of neighbors the two atoms have in common, the number of bonds among those common neighbors, and the number of bonds in the largest connected group those bonds form. An atom with 12 neighbors is fcc when all 12 signatures are (4, 2, 1), hcp when six are (4, 2, 1) and six (4, 2, 2), and icosahedral when all are (5, 5, 5). An atom with 14 neighbors is bcc when eight signatures are (6, 6, 6) and six (4, 4, 4). Any other atom is other.

Without cutoff, the analysis is adaptive: each atom has its own cutoff from its nearest neighbors, so strained or hot crystals of any lattice constant need no parameter. For fcc, hcp and icosahedral order it takes the 12 nearest neighbors \(r_1 \le \dots \le r_{12}\) and the cutoff

\[ r_c = \frac{1 + \sqrt 2}{2}\, \frac{1}{12} \sum_{j=1}^{12} r_j , \]

halfway between the first and second shells of fcc; neighbors and bonds between them count when they are no longer than \(r_c\). When that does not give fcc, hcp or icosahedral, it takes the 14 nearest neighbors for bcc and

\[ r_c = \frac{1 + \sqrt 2}{2}\, \frac{1}{14} \Big(\frac{2}{\sqrt 3} \sum_{j=1}^{8} r_j + \sum_{j=9}^{14} r_j\Big). \]

With cutoff, the conventional analysis, the neighbors of an atom are those closer than the cutoff, and an atom must have exactly 12 or 14 of them; the same cutoff decides the bonds between neighbors. For a lattice constant \(a\), a cutoff between the first and second shells of fcc is \(0.854\,a\); for bcc, whose 14 neighbors are its first two shells, a cutoff between the second and third is \(1.207\,a\).

In a system without periodic directions and fewer than 15 atoms, the neighbors of each atom are all the others.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• LAMMPS compute cna/atom, the conventional analysis.

Please cite

Honeycutt and Andersen (1987) and Faken and Jónsson (1994); for the adaptive analysis, also Stukowski (2012).

docs.title: Common neighbor parameter
docs.text:
CommonNeighborParameter measures how symmetrically the common neighbors of each atom and its neighbors are arranged: zero in perfect fcc, bcc and diamond, large at defects and surfaces, defined for any structure.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.identify import CommonNeighborParameter

# fcc copper of 4 x 4 x 4 cubic cells, with one atom missing
crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(4, 4, 4))
system = crystal.filter(np.arange(len(crystal)) > 0)

result = CommonNeighborParameter(cutoff=3.0).compute(system)
result.cnp.max()  # Å^2, at the neighbors of the vacancy
system = system.with_columns(result)  # the column 'cnp'

In a polycrystal, cut in half to show the boundaries inside:

from mdapy.build import build_crystal, build_polycrystal
from mdapy.visualization import render

grains = build_polycrystal(
    build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu"), mp.Box(50.0), 5, seed=4
)
cnp = CommonNeighborParameter(cutoff=3.08).compute(grains).cnp
render(grains, "images/cnp.png", atoms=grains["positions"][:, 0] < 25, color=cnp,
       colormap="plasma", value_range=(0, 20), width=800, height=600, legend="CNP (Å²)")  # fmt: skip

Zero inside the grains (dark blue), up to 20 Å² and more at the boundaries.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning cutoff float64 Å neighbors and common neighbors are closer than it

compute(system, *, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis. A given neighbor list must reach the cutoff.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A CommonNeighborParameterResult:

Attribute Type Unit Meaning cnp (N,) float64 Å² the parameter of each atom, NaN for an atom without neighbors; also its column cnp

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for a cutoff that is not positive; compute raises it for a neighbor list that does not fit.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an atom \(i\) with \(N_i\) neighbors \(j\), the common neighbors \(k\) of \(i\) and \(j\) are the atoms closer than the cutoff to both. With \(\mathbf r_{ik} = \mathbf x_i - \mathbf x_k\),

\[ Q_i = \frac{1}{N_i} \sum_{j} \Bigl| \sum_{k} (\mathbf r_{ik} + \mathbf r_{jk}) \Bigr|^2 . \]

It is zero in perfect fcc, bcc and diamond, and \(2a^2/3\) in ideal hcp of lattice constant \(a\) with the cutoff between its first and second shells. Unlike the centro-symmetry parameter it needs a cutoff rather than a number of neighbors.

Please cite

Tsuzuki et al. (2007).

docs.title: Coordination number
docs.text:
CoordinationNumber counts the neighbors of each atom, in total and by element, within one cutoff or a cutoff for each pair of elements.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.analysis import CoordinationNumber
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

# a CsCl-ordered CuZn crystal of 4 x 4 x 4 cubic cells
system = build_crystal("cscl", 2.95, elements=["Cu", "Zn"], repeat=(4, 4, 4))

result = CoordinationNumber(cutoff=3.2).compute(system)
result.coordination  # 14 for every atom: 8 unlike and 6 like neighbors
result.partial["Zn"]  # neighbors of element Zn
unlike = CoordinationNumber(cutoffs={("Cu", "Zn"): 2.7}).compute(system)
system = system.with_columns(result)  # coordination, coordination_Cu, ...

On a particle, the coordination shows the facets, edges and corners:

from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.visualization import render

crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(12, 12, 12))
center = crystal.box.matrix.diagonal() / 2
inside = np.linalg.norm(crystal["positions"] - center, axis=1) < 18.0
particle = crystal.filter(inside).with_box(mp.Box(12 * 3.615, pbc=False))

coordination = CoordinationNumber(cutoff=3.0).compute(particle).coordination
render(particle, "images/coordination.png", color=coordination, colormap="labels",
       box=False, width=800, height=700, legend="coordination")  # fmt: skip

A sphere of 18 Å radius cut from copper, with one color for each number of neighbors. The inside has 12, the (111) facets 9, the (100) facets 8 and the atoms at edges and corners fewer.

compute(system, *, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis. A given neighbor list must reach the largest cutoff; without one, the neighbors are counted as they are found, never stored. Partial counts and cutoffs need an element column.

docs.title: Centro-symmetry parameter
docs.text:
CentroSymmetryParameter measures how far the neighbors of each atom are from coming in opposite pairs: zero in perfect fcc and bcc, large at surfaces, dislocation cores and stacking faults.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.identify import CentroSymmetryParameter

# fcc copper of 4 x 4 x 4 cubic cells, with one atom missing
crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(4, 4, 4))
system = crystal.filter(np.arange(len(crystal)) > 0)

result = CentroSymmetryParameter(num_neighbors=12).compute(system)
result.csp.max()  # Å^2, at the neighbors of the vacancy
system = system.with_columns(result)  # the column 'csp'

Around a dislocation, the stacking fault and the partial dislocations stand out:

from mdapy.build import build_crystal, edge_dislocation
from mdapy.calculators import EAM
from mdapy.simulation import minimize
from mdapy.visualization import render, write_png

cell = build_crystal(
    "fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", orientation=[(1, -1, 0), (1, 1, -2), (1, 1, 1)]
)
edge = edge_dislocation(cell, (30, 6, 12))
relaxed = minimize(edge, EAM.zhou(["Cu"]), max_force=1e-3, max_steps=3000).system
csp = CentroSymmetryParameter().compute(relaxed).csp

z = relaxed["positions"][:, 2]
shown = (csp > 0.5) & (np.abs(z - z.mean()) < 15)  # not the free surfaces
write_png(
    "images/csp.png",
    render(relaxed, atoms=shown, color=csp, colormap="plasma", value_range=(0, 6),
           view="top", width=1000, height=500, legend="CSP (Å²)"),
)  # fmt: skip

A relaxed edge dislocation in copper seen from above its glide plane, the atoms with a parameter above 0.5 Å²: the stacking fault (yellow, about 5.7 Å²) between the cores of the two Shockley partials (purple, about 1.7 Å²).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning num_neighbors int32 12 number \(N\) of nearest neighbors, even: 12 for fcc, 8 for bcc

compute(system, *, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis. A given neighbor list must hold the num_neighbors nearest neighbors of every atom.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A CentroSymmetryResult:

Attribute Type Unit Meaning csp (N,) float64 Å² the parameter of each atom; also its column csp

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for a num_neighbors that is odd or below 2; compute raises it for a neighbor list that does not hold the num_neighbors nearest neighbors, or a system without periodic directions with no more atoms than num_neighbors.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Of the \(N\) nearest neighbors of an atom, at \(\mathbf r_1, \dots, \mathbf r_N\) from it, every pair \((a, b)\) gives \(|\mathbf r_a + \mathbf r_b|^2\), which is zero for opposite neighbors. The parameter is the sum of the \(N/2\) smallest of these values. It is zero in perfect fcc and bcc and \(a^2\) for the twelve neighbors of ideal hcp of lattice constant \(a\).

The sum of the smallest values is the definition of LAMMPS compute centro/atom; it can use one neighbor in two pairs.

Please cite

Kelchner et al. (1998).

docs.title: Diamond structure
docs.text:
DiamondStructure tells cubic diamond from hexagonal diamond (lonsdaleite) in silicon, germanium, carbon and other tetrahedrally bonded crystals, where common neighbor analysis of the four nearest neighbors says nothing.

import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.identify import DiamondStructure

# cubic diamond silicon of 3 x 3 x 3 cells
system = build_crystal("diamond", 5.431, elements="Si", repeat=(3, 3, 3))

result = DiamondStructure().compute(system)
result.counts()["cubic_diamond"]  # 216

In a polycrystal of silicon:

from mdapy.build import build_crystal, build_polycrystal
from mdapy.visualization import render

grains = build_polycrystal(
    build_crystal("diamond", 5.431, elements="Si"), mp.Box(60.0), 6, seed=4
)
structures = DiamondStructure().compute(grains)
render(
    grains, "images/diamond.png", color=structures, width=1100, height=640, legend=True
)

Six grains of silicon as built: cubic diamond in blue, its first and second neighbors in cyan and green. An atom is cubic diamond only if its second neighbors are in order too; the atoms of the boundaries next to the grains are their neighbors, the others white.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: DiamondStructure() has no parameters. compute(system, *, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis. A given neighbor list must hold the 4 nearest neighbors of every atom.

The types, their numbers and their colors are those of OVITO.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: compute raises InvalidParameter for a neighbor list that does not hold the 4 nearest neighbors, or a system without periodic directions of fewer than 5 atoms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The first neighbors of an atom are its 4 nearest. Each of them has 4 nearest neighbors of its own, one of which must be the atom itself; otherwise the atom is other. The other three of each give the 12 second neighbors of the atom, which form an fcc shell in cubic diamond and an hcp shell in hexagonal diamond. Common neighbor analysis of these 12, with the cutoff \(\frac{1+\sqrt 2}{2}\) times their mean distance, decides: fcc is cubic_diamond and hcp hexagonal_diamond. Then, atom by atom in the order of the system, an atom that is still other and among the 4 nearest of a diamond atom becomes its first neighbor (of cubic or hexagonal diamond, as that atom); after all first neighbors, an atom that is still other and among the 4 nearest of a first neighbor becomes a second neighbor of the same kind. The first atom in order to reach an atom decides its kind.

Please cite

Maras et al. (2016).

docs.title: Dislocation analysis
docs.text:
DislocationAnalysis finds the dislocations of a crystal, by the dislocation extraction algorithm (DXA) of OVITO: lines through the cores, the Burgers vector of each, and the junctions where they meet. Partial dislocations at the edges of stacking faults are found as well. The defects that are not dislocations, such as grain boundaries, free surfaces and voids, make the defect mesh around them.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import DislocationAnalysis
from mdapy.build import dislocation_quadrupole

# two edge dislocations of copper and their opposites, each split into two
# Shockley partials 10 Å apart
system = dislocation_quadrupole(
    "fcc edge", 3.615, (168.4, 121.4, 75.4), (14, 8, 6), elements="Cu", dissociation=10
)
result = DislocationAnalysis("fcc").compute(system)
len(result.lines)  # 4 partials
line = result.lines[0]
line.family  # 1/6<112>: a Shockley partial
line.burgers  # [-1/6, -1/3, 1/6] in the lattice frame, units of a
line.spatial_burgers  # Å, [-1.278, 0, 0.738] along the axes of the box
line.loop, line.infinite  # True, True: straight through the periodic box
line.length  # Å, 26.6
result.lengths()  # Å, {"1/2<110>": 0, "1/6<112>": 106.3, ..., "other": 0}
result.counts()  # atoms, {"other": 120, "fcc": 3630, "hcp": 138, ...}
system = system.with_columns(result)  # dxa_structure, dxa_crystal_cluster

A disc of vacancies in a (111) plane collapses into a Frank loop, which in copper turns into a stacking-fault tetrahedron: six Shockley partials and six stair-rod dislocations along its edges, meeting at junctions.

from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.calculators import EAM
from mdapy.simulation import minimize

copper = build_crystal(
    "fcc",
    3.615,
    elements="Cu",
    orientation=[(1, -1, 0), (1, 1, -2), (1, 1, 1)],
    repeat=(14, 8, 4),
)
p = copper["positions"] - copper.box.matrix.diagonal() / 2
plane = p[np.argmin(np.abs(p[:, 2])), 2]  # the (111) plane through the middle
disc = (np.abs(p[:, 2] - plane) < 0.3) & (np.linalg.norm(p[:, :2], axis=1) < 10)
relaxed = minimize(copper.filter(~disc), EAM.zhou(["Cu"]), max_force=1e-2).system

tetrahedron = DislocationAnalysis("fcc").compute(relaxed)
len(tetrahedron.lines), len(tetrahedron.junctions)  # 12 lines, 6 junctions
tetrahedron.lengths()  # Å, {"1/6<112>": 68.8, "1/6<110>": 56.7, ...}
tetrahedron.lines[0].junctions  # the junctions at its first and last point

The partials with the stacking faults between them, and the tetrahedron, drawn by the renderer in the colors of their families, with a legend of the atoms and the lines shown:

from mdapy.visualization import render, write_png

kinds = {"1/2<110>": "perfect", "1/6<112>": "Shockley", "1/6<110>": "stair-rod",
         "1/3<100>": "Hirth", "1/3<111>": "Frank"}  # fmt: skip


def legend(found, shown):
    """The structures of the atoms shown and the families of the lines."""
    names = {found.names[k]: found.colors[k] for k in np.unique(found.structure[shown])}
    palette = DislocationAnalysis.FAMILY_COLORS[found.crystal]
    for family in sorted({line.family for line in found.lines}):
        names[f"{kinds.get(family, 'other')} {family}"] = palette[family]
    return names


hcp = result.structure == result.names.index("hcp")
not_fcc = tetrahedron.structure != tetrahedron.names.index("fcc")
pictures = [
    render(
        system,
        atoms=hcp,
        color=result,
        legend=legend(result, hcp),
        radius=0.8,
        dislocations=result,
        burgers_vectors=True,
        burgers_scale=5,
        width=640,
        height=500,
    ),
    render(
        relaxed,
        atoms=not_fcc,
        color=tetrahedron,
        legend=legend(tetrahedron, not_fcc),
        radius=0.6,
        dislocations=tetrahedron,
        width=640,
        height=500,
    ),
]
write_png("images/dislocations.png", np.hstack(pictures))

Left: the four Shockley partials (green) with their Burgers vectors (gray arrows), and between each pair the two layers of hcp atoms (red) of its stacking fault, one across the periodic boundary. Right: the stacking-fault tetrahedron of the relaxed Frank loop, Shockley partials (green) and stair-rods (magenta) along its edges, with the hcp atoms of its faces and the other atoms of its corners (white).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning crystal str the crystal: fcc, hcp, bcc, cubic_diamond or hexagonal_diamond circuit_length int32 14 the number of edges of the longest Burgers circuit that finds a line; at least 3 stretch int32 9 the number of edges more a circuit may grow to follow a line perfect_only bool False find perfect dislocations only: the atoms of stacking faults are other, and partials make one line point_separation float64 2.5 how sparse the points along the lines are: each is the mean of a run of the points found, longer where the line is wider; 0 keeps them all smoothing int32 1 the number of smoothing steps of the lines mesh_smoothing int32 8 the number of smoothing steps of the defect mesh interface_mesh bool False also give the interface mesh, on which the circuits run

compute(system, *, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the progress and cancel of every analysis, but no neighbor list. No two atoms may be at the same position.

The structures are those of OVITO's dislocation analysis, found with the crystal: fcc and hcp for fcc or hcp (each the stacking fault of the other), bcc for bcc, cubic and hexagonal diamond for either diamond. Longer circuits find dislocations of wider cores, and take longer.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A DislocationResult:

Attribute or method Type Meaning crystal str the crystal analyzed lines tuple of DislocationLine the dislocation lines junctions (J, 3) float64 the points in Å where three or more lines meet, in the box structure (N,) int8 the structure of each atom, an index into names; its column dxa_structure names tuple of str other, fcc, hcp, bcc, cubic_diamond, hexagonal_diamond colors tuple of (3,) float64 the default color of each structure crystal_cluster (N,) int64 the crystal cluster of each atom, −1 for none; its column dxa_crystal_cluster clusters CrystalClusters the crystal clusters defect_mesh TriangleMesh the surface around the defects that are not dislocations, closed over the free ends of the lines, its normals pointing into the crystal defect_atoms (V,) int64 the atom at each vertex of the defect mesh, −1 at the end of a line interface_mesh TriangleMesh or None the mesh between the good crystal and the rest, with interface_mesh=True interface_atoms (V,) int64 or None the atom at each of its vertices lengths() dict of str to float64 the total length of the lines of each family of the crystal in Å, other last total_length float64 the total length of the lines in Å counts() dict of str to int64 the number of atoms of each structure, by name

A DislocationLine:

Attribute Type Meaning points (P, 3) float64 the points along the line in Å, unwrapped: consecutive points are close also across a periodic boundary burgers (3,) float64 the Burgers vector in the lattice frame of its crystal cluster, in units of the lattice constant spatial_burgers (3,) float64 the Burgers vector in Å along the axes of the box, as the crystal cluster is turned and stretched; where the lattice about the line, within 7 Å, is turned from the cluster by more than 3°, as when one cluster holds two grains, as that lattice is turned cluster int32 the crystal cluster of the lattice frame family str the family of the Burgers vector, or other length float64 the length in Å loop bool whether the line closes on itself: a loop, or a line through periodic boundaries infinite bool whether it closes through periodic boundaries junctions (int32, int32) the junctions at its first and last point, −1 for a free end and for the ends of a closed line

The families of Burgers vectors, by crystal:

Crystal Families fcc 1/2<110> perfect, 1/6<112> Shockley, 1/6<110> stair-rod of the Lomer–Cottrell lock, 1/3<100> Hirth, 1/3<111> Frank, 1/6<310> and 1/3<110> the stair-rods where Shockley partials on two {111} planes meet in other ways bcc 1/2<111>, <100>, <110> cubic_diamond 1/2<110>, 1/6<112>, 1/6<110>, 1/3<111> hcp 1/3<11-20>, <0001>, <1-100>, 1/3<1-100>, 1/3<11-23> hexagonal_diamond 1/3<11-20>, <0001>, <1-100>, 1/3<1-100>

A CrystalClusters:

Attribute Type Meaning structure (C,) int8 the structure of each cluster, an index into names sizes (C,) int64 the number of atoms of each orientation (C, 3, 3) float64 the matrix that takes vectors of its lattice frame, in units of the lattice constant, to vectors in Å along the axes of the box

The lattice frame of a cubic crystal is that of its cubic cell; that of hcp and hexagonal diamond has c along z and a1 along x, in units of the cubic lattice constant with the same nearest neighbors (√2 a for hcp). Of the frames the symmetry of the lattice allows, that of a cluster of the crystal is the one closest to the axes of the box, so that the lattice Burgers vectors of a crystal along the box read as usual.

render(system, dislocations=result) draws the lines as tubes in the colors of their families, cut at the periodic boundaries; their colors are DislocationAnalysis.FAMILY_COLORS[crystal]. With burgers_vectors=True an arrow from the middle of each line shows its Burgers vector in space, burgers_scale times as long. mesh=result.defect_mesh draws the defect mesh.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for an unknown crystal, a circuit_length below 3, a stretch, smoothing or mesh_smoothing that is not an integer of at least 0, and a point_separation that is negative or not finite; compute raises it for a periodic box so short that an atom meets its own periodic image or an edge of the mesh spans half of it (replicate the system first).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Grain boundaries. In low-angle grain boundaries and twin boundaries the analysis finds the dislocations well. In general grain boundaries it finds a part of them only, and it is not clear what the lines it finds there are; their number and length depend on which grain the atoms of the boundary are given to. Draw no conclusions from the lines in such boundaries. OVITO says the same of its own analysis.
  • Small loops come out shorter than 2πR, as the lines are smoothed: by 7 % for a radius of 10 Å, by 2 % for 18 Å.
  • Wide partials. With perfect_only, two partials more than about 12 Å apart are not joined into one perfect line, and are left out; larger circuit_length and stretch, such as 20 and 12, reach 20 Å.
  • Disorder. Lines hold in crystals whose atoms are moved at random by 0.15 Å; at 0.2 Å they break, at 0.25 Å none is found. The atoms of copper vibrate by about 0.08 Å at room temperature.
  • Units. Positions are in Å: the test of empty space between atoms takes five times the cutoff as a square of a length, as OVITO does, so that lengths in other units find nothing.
  • Order of the atoms. Where a circuit could go two ways, the order of the atoms decides; another order changes the lengths by about 1 %. For the same order the results are the same on every run and for any number of threads.
  • Turned lattices. Where the lattice about a line is turned by more than 3° from the mean orientation of its cluster, as in a cluster that holds two grains or in a strongly bent crystal, the spatial Burgers vector is that of the lattice about the line. The spatial vectors of lines in differently turned lattices then need not add up to zero at a junction; the lattice vectors burgers of one cluster do.

docs.title: Where the results differ from OVITO
docs.text:
On straight, split and bent dislocations, loops, locks, stacking-fault tetrahedra, twins, low-angle boundaries and crystals at temperature the two programs find the same lines, of the same families and Burgers vectors, with lengths within about 0.5 %. They differ in these ways:

  • Junctions. Where lines meet, one program can give a short junction line where the other gives a node of four lines, or split a line in two; the Burgers vectors add up the same. Two crossing loops of bcc make one node of eight lines in MDAPY and two of four in OVITO, 4 % longer in all.
  • Slivers of crystal. A line traced in a cluster of fewer than 100 atoms, such as the layer of crystal inside an extrinsic fault next to a lock, is given in the largest crystal cluster related to it. OVITO keeps the frame of the sliver, whose orientation is poorly fitted: its Burgers vector there is off by up to 0.5 Å and need not be a lattice vector.
  • Grain boundaries. An atom outside the crystal takes the cluster of most of the crystal atoms around it, where OVITO takes that of the first its tessellation lists. The interface mesh of MDAPY then lies on the atoms of the boundary, OVITO's a layer further out, and MDAPY finds 6 to 11 % more line length in general boundaries; OVITO's own length changes by about 4 % with the order of the atoms.
  • Turned lattices. MDAPY gives the spatial Burgers vector of the lattice about a line, as above; OVITO that of the mean orientation of the cluster.
  • Families. OVITO names the stair-rods 1/6<310> and 1/3<110> of fcc "Other".
  • Ties of the tessellation. In a perfect lattice four atoms on a circle can be split along either diagonal. MDAPY moves the atoms by up to \(10^{-4}\) Å to settle it, OVITO has its own rule: the triangles of the meshes there can differ, their areas do not.
  • Lattice frames. Of the frames the symmetry of the lattice allows, both give a cluster the one closest to the axes of the box; when two are as close, they may take different ones, and the lattice Burgers vectors then differ by a rotation of the lattice, the spatial ones do not.

OVITO's options to analyze the selected atoms only and to mark the atoms of the cores, and its export to CA files, are not here.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The atoms of the crystal are found by common neighbor analysis with adaptive cutoffs, with the rules of OVITO's dislocation analysis, and their neighbors put in the order of the ideal ones of their lattice. Neighboring atoms of one structure whose neighbors map onto each other by a rotation of the lattice make a crystal cluster, with one lattice frame; two clusters that touch, or both touch a third, are related by the rotation between their frames. Each edge of the Delaunay tessellation of the atoms gets an ideal vector, the vector between its atoms in the perfect crystal, along the neighbors of the crystal atoms, at most four steps; an atom of no cluster takes that of most of the crystal atoms it neighbors.

A tetrahedron is good when the ideal vectors of its six edges are known and add up to zero around each of its faces, the rotations between the frames too, the elastic mapping compatible there. The interface mesh is made of the faces between the good tetrahedra and the rest. A Burgers circuit is a closed path of \(n\) edges along it; its Burgers vector

\[ \mathbf b = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \mathsf R_k \, \mathbf v_k \]

adds up the ideal vectors \(\mathbf v_k\) of its edges, each turned by \(\mathsf R_k\) into the frame of the first. Circuits that do not close, \(\mathbf b \neq 0\), enclose dislocations: found shortest first, up to circuit_length edges, each is swept along its line in both directions over the triangles of the mesh, taking them, and the centers of the circuits on the way are the points of the line. Lines whose circuits close in on each other meet in a junction, or, two of them, join; circuits around the holes left between others find the lines missing there. The faces of the mesh no circuit took, closed over the free ends of the lines, are the defect mesh. Burgers vectors are then given in the frame of a cluster of the crystal, each line runs along the axis it runs along most, and the lines are coarsened and smoothed.

The sense of a line and its Burgers vector are those of OVITO, which insert_dislocation and the dislocation models of the structure builder follow too: along +z the analysis finds the Burgers vector put in. In the convention of Hirth and Lothe (FS/RH) it is the opposite.

Please cite

Stukowski and Albe (2010) and Stukowski, Bulatov and Arsenlis (2012).
