docs.title: Atomic displacement
docs.text:
AtomicDisplacement gives the displacement of each atom from its position in a reference configuration, the atoms matched by their ids, across the periodic boundaries by the nearest image.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import AtomicDisplacement
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

reference = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(8, 8, 16))
reference = reference.with_columns(id=np.arange(1, len(reference) + 1))

# the crystal twisted about z: each layer turned by an angle that grows with z
center = reference.box.matrix.diagonal()[:2] / 2
x = reference["positions"]
angle = 0.2 * x[:, 2] / reference.box.matrix[2, 2]
c, s = np.cos(angle), np.sin(angle)
turned = x.copy()
turned[:, 0] = center[0] + c * (x[:, 0] - center[0]) - s * (x[:, 1] - center[1])
turned[:, 1] = center[1] + s * (x[:, 0] - center[0]) + c * (x[:, 1] - center[1])
twisted = reference.with_columns(positions=turned)

result = AtomicDisplacement(reference).compute(twisted)
result.displacement  # (N, 3) Å
result.magnitude  # Å, largest at the top, far from the axis
twisted = twisted.with_columns(result)  # displacement, displacement_magnitude

from mdapy.visualization import render

render(
    twisted,
    "images/displacement.png",
    color="displacement_magnitude",
    colormap="plasma",
    view=[1, -1, 0.6],
    width=500,
    height=600,
    legend="displacement (Å)",
)

The crystal colored by the length of the displacements: zero at the bottom, growing with the height and the distance from the axis.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
AtomicDisplacement(reference, *, minimum_image=True, affine=False)

Name Type Default Meaning reference System the reference configuration minimum_image bool True along each periodic direction, the periodic image of the reference position nearest the atom affine bool False measure in the reference box: the current positions mapped into it first, which removes the homogeneous deformation of the box

compute(system) takes the current configuration. The atoms are matched by the column id when both systems have it, in any order; without ids, the two must have the same atoms in the same order.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
An AtomicDisplacementResult:

Attribute Type Meaning displacement (N, 3) float64 the displacement of each atom in Å, in the order of the system; its column displacement magnitude (N,) float64 its length in Å; its column displacement_magnitude

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: compute raises InvalidParameter for an atom whose id is not in the reference, and, without ids, for systems of different numbers of atoms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The displacement of an atom is \(\mathbf u = \mathbf x - \mathbf x_0\), with \(\mathbf x_0\) its position in the reference. With affine, \(\mathbf x\) is first mapped into the reference box: \(\mathbf x \to (\mathbf x - \mathbf o) H^{-1} H_0 + \mathbf o_0\), with \(H\), \(H_0\) the matrices of the box vectors as rows and \(\mathbf o\), \(\mathbf o_0\) the origins. With minimum_image, the fractional coordinates of \(\mathbf u\) along the periodic vectors are rounded to the nearest integers and those taken away.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• OVITO Displacement vectors, with and without the minimum image and the affine mapping to the reference.
  • Mean squared displacement over a trajectory, and Atomic strain against a reference.

docs.title: Center-of-mass drift
docs.text:
remove_drift moves each frame of a trajectory so that the center of mass of its atoms stays where it is in a reference frame, as OVITO's center of mass correction does. It takes away the drift of the whole system, from a thermostat that does not keep the momentum or a cluster that flies off, before positions are averaged or paths drawn.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.analysis import trajectory_lines
from mdapy.transform import remove_drift
from mdapy.visualization import colormap, render

# ten atoms that wander and drift together through a periodic box
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
box = mp.Box(20.0)
steps = rng.normal(0, 0.3, (200, 10, 3)) + [0.08, 0.05, 0.0]
walk = rng.random((10, 3)) * 20 + np.cumsum(steps, axis=0)
frames = [mp.System(box.wrap(x)[0], box, elements="Ar") for x in walk]

steady = remove_drift(frames)  # the frames moved, read when they are used
colors = colormap(np.arange(10), "labels")  # one for each atom and its path
for name, these in (("drift", frames), ("steady", steady)):
    paths = trajectory_lines(these)  # unwrapped, (10, 200, 3)
    render(
        these[-1].with_columns(positions=paths[:, -1]),
        f"images/{name}.png",
        color=colors,
        radius=0.8,
        lines=paths,
        line_radius=0.12,
        line_color=colors,
        view=(0.0, 0.0, -1.0),
        width=420,
        height=420,
    )

The unwrapped paths of ten atoms over 200 frames, seen along the z axis, each in the color of its atom, and the atoms where they end: with the drift of the whole system toward the upper right (left), and with the center of mass kept where it is in the first frame (right).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
remove_drift(frames, reference=0, *, atoms=None, unwrap=True)

Name Type Default Meaning frames sequence of System the frames, such as a Trajectory, a slice of one or a list reference int32 0 the frame whose center of mass is kept; negative counts from the end atoms mask or indices all the atoms of the first frame whose center of mass is kept, as OVITO's only selected unwrap bool True follow the atoms through the periodic boundaries to find the center of mass, or take the positions as they are

The masses are the mass column of the first frame, else the masses of its elements, else all equal, which gives the geometric center. The atoms are matched by their ids and followed through the periodic boundaries as for the mean squared displacement: by the image flags, or else through the nearest periodic image of each step. OVITO takes the positions as they are, the same as unwrap=False; of wrapped positions, whose center of mass jumps when an atom crosses a boundary, it gives the right drift only after its unwrap trajectories modifier, the same as unwrap=True.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: A sequence of the frames, as long as frames, read when they are used like a Trajectory: indexing with an integer gives one frame, with a slice the frames it selects, and iterating goes through them in turn. Each frame has all its atoms moved by one translation, its other columns and its box unchanged; atoms may stand outside the box after the move, and wrap puts them back. Its shifts are the (T, 3) translations in Å, the drift of the center of mass with the sign turned. The centers of mass are found in one pass over the frames when remove_drift is called.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: remove_drift raises InvalidParameter for no frames, a reference that is not one of the frames, atoms that are not a mask or indices of the first frame, chosen atoms whose masses add up to zero, and frames that do not hold the same atoms, as the mean squared displacement does.

docs.title: Elastic strain
docs.text:
ElasticStrain gives the elastic strain of each atom of a crystal: how its nearest neighbors are stretched and sheared from those of the ideal crystal of given lattice constants, as OVITO's elastic strain calculation does. Unlike the atomic strain, it needs no reference configuration, and it leaves out the slip of dislocations, which moves atoms without straining the lattice.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.analysis import ElasticStrain
from mdapy.build import build_crystal, dislocation_quadrupole
from mdapy.visualization import render

# copper squeezed by 1 % along x: the strain of the deformation
cu = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(5, 5, 5))
squeezed = cu.with_box(mp.Box(cu.box.matrix * [[0.99], [1], [1]]), scale_positions=True)
result = ElasticStrain("fcc", 3.615).compute(squeezed)
result.strain_tensor[0]  # (3, 3), -0.0102 along x
squeezed = squeezed.with_columns(
    result
)  # elastic_strain_structure, elastic_strain, elastic_volumetric_strain

# hcp magnesium of other constants than the ideal ratio
ElasticStrain("hcp", 3.21, c=5.21)

# two dissociated edge dislocations of copper in a periodic box, along their lines
dipole = dislocation_quadrupole("fcc edge", 3.615, (168.4, 121.4, 75.4), (14, 8, 3),
                                elements="Cu", dissociation=10)  # fmt: skip
strain = ElasticStrain("fcc", 3.615).compute(dipole)
render(dipole, "images/elastic-strain.png", color=strain.volumetric, colormap="coolwarm",
       value_range=(-0.02, 0.02), view="top", box=False, width=780, height=740, legend="volumetric strain")  # fmt: skip

The volumetric elastic strain about two edge dislocations of copper of opposite sign, seen along their lines, each split into two Shockley partials with a stacking fault between them: the crystal is squeezed (blue) between their glide planes and stretched (red) beyond them; the atoms of the faults and the cores, which are not fcc, have none (white).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
ElasticStrain(crystal, a, c=None)

Name Type Default Unit Meaning crystal str "fcc", "hcp", "bcc", "cubic_diamond" or "hexagonal_diamond" a float64 Å the lattice constant of the unstrained crystal: of the cubic cell, or a of the hexagonal cell c float64 a √(8/3) Å the lattice constant c of the unstrained hexagonal cell; only for hcp and hexagonal diamond

compute(system, *, progress=None, cancel=None) finds the atoms of the crystal as the dislocation analysis does, with the stacking faults of fcc and hcp in each other's structure and those of the two diamonds in each other's, and their neighbors: the 12 nearest of fcc and hcp, the 14 nearest of bcc, and of the diamonds the 4 nearest and their 3 nearest each.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
An ElasticStrainResult:

Attribute Type Meaning structure (N,) int8 the structure of each atom, an index into names; its column elastic_strain_structure names, colors tuple of str, tuple of (3,) float64 other, fcc, hcp, bcc, cubic_diamond, hexagonal_diamond, and their colors, those of PTM strain_tensor (N, 3, 3) float64 the elastic strain \(\varepsilon\) of each atom of the crystal in the spatial frame, zero for the other atoms; its column elastic_strain volumetric (N,) float64 \(\operatorname{tr}\varepsilon / 3\), zero for the atoms not of the crystal; its column elastic_volumetric_strain

Where OVITO joins crystal regions across a stacking fault of a hexagonal crystal, it keeps the relation between them in single precision, so its strains of those atoms differ from these by up to 1e-7. OVITO can also give the strain in the frame of the lattice and the deformation gradient, which depend on which of the equivalent frames of the lattice it takes for a crystal region; MDAPY gives the strain in the spatial frame only, OVITO's default.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for an unknown crystal, a lattice constant that is not positive, and c for a cubic crystal; compute raises it for a box so short along a periodic direction that an atom meets its own periodic image among its neighbors, which replicating the system along that direction mends.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The neighbors of an atom of the crystal are at the vectors \(\mathbf d_k\), each the nearest periodic image, and are matched to the ideal vectors \(\mathbf v_k\) of the crystal by the bonds among them, as the structure identification orders them. The ideal vectors are those of the cubic cell of constant \(a\); those of hcp and hexagonal diamond, of the cubic crystal with the same nearest neighbors, are stretched along c by \((c/a)/\sqrt{8/3}\). The elastic deformation gradient minimizes \(\sum_k |\mathbf d_k - F \mathbf v_k|^2\):

\[ F = \Big(\sum_k \mathbf d_k \mathbf v_k^T\Big)\Big(\sum_k \mathbf v_k \mathbf v_k^T\Big)^{-1}, \qquad \varepsilon = \tfrac{1}{2}\big(I - F^{-T} F^{-1}\big), \]

the Euler–Almansi strain, which does not depend on how the lattice of the crystal is turned, nor on which of its equivalent frames the ideal vectors are taken in.

  • Atomic strain, against a reference configuration.

Please cite

Stukowski and Arsenlis (2012).

docs.title: Entropy fingerprint
docs.text:
EntropyFingerprint gives the pair entropy fingerprint of each atom, a measure of local order that needs no reference structure: low (more negative) in crystals, high in liquids and gases.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.analysis import EntropyFingerprint
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

# fcc copper of 4 x 4 x 4 cubic cells, slightly disordered
crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(4, 4, 4))
shake = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(0, 0.05, (len(crystal), 3))
system = crystal.with_columns(positions=crystal["positions"] + shake)

result = EntropyFingerprint(cutoff=5.0, sigma=0.2, average_cutoff=3.0).compute(system)
result.entropy  # in units of the Boltzmann constant
system = system.with_columns(result)  # the column entropy_average

In a polycrystal, cut in half:

from mdapy.build import build_crystal, build_polycrystal
from mdapy.visualization import render

grains = build_polycrystal(
    build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu"), mp.Box(50.0), 5, seed=4
)
fingerprint = EntropyFingerprint(cutoff=5.0, sigma=0.2, average_cutoff=3.0).compute(
    grains
)
render(grains, "images/entropy.png", atoms=grains["positions"][:, 0] < 25,
       color=fingerprint.entropy, width=800, height=600, legend="entropy")  # fmt: skip

The averaged entropy is lowest in the ordered grains (dark) and highest at the boundaries and their junctions (green and yellow).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning cutoff float64 Å neighbors are closer than it sigma float64 0.2 Å width of the Gaussian of each neighbor, below cutoff local_density bool False use the density of each atom's neighbors instead of that of the system average_cutoff float64 None Å average each value with those of the neighbors closer than it

compute(system, *, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis. A given neighbor list must reach the larger of cutoff and average_cutoff; without one, the neighbors within cutoff are found and used at once, never stored.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
An EntropyResult:

Attribute Type Meaning entropy (N,) float64 the fingerprint of each atom, in units of the Boltzmann constant; its column entropy, with the options in the name: entropy_average, entropy_local_density, entropy_average_local_density average bool whether the values are averaged

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for a cutoff that is not positive, a sigma not between 0 and the cutoff, or an average_cutoff that is not positive; compute raises it for a neighbor list that does not fit.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For each atom \(i\) a local radial distribution is built from its neighbors \(j\) closer than the cutoff \(r_c\), each smeared by a Gaussian of width \(\sigma\):

\[ g_i(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi\rho r^2} \sum_j \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma} e^{-(r - r_{ij})^2 / 2\sigma^2}, \qquad s_i = -2\pi\rho \int_0^{r_c} \big[g_i \ln g_i - g_i + 1\big]\, r^2 \,\mathrm dr , \]

where \(\rho\) is the number density of the system or, with local_density, the number of neighbors over the volume of the cutoff sphere. \(g_i\) is evaluated at \(r = k\sigma\) up to the cutoff and the integral is the trapezoid rule over those points, as in LAMMPS; where \(g_i < 10^{-10}\) the integrand is \(r^2\). With average_cutoff, \(s_i\) is averaged with the values of the neighbors closer than it.

LAMMPS compute entropy/atom spreads each neighbor over seven points only; MDAPY uses the whole Gaussian, so that equivalent atoms get equal values. The two agree to within about 0.7 %.

docs.text:

Piaggi and Parrinello (2017).

docs.title: Difference between frames
docs.text:
FrameDifference gives the change of a column of each atom from a reference frame, such as the first of a trajectory, the atoms matched by their ids, as OVITO's difference between frames. It adds the column <name>_change to a system.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import CoordinationNumber, FrameDifference
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

# copper with ids, then the same atoms shaken by 0.4 Å and in another order
copper = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(8, 8, 8))
copper = copper.with_columns(id=np.arange(1, len(copper) + 1))
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
hot = copper.with_columns(
    positions=copper["positions"] + rng.normal(0, 0.4, (len(copper), 3))
)
hot = hot.gather(rng.permutation(len(hot)))

coordination = CoordinationNumber(3.0)
before = copper.with_columns(coordination.compute(copper))
after = hot.with_columns(coordination.compute(hot))
change = FrameDifference("coordination").compute(after, before)
after = after.with_columns(change)  # the column coordination_change

The atoms colored by the change of their number of neighbors:

from mdapy.visualization import render, write_png

write_png(
    "images/frame-difference.png",
    render(
        after,
        color="coordination_change",
        colormap="coolwarm",
        value_range=(-6, 6),
        view="iso",
        width=680,
        height=500,
        legend=True,
    ),
)

Each atom of the crystal had 12 neighbors within 3 Å; shaken, most have fewer (blue) and a few more (orange).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
FrameDifference(column)

Name Type Meaning column str a column of numbers, a component such as "velocities.z" or an expression over the columns

compute(system, reference) takes the frame and the reference frame. Their atoms are matched by the id column where both have one, else taken in the same order. Positions change through the periodic boundaries as they are given; the atomic displacement follows them.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A FrameDifferenceResult:

Attribute Type Meaning difference (N,) or (N, k) float64 the value of each atom of the system minus its value in the reference name str the column

System.with_columns(result) adds difference as the column, its dots as underscores, followed by _change, such as velocities_z_change.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for a column that is not a name; compute raises it for a column of text, repeated ids in the reference, or without ids a reference of another number of atoms, and MissingProperty for an atom that is not in the reference.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:

  • OVITO Difference between frames.

docs.title: Frozen values
docs.text:
freeze gives the atoms of one frame the values a column has in another, such as the first of a trajectory, matched by their ids, as OVITO's freeze property. It keeps a property of the start, such as where each atom was or its structure, at hand in every later frame, to compare with what the atom is now.

Copper melts at 2500 K, here in LAMMPS for 10 ps. Where did each atom of the liquid start?

import numpy as np
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.calculators import EAM, LAMMPS
from mdapy.identify import CommonNeighborAnalysis
from mdapy.simulation import MolecularDynamics
from mdapy.transform import freeze

copper = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(12, 6, 6))
copper = copper.with_columns(id=np.arange(1, len(copper) + 1))
EAM.zhou(["Cu"]).write("Cu.eam.alloy")
potential = LAMMPS(
    "pair_style eam/alloy\npair_coeff * * Cu.eam.alloy Cu", elements=["Cu"]
)
with MolecularDynamics(copper, potential, timestep=0.002) as md:
    md.velocities(5000, seed=1)
    md.run(5000, ensemble="npt", temperature=2500.0, pressure=0.0)
    liquid = md.system

liquid = freeze(liquid, copper, "positions.x")  # the column positions_x_frozen

# the same for the structure: the atoms that are no longer what they were
cna = CommonNeighborAnalysis()
start = copper.with_columns(cna.compute(copper))
liquid = freeze(liquid.with_columns(cna.compute(liquid)), start, "cna_structure")
changed = liquid.where("cna_structure != cna_structure_frozen")
changed.sum()  # 1728: every atom, the crystal has melted

The crystal and the liquid, each atom in the color of where it started along x:

from mdapy.visualization import render, write_png

options = dict(
    colormap="jet",
    value_range=(0, copper.box.matrix[0, 0]),
    legend="x at the start (Å)",
    view="front",
    width=640,
    height=420,
)
write_png(
    "images/freeze.png",
    np.hstack(
        [
            render(copper, color=copper["positions.x"], **options),
            render(liquid, color="positions_x_frozen", **options),
        ]
    ),
)

Left: the crystal, colored from blue to red along x. Right: the liquid after 10 ps, each atom still in the color of where it started: the stripes have mixed over some ångströms, and atoms that crossed the periodic boundary at the ends of the box carry their color to the other side.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
freeze(system, reference, column, *, name=None)

Name Type Default Meaning system System the frame that takes the values reference System the frame of the values, its atoms matched by the id column where both have one, else in the same order column str a column, a component such as "positions.z" or an expression over the columns name str None the new column; by default the column, its dots as underscores, followed by _frozen

docs.title: Results
docs.text: The system with the values of the reference in the new column; its other columns as they are.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: MissingProperty if an atom of the system is not in the reference; InvalidParameter for repeated ids in the reference or, without ids, a reference of another number of atoms.

docs.title: Grain segmentation
docs.text:
GrainSegmentation finds the grains of a polycrystal: groups of crystalline atoms whose lattices have nearly the same orientation, from the orientations polyhedral template matching gives, as OVITO's Grain segmentation does, with the centers of mass and the radii of the grains.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.build import build_crystal, build_polycrystal
from mdapy.identify import GrainSegmentation

# eight grains of copper, the atoms displaced by about 0.04 Å
copper = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu")
grains = build_polycrystal(copper, mp.Box(60.0), 8, seed=2)
shake = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(0, 0.04, (len(grains), 3))
grains = grains.with_columns(positions=grains["positions"] + shake)

result = GrainSegmentation().compute(grains)
result.count  # 8
result.sizes  # [2885, 2666, ..., 1353] atoms, about largest first
result.orientation[0]  # mean lattice orientation of the largest, (x, y, z, w)
result.center[0], result.radius_of_gyration[0]  # Å
grains = grains.with_columns(result)  # the column grain, -1 for none

# merged along the bonds of least misorientation, up to 3 degrees
tree = GrainSegmentation(3.0, method="spanning_tree").compute(grains)

Each atom in the color of its grain, and the merges of the clusters with the threshold chosen:

from mdapy.visualization import plot, render

names = [f"grain {k}: {n} atoms" for k, n in enumerate(result.sizes)]
render(
    grains,
    "images/grain-segmentation.png",
    color=result.atom_colors(),
    legend=dict(zip(names, result.colors)),
    width=1000,
    height=600,
)

with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    ax.scatter(np.log(result.merge_distance), result.merge_size, s=4)
    ax.axvline(result.threshold, color="0.5", linestyle="--")
    ax.set_xlabel("Log merge distance")
    ax.set_ylabel("Merge size (atoms)")
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    plot.save(fig, "images/grain-merges", formats=("png",))

The eight grains, each in its own color; the atoms of the boundaries have joined the nearest grain.

The merges of two clusters of at least 20 atoms, larger clusters merging at larger distances. All are within grains: the grains here are misoriented by more than 4°, so no bond joins two of them. The threshold (dashed) is the largest distance of the merges that follow the trend; merges of distinct grains or subgrains, misoriented by less, would stand out beyond it.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
GrainSegmentation(threshold=None, *, method="graph", min_grain_size=100, stacking_faults=True, adopt_orphans=True, structures=("fcc", "hcp", "bcc"), rmsd_cutoff=0.1)

Name Type Default Unit Meaning threshold float64 None "graph": the largest log merge distance of the merges kept, by default chosen from the merges; "spanning_tree": the largest misorientation, needed method str "graph" "graph": node pair sampling of the graph of bonds; "spanning_tree": merges along the bonds of least misorientation min_grain_size int64 100 atoms smaller clusters are no grains stacking_faults bool True the atoms of stacking faults and twin boundaries (hcp in fcc, hexagonal in cubic diamond, or the other way round) join the grains around them adopt_orphans bool True atoms in no grain join the grain nearest along their bonds structures, rmsd_cutoff those of polyhedral template matching, done when no result of it is given

The threshold of the spanning tree is in degrees. The structures must include those of the grains; a grain of hcp atoms needs "hcp", a grain of silicon "cubic_diamond".

compute(system, *, ptm=None, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis and a PTMResult of the system, from PolyhedralTemplateMatching(template_neighbors=True), to reuse; the box must be at least twice as wide as the bonds along its periodic directions.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A GrainResult:

Attribute Type Unit Meaning grain (N,) int64 the grain of each atom, an index into the arrays below; -1 for none sizes (G,) int64 atoms of each grain; the grains are ranked by size before adopt_orphans adds the atoms in no grain, as in OVITO, so a grain can end a little larger than the one before it structure (G,) int8 structure of each grain, an index into names names tuple of str the structures of polyhedral template matching orientation (G, 4) float64 mean lattice orientation, a quaternion (x, y, z, w) as those of the atoms center (G, 3) float64 Å center of mass, inside the box radius (G,) float64 Å of the smallest sphere about the center that holds the grain radius_of_gyration (G,) float64 Å colors (G, 3) float64 a distinct color for each grain, RGB from 0 to 1 atom_colors(*, ungrouped=(0.8, 0.8, 0.8)) (N, 3) float64 the color of the grain of each atom, ungrouped for atoms in no grain threshold float64 the threshold applied: log merge distance, or degrees for the spanning tree merge_distance, merge_size (M,) float64 , atoms the merges of two clusters of at least 20 atoms, in order: merge distance (degrees for the spanning tree) and the atoms of the smaller cluster count int32 the number of grains

with_columns(result) adds the column grain. The centers of mass weigh the atoms by the column mass when there is one. A grain that reconnects to itself through the periodic boundaries has no center of mass: its center and radii are those of whichever of its atoms are unwrapped together.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for an unknown method, a spanning tree without a positive threshold, a threshold that is not finite, or a minimum size that is not a positive integer; compute raises it for a template matching without its neighbors or of another system, and for a box too short for the bonds.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Polyhedral template matching gives each atom a structure and a lattice orientation. Each atom is bonded to the neighbors of its template, an atom of no structure to its 8 nearest. The misorientation of a bond is the smallest angle that turns the lattice of one atom into that of the other, over the rotations of the lattice that leave it unchanged; it is defined for atoms of the same structure. With stacking_faults, the atoms of the less common of fcc and hcp (of cubic and hexagonal diamond) take, one after the other from the bond of least misorientation, the structure and the equivalent orientation of their neighbors across a coherent interface.

The clusters grow from single atoms by merges along the bonds misoriented by less than 4°, each merge adding to a cluster the orientation of the other, turned to the nearest equivalent:

  • "graph": the bonds are the edges of a graph of weights \(\exp(-\theta^2/3)\), \(\theta\) in degrees; node pair sampling (Bonald et al. 2018) merges the pair of clusters \(a\), \(b\) of least distance \(w_a w_b / w_{ab}\), where \(w\) are the weights of the clusters and of the edges between them, the distance of a merge. The automatic threshold fits the logarithm of the merge distance against that of the merge size (the harmonic mean of the sizes of the two clusters) with a line, by least absolute deviations, and keeps the merges up to the last one that lies less than 1.5 median deviations above it.
  • "spanning_tree": the bonds are taken from the least misoriented up, as in a minimum spanning tree; the distance of a merge is the misorientation of its bond (Panzarino and Rupert 2014).

The merges up to the threshold make the clusters; those of at least min_grain_size atoms are the grains, numbered from the largest. The other atoms, the orphans (Hoffrogge and Barrales-Mora 2017), join the grain whose nearest atom is the closest along the bonds. The orientations of the atoms enter in single precision, as OVITO keeps them.

Please cite

Larsen et al. (2016) for polyhedral template matching and Bonald et al. (2018) for node pair sampling.

docs.title: Histograms
docs.text:
Histogram counts the values of a column of the atoms in bins of equal width, as OVITO's histogram: a column, a component such as "velocities.x" or an expression over the columns, of all atoms or of those chosen.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import Histogram
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

# copper at 300 K: velocities in Å/ps of the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
copper = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(10, 10, 10))
kT, mass = 0.025852, 63.546  # eV, amu
sigma = np.sqrt(kT / mass / 1.0364269e-4)  # (Å/ps)², from eV/amu
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
copper = copper.with_columns(velocities=rng.normal(0, sigma, (len(copper), 3)))

histogram = Histogram("velocities.x", bins=40).compute(copper)
histogram.center, histogram.counts  # bin centers, atoms in each bin
fast = Histogram("velocities.x", bins=40, range=(-10, 10)).compute(
    copper, atoms=copper.where("velocities.y > 0")
)

The distribution of one component and the Gaussian it follows:

from mdapy.visualization import plot

with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    width = histogram.edges[1] - histogram.edges[0]
    ax.bar(histogram.center, histogram.density, width=width, color="#9ec5e8")
    v = np.linspace(histogram.edges[0], histogram.edges[-1], 200)
    ax.plot(v, np.exp(-0.5 * (v / sigma) ** 2) / (sigma * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)), "k")
    ax.set_xlabel("$v_x$ (Å/ps)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Density (ps/Å)")
    plot.save(fig, "images/histogram", formats=("png",))

4000 values of \(v_x\) in 40 bins, normalized as a density, against the Gaussian of variance \(k_BT/m\).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Histogram(column, bins=50, range=None)

Name Type Default Unit Meaning column str a column of numbers, a component such as "positions.z" or an expression over the columns bins int32 50 number of bins of equal width range (float64, float64) None that of the column lowest and highest value of the bins; values outside are not counted. By default from the lowest to the highest finite value, or one unit above a single value

compute(system, *, atoms=None) counts the atoms given as a boolean mask or indices, such as those of System.where, or all. NaN and infinite values are left out and counted apart.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A HistogramResult:

Attribute Type Meaning center (bins,) float64 bin centers edges (bins + 1,) float64 bin edges; the last bin holds its upper edge counts (bins,) int64 number of values in each bin frequency (bins,) float64 the counts divided by the number of values counted density (bins,) float64 the frequency divided by the width of a bin nonfinite int64 the number of values left out as NaN or infinite name str the column

docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for fewer than one bin or a range that does not increase; compute raises it for a column of text, a column of several components (give one of them) or a wrong mask.

docs.title: Isosurfaces and voxels
docs.text:
isosurface gives the surface where a field on a grid over the box, such as a property of the atoms binned along the three box vectors, crosses a level: the boundary of the regions of high density, of one element, of large strain. voxel_faces shows the grid itself, as colors of its cells on the faces of the box.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import SpatialBinning, isosurface
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.visualization import colormap, render, voxel_faces

# nickel with twelve spherical copper precipitates of radius 8 Å
nickel = build_crystal("fcc", 3.55, elements="Ni", repeat=(16, 16, 16))
box = nickel.box
centers = np.random.default_rng(3).random((12, 3))
step = box.to_fractional(nickel["positions"])[:, None, :] - centers
step -= np.round(step)
inside = (np.linalg.norm(step @ box.matrix, axis=-1) < 8).any(axis=1)
alloy = nickel.with_columns(
    element=np.where(inside, "Cu", "Ni"), copper=inside.astype(float)
)

# the copper fraction in 14 x 14 x 14 cells, and where it is one half
fraction = SpatialBinning("copper", 14, axes=(0, 1, 2)).compute(alloy)
surface = isosurface(fraction.values, box, 0.5)  # a TriangleMesh
surface.area  # Å²

render(alloy, "images/isosurface.png", atoms=[], mesh=surface, mesh_color="#c8a24a",
       width=600, height=600)  # fmt: skip
faces, values = voxel_faces(fraction.values, box)
render(alloy, "images/voxels.png", atoms=[], mesh=faces,
       mesh_color=colormap(values, "viridis", (0, 1)), width=600, height=600)  # fmt: skip

Left: the surface where the copper fraction is one half, which wraps the precipitates, cut at the faces of the box where it crosses them and moved in through the opposite faces. Right: the copper fraction of the cells at the faces of the box, from none (purple) to all (yellow), where the precipitates are cut by them.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
isosurface(values, box, level) and voxel_faces(values, box)

Name Type Unit Meaning values (na, nb, nc) float64 the field at the centers of the cells of a grid that divides the box into na, nb and nc cells along a, b and c, such as SpatialBinning(..., axes=(0, 1, 2)).compute(system).values box Box the box the grid divides level float64 as the field the value on the surface

The values must be finite: the mean of a property in a bin without atoms is NaN, and np.nan_to_num or a sum or density instead of the mean mends that.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
isosurface gives a TriangleMesh, the triangles of the surface, whose normals point toward lower values, from inside the regions above the level to outside; it crosses the periodic boundaries of the box, and ends at the outermost cell centers along the box vectors that are not periodic. Its area is the area in Å². Where the field does not cross the level, the mesh is empty.

voxel_faces gives a TriangleMesh of the six faces of the box, two triangles for each cell at each face, and the value of the cell of each triangle; colormap(values, name, value_range) makes them colors, and render(mesh=..., mesh_color=...) draws them, as OVITO shows a voxel grid.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Both raise InvalidParameter for values that are not a three-dimensional grid of finite numbers, and isosurface for a level that is not finite.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The samples of the field are at the centers of the cells; between each eight neighboring samples, along the periodic box vectors also across the boundary, lies a cube of the dual grid. Each cube is cut into six tetrahedra that share its diagonal from corner (0, 0, 0) to (1, 1, 1), which neighboring cubes cut alike, so that their faces meet. A sample above the level is inside. In each tetrahedron whose corners are some inside and some not, the surface crosses each edge between an inside and an outside corner where the field, linear along the edge, equals the level: one triangle where one corner is on its own side, two where two are inside. Neighboring tetrahedra share the crossings on their common edges, so that the surface is one piece without gaps, closed where the regions above the level do not reach a box face that is not periodic. Unlike marching cubes, the tetrahedra leave no case ambiguous.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Spatial binning, which gives the grids.
  • Surface mesh, the surface of the solid of the atoms themselves.
  • Rendering.

docs.title: Lindemann index
docs.text:
LindemannIndex measures how much the distances between atoms fluctuate over a trajectory, relative to their mean; it rises sharply at melting, which makes it a criterion of melting for clusters and nanoparticles.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.analysis import LindemannIndex

# a cluster of 30 atoms vibrating about its sites for 50 frames
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
sites = rng.random((30, 3)) * 8 + 10
box = mp.Box(30.0, pbc=False)
frames = [
    mp.System(sites + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=(30, 3)), box, elements="Ar")
    for _ in range(50)
]

result = LindemannIndex().compute(frames)
result.index  # over every pair of atoms
result.running  # of the frames up to each one
system = frames[0].with_columns(result)  # the column 'lindemann'

The same cluster with atoms that wander away, as in a liquid, against the one that vibrates:

from mdapy.visualization import plot

steps = rng.normal(scale=0.15, size=(50, 30, 3))
liquid = [
    mp.System(sites + walk, box, elements="Ar") for walk in np.cumsum(steps, axis=0)
]
melted = LindemannIndex().compute(liquid)

with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    ax.plot(result.running, label="vibrating about sites")
    ax.plot(melted.running, label="wandering away")
    ax.axhline(0.1, color="0.5", linestyle="--")
    ax.set_xlabel("Frame")
    ax.set_ylabel("Lindemann index")
    ax.legend()
    plot.save(fig, "images/lindemann", formats=("png",))

The running index levels off for atoms that vibrate about their sites and keeps rising for atoms that wander away. The dashed line marks 0.1, about where the index of a solid stands when it melts.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning unwrap bool True follow the atoms through the periodic boundaries, or take the positions as they are, already unwrapped

compute(frames, *, progress=None, cancel=None) takes a sequence of systems as the mean squared displacement does, with the atoms matched by their ids and unwrapped in the same way, and the progress and cancel of every analysis. The distances are those between the unwrapped positions, not between the nearest periodic images.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A LindemannResult:

Attribute Type Meaning index float64 the index \(\delta\) over every pair of atoms and every frame atomic (N,) float64 the index \(\delta_i\) of each atom, averaged over its pairs, the atoms in the order of the first frame; its column lindemann running (T,) float64 \(\delta\) over the frames from the first to each one; 0 for the first

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: compute raises InvalidParameter as the mean squared displacement does and for fewer than two atoms, and Cancelled when cancelled.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
With \(r_{ij}\) the distance between atoms \(i\) and \(j\) and \(\langle \cdot \rangle\) the average over the frames, for \(N\) atoms,

\[ \delta = \frac{2}{N(N-1)} \sum_{i<j} \frac{\sqrt{\langle r_{ij}^2 \rangle - \langle r_{ij} \rangle^2}}{\langle r_{ij} \rangle} , \qquad \delta_i = \frac{1}{N-1} \sum_{j \ne i} \frac{\sqrt{\langle r_{ij}^2 \rangle - \langle r_{ij} \rangle^2}}{\langle r_{ij} \rangle} . \]

\(\delta\) is the mean of the \(\delta_i\). A rigid motion of all atoms leaves every distance unchanged and gives 0.

Please cite

Lindemann (1910); for this index of the distances, Zhou et al. (2002).

docs.title: Mean squared displacement
docs.text:
MeanSquaredDisplacement gives the mean squared displacement of the atoms of a trajectory against the lag between frames, from which the diffusion coefficient follows.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.analysis import MeanSquaredDisplacement

# 100 frames of 50 atoms on a random walk in a 10 Å box, positions wrapped
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
box = mp.Box(10.0)
walk = np.cumsum(rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=(100, 50, 3)), axis=0)
frames = [mp.System(box.wrap(x)[0], box, elements="Ar") for x in walk]

result = MeanSquaredDisplacement().compute(frames)  # or a Trajectory
result.lag, result.msd  # lag in frames, MSD in Å²
dt = 0.1  # ps between frames
slope = np.polyfit(result.lag[1:50] * dt, result.msd[1:50], 1)[0]
diffusion = slope / 6  # Å²/ps, about 0.05

from mdapy.visualization import plot

with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    plot.msd(result, timestep=dt, ax=ax, fit=(1, 50))
    plot.save(fig, "images/msd", formats=("png",))

The random walk spreads linearly in time; the slope of the fit over 6 is the diffusion coefficient in the legend.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning window bool True average over every time origin, or measure from the first frame only unwrap bool True follow the atoms through the periodic boundaries, or take the positions as they are, already unwrapped

compute(frames) takes a sequence of systems, such as a list or a Trajectory, with the same atoms in every frame. Where the first frame has an id column, as a LAMMPS dump does, every frame needs one and the atoms are matched by their ids, in whatever order each frame lists them; without ids, the atoms are in the same order in every frame.

With unwrap=True, each atom is followed from frame to frame through the periodic boundaries:

  • by its image flags, the image column, as in a LAMMPS dump with ix iy iz, where two consecutive frames both have them;
  • otherwise by the periodic image nearest to its position in the previous frame, which needs every atom to move less than half the box between two frames.

The box may change from frame to frame. With image flags, the position of an atom in a frame is its position plus its flags times the lattice vectors of that frame, as LAMMPS and OVITO unwrap it: when the box changes, an atom some boxes away from where it started moves with the box by that many times the change. With unwrap=False, for positions already unwrapped, such as xu yu zu of a LAMMPS dump, the positions are used as they are.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A DisplacementResult:

Attribute Type Meaning lag (T,) int64 the lag \(m\) in frames, from 0 to T − 1; the lag time is \(m\) times the time between frames msd (T,) float64 the mean squared displacement in Å² for each lag components (T, 3) float64 its x, y and z parts in Å²

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: compute raises InvalidParameter without frames, for frames with different numbers of atoms, for frames without atoms, and, where the first frame has ids, for repeated ids or a frame without the same ids.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
With the positions \(\mathbf r_i(k)\) of the \(N\) atoms in frame \(k\) of \(T\), unwrapped as above, the mean squared displacement averaged over every time origin (window=True) is

\[ \text{MSD}(m) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_i \frac{1}{T - m} \sum_{k=0}^{T-m-1} \lvert \mathbf r_i(k + m) - \mathbf r_i(k) \rvert^2 , \]

computed with fast Fourier transforms as described by Calandrini et al. (2011); from the first frame only (window=False) it is

\[ \text{MSD}(m) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_i \lvert \mathbf r_i(m) - \mathbf r_i(0) \rvert^2 . \]

The average over every origin is smoother, but the largest lags have few origins: \(T - m\), only one at \(m = T - 1\). For atoms that diffuse with the coefficient \(D\), \(\text{MSD} \to 6 D t\) at long times \(t\), and each component tends to \(2 D t\).

Please cite

With window=True, Calandrini et al. (2011).

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
Every analysis in MDAPY is used the same way: a class named after what it computes takes the parameters, and its compute method takes a system and returns a result.

import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.analysis import RadialDistributionFunction
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.identify import CommonNeighborAnalysis

system = build_crystal("fcc", 3.6, elements="Cu", repeat=(4, 4, 4))

result = CommonNeighborAnalysis().compute(system)
result.counts()  # {'other': 0, 'fcc': 256, ...}
system = system.with_columns(result)  # adds the column cna_structure

nl = mp.NeighborList.build(system, 6.0)  # one search for several analyses
rdf = RadialDistributionFunction(cutoff=6.0).compute(system, neighbors=nl)

Structure identification is in mdapy.identify; every other analysis, the space group among them, is in mdapy.analysis.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
The constructor of an analysis takes its parameters and checks them, so a wrong value fails before any computation. compute takes:

Name Type Default Meaning system System the atoms, with the columns the analysis needs, such as element or velocities neighbors NeighborList None a neighbor list of this system to use instead of a new search, for analyses that take one progress, cancel None progress reports and cancellation, as described in Parallelism

Analyses of a trajectory, such as the mean squared displacement and the Lindemann index, take a sequence of systems, frames, instead of system. The Voronoi analysis takes no neighbor list: it searches as far as each cell needs.

A neighbor list passed as neighbors must fit the system: the one it was built for, or any with the same positions in the same box. An analysis of the neighbors within a cutoff needs a list with at least that cutoff. An analysis of the k nearest neighbors of each atom takes either a list of nearest neighbors or a list within a cutoff, with at least k neighbors for every atom. The results are those of the analysis's own search: for nearest neighbors exactly, for a cutoff up to the order in which values are summed.

Without neighbors, most analyses within a cutoff count each atom's neighbors as the search finds them, without storing the pairs, which keeps the memory small for large systems. Pass a list when several analyses need the same neighbors.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A result is an immutable object whose arrays are read-only; all derive from mdapy.core.Result.

Method Returns columns() the per-atom values by column name; empty for results of a whole system, such as a radial distribution function

system.with_columns(result) adds these columns to a system, for example to write them to a file.

Structure identification returns a StructureResult:

Attribute or method Type Meaning structure (N,) int8 the type of each atom, an index into names; its column is named after the method, as cna_structure names tuple of str the name of each type, in lower case, such as "fcc"; type 0 is always "other" colors tuple of (3,) float64 the default color of each type, from 0 to 1 counts() dict of str to int64 the number of atoms of each type, by name

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructors raise InvalidParameter for invalid parameters. compute raises InvalidParameter for a neighbor list that does not fit, as above; MissingProperty when the system lacks a column the analysis needs; and Cancelled when cancelled.

docs.title: Planar faults
docs.text:
PlanarFaults finds the planar faults of fcc crystals, stacking faults and coherent twin boundaries, from the hcp-like atoms that polyhedral template matching finds in their {111} planes, and estimates their areas, as OVITO's Identify fcc planar faults does.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.build import build_crystal, slip
from mdapy.identify import PlanarFaults
from mdapy.transform import replicate

# fcc copper with z along [111], slipped by a/6 [11-2] above one plane
a = 3.615
cell = build_crystal(
    "fcc", a, elements="Cu", orientation=[(1, -1, 0), (1, 1, -2), (1, 1, 1)]
)
crystal = replicate(cell, (6, 4, 8))
faulted = slip(crystal, [0, a / np.sqrt(6), 0], height=0.51)

result = PlanarFaults().compute(faulted)
result.counts()["intrinsic stacking fault"]  # 96: two planes of 48 atoms
result.areas()["intrinsic stacking fault"]  # 271.6 Å², the area of the box
faulted = faulted.with_columns(result)  # planar_fault

An intrinsic and an extrinsic stacking fault and a twin in one crystal, made by slipping above chosen (111) planes:

from mdapy.visualization import render

crystal = replicate(cell, (6, 4, 20))  # 60 (111) planes
b = [0, a / np.sqrt(6), 0]
faults = slip(crystal, b, height=10.5 / 60)  # intrinsic
for plane in (25.5, 26.5):  # extrinsic: two neighboring planes
    faults = slip(faults, b, height=plane / 60)
for plane in range(6):  # a twin six planes thick: six planes in a row
    faults = slip(faults, b, height=(40.5 + plane) / 60)

found = PlanarFaults(extrinsic=True).compute(faults)
colors = np.asarray(found.colors)[found.fault]
render(
    faults,
    "images/planar-faults.png",
    color=colors,
    view="left",
    width=760,
    height=900,
    legend=dict(zip(found.names, found.colors)),
)

Seen along x. From the bottom: the intrinsic stacking fault (orange, two planes), the extrinsic stacking fault (purple, two planes with one fcc plane between) and the two coherent twin boundaries (blue) around the twin, whose rows of atoms turn the other way.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
PlanarFaults(structures=("fcc", "hcp", "bcc"), *, rmsd_cutoff=0.1, extrinsic=False)

Name Type Default Unit Meaning structures iterable of str ("fcc", "hcp", "bcc") the structures polyhedral template matching looks for, fcc and hcp among them rmsd_cutoff float64 0.1 atoms that deviate more from their best template are other; 0 for no cutoff extrinsic bool False also find extrinsic stacking faults, which are otherwise two coherent twin boundaries

compute(system, *, ptm=None, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) runs polyhedral template matching, or takes a PTMResult of the same system already computed with template_neighbors=True; neighbors, progress and cancel are those of every analysis.

docs.text:
A PlanarFaultResult:

Attribute or method Type Meaning fault (N,) int8 the type of each atom, an index into names names tuple of str non-hcp, other hcp, intrinsic stacking fault, coherent twin boundary and multilayer stacking fault, numbered as in OVITO, and extrinsic stacking fault colors tuple of (3,) float64 OVITO's colors of the types interatomic_distance (N,) float64 the distance in Å between nearest neighbors of the lattice each atom matched counts() dict of str to int64 the number of atoms of each type areas() dict of str to float64 the area in Å² of the intrinsic stacking faults, the coherent twin boundaries and the extrinsic stacking faults

The column is planar_fault.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for structures without fcc and hcp, or a negative RMSD cutoff; compute raises it for a PTMResult of another system or without the neighbors in the order of the templates.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An hcp-like atom has six neighbors in its basal plane, a {111} plane of the fcc crystal, and three above and three below it. Two hcp-like atoms one above the other are stacked, their basal planes parallel, unless an atom lies in both their basal planes. Each hcp-like atom is first classified by its hcp-like neighbors in its basal plane, those stacked above and below it, and its fcc neighbors above and below:

  • stacked hcp-like neighbors on one side only: an intrinsic stacking fault, two planes of hcp-like atoms;
  • no stacked hcp-like neighbors, at least one hcp-like neighbor in the basal plane and fcc neighbors on both sides: a coherent twin boundary, one plane;
  • stacked hcp-like neighbors on both sides: a multilayer stacking fault, three planes or more;
  • otherwise other hcp, an hcp-like atom of no planar fault.

A second pass then goes through the hcp-like atoms in the order of their indices, as OVITO does, and changes the types as it goes: a twin-boundary or other atom whose hcp-like basal neighbors include stacking-fault atoms and no twin-boundary atoms becomes a stacking-fault atom, and the other way round; the stacking-fault atoms stacked on a multilayer atom become multilayer atoms. Atoms at the edges of faults, next to partial dislocations, may thus depend on the order of the atoms.

With extrinsic, a last pass makes extrinsic stacking faults of the twin-boundary atoms next to a single plane of fcc atoms between two planes of hcp-like atoms: a twin-boundary atom with an fcc neighbor above or below that has at least five hcp-like and five fcc neighbors, as an fcc atom with six hcp-like neighbors in the planes above and below it and six fcc neighbors in its own plane has. An extrinsic stacking fault, a plane inserted into the stacking, is such a twin of two planes. This pass reads the types the others left and does not depend on the order of the atoms.

The area of an atom in a {111} plane is \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}d^2\), with \(d\) the interatomic distance; a stacking fault is two planes of atoms, a twin boundary one, an extrinsic stacking fault two:

\[ A_\mathrm{ISF} = \frac{\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{i \in \mathrm{ISF}} d_i^2, \qquad A_\mathrm{TB} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\sum_{i \in \mathrm{TB}} d_i^2, \qquad A_\mathrm{ESF} = \frac{\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{i \in \mathrm{ESF}} d_i^2 . \]

Adjacent faults of different kinds can look alike: a multilayer stacking fault may be several stacking faults or twin boundaries on neighboring planes.

docs.text:
• Polyhedral template matching, which finds the hcp-like atoms.
  • OVITO Identify fcc planar faults.

docs.title: Polyhedral template matching
docs.text:
PolyhedralTemplateMatching gives each atom the crystal structure of its neighborhood, the rotation of that crystal, its elastic deformation and the chemical ordering of its elements, by matching the polyhedron of its nearest neighbors to the templates of nine structures, by the method of Larsen, Schmidt and Schiøtz.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.identify import PolyhedralTemplateMatching

# Cu3Au: an fcc lattice ordered in the L1_2 structure, slightly disordered
alloy = build_crystal("l1_2", 3.75, elements=("Cu", "Au"), repeat=(4, 4, 4))
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
alloy = alloy.with_columns(
    positions=alloy["positions"] + rng.normal(scale=0.05, size=(256, 3))
)

ptm = PolyhedralTemplateMatching(deformation_gradient=True, ordering=True)
result = ptm.compute(alloy)
result.counts()["fcc"]  # 256
result.interatomic_distance.mean()  # about 2.65 Å, 3.75 / sqrt(2)
result.orientation[0]  # near (0, 0, 0, 1): the cubic axes along x, y and z
result.ordering_names[result.ordering[0]]  # "L12_B": an Au site, at a corner
alloy = alloy.with_columns(result)  # structure, rmsd, orientation and more

docs.title: The structures
docs.text:
PTM knows nine types: other and eight structures. The structures to look for are chosen with structures; by default fcc, hcp and bcc, as in OVITO. Each is matched by the polyhedron of the nearest neighbors of an atom:

Structure Neighbors matched For example fcc 12 Cu, Al, Ni, and the A1, L10 and L12 alloys hcp 12 Mg, Ti, Zn, and the stacking faults and twins of fcc bcc 14, 8 first and 6 second Fe, W, Mo, and B2 alloys ico 12 the centers of icosahedra, in metallic glasses and clusters sc 6 α-Po, and rocksalt, whose two elements the structure does not tell apart cubic_diamond 4 first and 12 second Si, Ge, diamond, and zincblende hexagonal_diamond 4 first and 12 second lonsdaleite, and wurtzite graphene 3 first and 6 second graphene, and hexagonal boron nitride

Each crystal, and a Mackay icosahedron of 309 atoms cut in half, with all eight structures looked for:

import itertools
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.visualization import render, write_png


def mackay(shells, d):
    """A Mackay icosahedron: on each shell, triangular lattices on 20 faces."""
    g = (1 + 5**0.5) / 2
    corners = [(0, s, t * g) for s, t in itertools.product((-1, 1), repeat=2)]
    corners = np.array([np.roll(c, k) for c in corners for k in range(3)]) * d / 2
    faces = [
        f
        for f in itertools.combinations(range(12), 3)
        if all(
            np.isclose(np.linalg.norm(corners[i] - corners[j]), d)
            for i, j in itertools.combinations(f, 2)
        )
    ]
    points = [np.zeros(3)]
    for n in range(1, shells + 1):
        for a, b, c in faces:
            for i in range(n + 1):
                for j in range(n + 1 - i):
                    points.append(
                        i * corners[a] + j * corners[b] + (n - i - j) * corners[c]
                    )
    points = np.unique(np.round(points, 6), axis=0)
    return mp.System(points + 30.0, mp.Box(60.0, pbc=False), elements="Cu")


everything = PolyhedralTemplateMatching(PolyhedralTemplateMatching.NAMES[1:])
crystals = [
    build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(3, 3, 3)),
    build_crystal("hcp", 3.21, c=5.21, elements="Mg", repeat=(4, 4, 3)),
    build_crystal("bcc", 2.865, elements="Fe", repeat=(4, 4, 4)),
    build_crystal("sc", 3.35, elements="Po", repeat=(4, 4, 4)),
    build_crystal("diamond", 5.431, elements="Si", repeat=(2, 2, 2)),
    build_crystal("lonsdaleite", 2.52, c=4.12, elements="C", repeat=(4, 4, 3)),
    build_crystal("graphene", 2.46, c=10.0, elements="C", repeat=(5, 5, 1)),
]
pictures = []
for crystal in crystals:
    found = everything.compute(crystal)
    pictures.append(render(crystal, color=found, legend=True, width=520, height=440))
icosahedron = mackay(4, 2.55)
found = everything.compute(icosahedron)
found.counts()  # 1 ico at the center, 90 hcp, 20 fcc, 198 other
pictures.append(
    render(
        icosahedron,
        atoms=icosahedron["positions.z"] < 30.5,
        color=found,
        view="top",
        box=False,
        legend=True,
        width=520,
        height=440,
    )
)
write_png(
    "images/ptm-structures.png",
    np.vstack([np.hstack(pictures[:4]), np.hstack(pictures[4:])]),
)

Top: fcc copper, hcp magnesium, bcc iron and simple cubic polonium. Bottom: cubic diamond silicon, hexagonal diamond (lonsdaleite), graphene, and half of a Mackay icosahedron: its center is icosahedral, the planes between its twenty tetrahedra hcp, the insides of the tetrahedra fcc, and the surface other.

Look only for the structures the system can have: each structure added is one more template that an atom of another structure, or of a defect, may match by accident. Atoms of a liquid, of a surface or of a grain boundary are other.

docs.title: The RMSD and its cutoff
docs.text:
Thermal motion moves the neighbors away from the template; the RMSD measures how far, after the template is scaled and rotated onto them. An atom whose best RMSD is above rmsd_cutoff is other. With no cutoff, the RMSD of every atom shows where the crystal ends and the disorder begins:

from mdapy.visualization import plot

crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(8, 8, 8))
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
no_cutoff = PolyhedralTemplateMatching(rmsd_cutoff=0)
with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    for shake in (0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4):
        moved = crystal["positions"] + rng.normal(0, shake, (len(crystal), 3))
        rmsd = no_cutoff.compute(crystal.with_columns(positions=moved)).rmsd
        ax.hist(rmsd, bins=np.linspace(0, 0.4, 81), histtype="step", label=f"{shake} Å")
    ax.axvline(0.1, color="0.5", ls="--")
    ax.set_xlabel("RMSD")
    ax.set_ylabel("Atoms")
    ax.legend(title="shaken by")
    plot.save(fig, "images/ptm-rmsd", formats=("png",))

Copper with every atom shaken by a normal distribution of 0.05 to 0.4 Å along each axis; at room temperature the atoms of copper vibrate by about 0.08 Å along each axis. The default cutoff of 0.1 (dashed) keeps a crystal shaken by 0.05 Å and a good part of one shaken by 0.1 Å; a crystal shaken by 0.4 Å is no longer one. Raise the cutoff for hot crystals, or use 0 to classify every atom by its best template.

docs.title: Orientations
docs.text:
orientation is the rotation of the lattice of each atom from its standard orientation, the cubic axes along x, y and z for the cubic structures, as a quaternion (x, y, z, w) reduced by the symmetry of the lattice. Atoms of one grain have nearly the same; grain segmentation groups them. Here the x, y and z of the quaternion color each atom:

from mdapy.build import build_polycrystal

grains = build_polycrystal(
    build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu"), mp.Box(50.0), 8, seed=3
)
grains = grains.with_columns(
    positions=grains["positions"] + rng.normal(0, 0.05, (len(grains), 3))
)
found = PolyhedralTemplateMatching().compute(grains)
rotation = np.clip(0.5 + 1.25 * found.orientation[:, :3], 0, 1)
rotation[found.structure == 0] = 0.95  # other
write_png(
    "images/ptm.png",
    np.hstack(
        [
            render(grains, color=found, legend=True, width=520, height=440),
            render(grains, color=rotation, width=440, height=440),
        ]
    ),
)

A copper polycrystal of eight grains. Left: the structure of each atom, fcc inside the grains, other at the boundaries, and some hcp where two grains share a plane of atoms. Right: the orientation of each atom, one color for each grain.

interatomic_distance gives the distance between nearest neighbors of the matched lattice of each atom, and, with deformation_gradient=True, the elastic deformation gradient maps the template, scaled to that distance, onto the neighbors: from it the elastic strain of each atom follows.

docs.title: Chemical ordering
docs.text:
With ordering=True and an element column, PTM also compares the elements of the neighbors with the sublattices of the ordered crystals of each structure:

Ordering Structure Its atoms pure any all neighbors of the element of the atom L10 fcc layers of two elements alternating along a cube axis, as CuAu L12_A fcc the face centers of L12, as Cu in Cu3Au L12_B fcc the corners of L12, as Au in Cu3Au B2 bcc the eight first neighbors of the other element, as CuZn zincblende_wurtzite cubic_diamond, hexagonal_diamond the four first neighbors of the other element, as GaAs and ZnO boron_nitride graphene the three first neighbors of the other element, as hexagonal BN other any none of these, such as a random alloy 
ordered = PolyhedralTemplateMatching(
    PolyhedralTemplateMatching.NAMES[1:], ordering=True
)
alloys = [
    build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(3, 3, 3)),
    build_crystal("fcc", 3.8, elements=("Cu", "Au"), repeat=(3, 3, 3)),
    build_crystal("l1_2", 3.75, elements=("Cu", "Au"), repeat=(3, 3, 3)),
    build_crystal("cscl", 2.95, elements=("Cu", "Zn"), repeat=(4, 4, 4)),
    build_crystal("zincblende", 5.65, elements=("Ga", "As"), repeat=(2, 2, 2)),
    build_crystal("wurtzite", 3.25, c=5.21, elements=("Zn", "O"), repeat=(4, 4, 3)),
    build_crystal("graphene", 2.50, c=10.0, elements=("B", "N"), repeat=(5, 5, 1)),
]
side = [1.0, 0.5, 0.35]  # off the rows of atoms along [111]
pictures = []
for crystal in alloys:
    found = ordered.compute(crystal)
    title = ", ".join(found.ordering_names[k] for k in np.unique(found.ordering))
    pictures.append(
        render(crystal, radius=0.8, view=side, legend=title, width=520, height=440)
    )

# Cu3Au with 4 pairs of Cu and Au swapped: the atoms around them are other
mixed = build_crystal("l1_2", 3.75, elements=("Cu", "Au"), repeat=(4, 4, 4))
element = np.asarray(mixed["element"]).copy()
copper = rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(element == "Cu"), 4, replace=False)
gold = rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(element == "Au"), 4, replace=False)
element[copper], element[gold] = "Au", "Cu"
found = ordered.compute(mixed.with_columns(element=element))
colors = np.array(PolyhedralTemplateMatching.ORDERING_COLORS)
names = {found.ordering_names[k]: colors[k] for k in np.unique(found.ordering)}
pictures.append(
    render(
        mixed,
        color=colors[found.ordering],
        radius=0.8,
        view=side,
        legend=names,
        width=520,
        height=440,
    )
)
write_png(
    "images/ptm-ordering.png",
    np.vstack([np.hstack(pictures[:4]), np.hstack(pictures[4:])]),
)

The ordered crystals in the colors of their elements, each titled with the orderings found. Top: pure copper, L10 CuAu, L12 Cu3Au with its two sublattices, and B2 CuZn. Bottom: zincblende GaAs, wurtzite ZnO, hexagonal boron nitride, and Cu3Au with 4 of its 64 Au atoms swapped with Cu atoms, in the colors of the orderings: the atoms whose neighbors no longer match a sublattice are other.

The ordering of an atom is that of the best template of its structure; an atom of other structure gets the ordering other. In a random solid solution most atoms are other too, and the share of an ordering is a measure of chemical order next to the Warren–Cowley parameters.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
PolyhedralTemplateMatching(structures=("fcc", "hcp", "bcc"), *, rmsd_cutoff=0.1, deformation_gradient=False, ordering=False, template_neighbors=False)

Name Type Default Unit Meaning structures iterable of str ("fcc", "hcp", "bcc") the structures to look for: fcc, hcp, bcc, ico, sc, cubic_diamond, hexagonal_diamond and graphene rmsd_cutoff float64 0.1 atoms that deviate more from their best template are other; 0 for no cutoff deformation_gradient bool False compute the elastic deformation gradient of each atom ordering bool False identify the chemical ordering from the element column template_neighbors bool False give the neighbors of each atom in the order of its template

compute(system, *, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis. A given neighbor list must hold the 18 nearest neighbors of every atom.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A PTMResult, a StructureResult with the types other, fcc, hcp, bcc, ico, sc, cubic_diamond, hexagonal_diamond and graphene, numbered as in OVITO, and:

Attribute Type Unit Meaning rmsd (N,) float64 the root-mean-square deviation from the best template, after scaling; 0 where none matches interatomic_distance (N,) float64 Å the distance between nearest neighbors of the matched lattice orientation (N, 4) float64 the rotation of the lattice from its standard orientation, a quaternion (x, y, z, w) deformation_gradient (N, 3, 3) float64 or None the elastic deformation gradient, from the template scaled to the interatomic distance to the neighbors ordering (N,) int8 or None the chemical ordering, an index into ordering_names: other, pure, L10, L12_A, L12_B, B2, zincblende_wurtzite and boron_nitride correspondences (N,) uint64 the order of the neighbors that matches the template, encoded as OVITO's Correspondences template_index (N,) int8 which of the equivalent templates of the structure matched neighbors (N, 16) index_dtype or None the neighbors of each atom in the order of the points of its template, -1 beyond its count

The columns are ptm_structure, ptm_rmsd, ptm_interatomic_distance, ptm_orientation, and when computed ptm_deformation_gradient (9 values per atom, by rows) and ptm_ordering. As in OVITO, an atom above the RMSD cutoff is other but keeps the other results of its best template; an atom that matches no template gets zeros.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for an unknown structure, no structure, or a negative RMSD cutoff; compute raises it for a neighbor list that does not hold the 18 nearest neighbors, and MissingProperty for the ordering without an element column.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The 18 nearest neighbors of an atom are first ordered by the solid angles of the faces of its Voronoi cell, which they share. For fcc, hcp, icosahedral, bcc and simple cubic, the first 12, 14 or 6 of them form a convex hull; its graph of edges, put in a canonical form, finds the templates of the same graph and every way the neighbors can map onto the points of a template. For the diamond structures, the 4 nearest neighbors and 3 of each of their own neighbors are matched together, and for graphene 3 and 2 of each. For every mapping, the neighbors are centered and scaled, and the rotation that brings the template closest to them is found by the quaternion method; the root-mean-square deviation of that fit, the RMSD, picks the best mapping and structure. The interatomic distance comes from the scale of the fit, and the deformation gradient is the linear map that brings the scaled template closest to the neighbors. The chemical ordering compares the elements of the neighbors with the sublattices of the ordered structures on the same template.

Neighbors at exactly the same distance, as in a perfect crystal, may come in an order other than OVITO's. The structure types are then the same, but an atom that matches no structure may report another best template.

Larsen, Schmidt and Schiøtz (2016).

docs.title: Radial distribution function
docs.text:
RadialDistributionFunction gives the radial distribution function g(r) of a system and its partial functions for each pair of elements.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import RadialDistributionFunction
from mdapy.build import build_crystal, random_alloy

# a random Cu-Ni alloy on an fcc lattice of 5 x 5 x 5 cubic cells
crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.6, elements="Cu", repeat=(5, 5, 5))
system = random_alloy(crystal, {"Cu": 0.5, "Ni": 0.5}, seed=0)

rdf = RadialDistributionFunction(cutoff=8.0, bins=160).compute(system)
rdf.r, rdf.g  # bin centers in Å and g(r)
rdf.pair("Cu", "Ni")  # a partial function
rdf.coordination[-1]  # mean number of neighbors closer than 8 Å

Plotted with mdapy.visualization.plot, for a larger alloy whose atoms are shaken by 0.12 Å as at a finite temperature:

from mdapy.build import build_crystal, random_alloy
from mdapy.visualization import plot

alloy = random_alloy(
    build_crystal("fcc", 3.6, repeat=(6, 6, 6)), {"Cu": 1, "Ni": 1}, seed=1
)
shake = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(0, 0.12, (len(alloy), 3))
hot = alloy.with_columns(positions=alloy["positions"] + shake)
partials = RadialDistributionFunction(cutoff=8.0, bins=160).compute(hot)
with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    plot.rdf(partials, ax=ax, partial=True)
    plot.save(fig, "images/rdf", formats=("png",))

The three partial functions of the random alloy agree: Cu and Ni share the sites at random. The peaks are the neighbor shells of fcc at a/√2, a, a√(3/2), a√2 and beyond.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning cutoff float64 Å largest distance; it may exceed half the box, periodic images count bins int32 200 number of bins of equal width from 0 to cutoff

compute(system, *, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis. A given neighbor list must reach cutoff; without one, the pairs are counted as they are found, never stored. Partial functions need an element column.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A RadialDistributionResult:

Attribute or method Type Meaning r (bins,) float64 bin centers in Å edges (bins + 1,) float64 bin edges in Å g (bins,) float64 g(r) coordination (bins,) float64 mean number of neighbors closer than the upper edge of each bin partial dict of (str, str) to (bins,) float64 g_ab(r) of each pair of elements (a, b), a not after b by atomic number pair(a, b) (bins,) float64 g_ab(r), with a and b in either order

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for a cutoff that is not positive or fewer than one bin; compute raises it for a neighbor list that does not fit, and pair for a pair of elements without a function.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
With \(n_k\) the number of ordered pairs \((i, j)\), \(j\) any atom or periodic image other than \(i\) itself, at a distance in bin \(k\) from \(r_k\) to \(r_{k+1}\), and \(n^{ab}_k\) those with \(i\) of element \(a\) and \(j\) of element \(b\),

\[ g(r_k) = \frac{V}{N^2}\, \frac{n_k}{\tfrac{4}{3}\pi\,(r_{k+1}^3 - r_k^3)}, \qquad g_{ab}(r_k) = \frac{V}{N_a N_b}\, \frac{n^{ab}_k}{\tfrac{4}{3}\pi\,(r_{k+1}^3 - r_k^3)}, \]

with \(V\) the volume of the box, \(N\) the number of atoms and \(N_a\) that of element \(a\); a pair at distance \(r\) is in bin \(\lfloor r / \Delta r \rfloor\). The partial functions add up as \(g = \sum_{a,b} x_a x_b\, g_{ab}\) with the fractions \(x_a = N_a / N\). The volume is that of the box also along directions that are not periodic, where \(g\) does not tend to 1.

This is the normalization of OVITO. LAMMPS compute rdf divides by \(N(N - 1)\) instead of \(N^2\), and by \(N_a(N_a - 1)\) for like pairs, so its values are larger by about \(N / (N - 1)\).

docs.title: Reductions
docs.text:
reduce gives one number from the values of a column of the atoms: their mean, sum, extremes, median, spread, the number of those not zero or the atom of the lowest or highest, as OVITO's reduce property. Over the frames of a trajectory, TimeSeries takes one such number from each frame.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import reduce
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

copper = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(6, 6, 6))
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
copper = copper.with_columns(
    velocities=rng.normal(0, 2.0, (len(copper), 3)),
    charge=rng.normal(0, 0.1, len(copper)),
)

reduce(copper, "charge", "sum")  # the total charge
reduce(copper, "velocities", "mean")  # (3,) the mean of each component
reduce(copper, "velocities.z", "max")  # the fastest along z
fastest = reduce(
    copper, "velocities.x**2 + velocities.y**2 + velocities.z**2", "argmax"
)
reduce(copper, "charge", "std", atoms=copper.where("positions.z > 10"))

fastest is the index of the fastest atom among all atoms, also when atoms chooses some of them.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
reduce(system, column, operation="mean", *, atoms=None)

Name Type Default Meaning system System the atoms column str a column of numbers, a component such as "positions.z" or an expression over the columns operation str "mean" one of OPERATIONS, below atoms (N,) bool or indices None a boolean mask or indices of the atoms to take, such as those of System.where; all by default Operation Gives "mean" the mean "sum" the sum; 0 of no values "min", "max" the lowest and highest value "median" the median, the mean of the two middle values for an even number "variance", "std" the variance and standard deviation of a sample, divided by the number of values minus one "nonzero" the number of values not zero "argmin", "argmax" the index of the atom of the lowest and highest value, the first of equal ones

NaN values are left out of every operation. The mean, extremes and median of no values are NaN, and so are the variance and standard deviation of fewer than two.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: A float64, or an int64 for "nonzero", "argmin" and "argmax"; for a column of several components, such as "velocities", an array of one per component.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: InvalidParameter for an unknown operation, a column of text, a wrong mask, or "argmin" or "argmax" of no values.
