• Histograms.
  • OVITO Reduce property.

docs.title: Ring statistics
docs.text:
RingStatistics finds the rings of a network of bonds, as in silica, amorphous silicon, carbon or ice: closed paths of bonds through distinct atoms in which no two atoms are closer through the network than along the ring, the shortest-path rings of Franzblau. It gives each ring, how many there are of each size and how many rings each atom is in.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import RingStatistics
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.visualization import colormap, render

# graphene with a Stone-Wales defect: one bond turned by 90 degrees
sheet = build_crystal("graphene", 2.46, c=10.0, elements="C", repeat=(8, 8, 1))
x = sheet["positions"].copy()
middle = sheet.box.matrix.sum(axis=0) / 2
first = int(np.argmin(np.linalg.norm(x[:, :2] - middle[:2], axis=1)))
second = int(np.argsort(np.linalg.norm(x - x[first], axis=1))[1])
center = (x[first] + x[second]) / 2
turn = np.array([[0.0, -1, 0], [1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1]])
x[[first, second]] = center + (x[[first, second]] - center) @ turn.T
defect = sheet.with_columns(positions=x)

rings = RingStatistics(8, cutoff=1.7).compute(defect)
rings.counts  # [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 60, 2, 0]: two pentagons, two heptagons
rings.atoms[0], rings.sizes[0]  # the atoms of the first ring and its size
defect = defect.with_columns(rings)  # the number of rings of each atom

mesh, ring = rings.polygons(defect)  # a fan of triangles about each ring
size = rings.sizes[ring]
named = {f"{n} atoms": colormap([n], "coolwarm", (5, 7))[0] for n in (5, 6, 7)}
render(defect, "images/rings.png", radius=0.35, bonds=1.7, mesh=mesh,
       mesh_color=colormap(size, "coolwarm", (5, 7)), view="top", box=False,
       legend=named, width=860, height=520)  # fmt: skip

The rings of graphene with a Stone–Wales defect, colored by size: the turned bond makes two pentagons (blue) and two heptagons (red) among the hexagons.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
RingStatistics(max_size=8, *, min_size=3, cutoff=None, cutoffs=None)

Name Type Default Unit Meaning max_size int32 8 the largest ring, at most 36 min_size int32 3 the smallest ring, at least 3 cutoff float64 None Å atoms closer than it are bonded cutoffs dict of (str, str) to float64 None Å the bond length of each pair of elements (a, b), in either order; pairs not given are never bonded, as for clusters

Without cutoff or cutoffs, the bonds are those of the topology of the system, such as those of a LAMMPS data file, each between the nearest periodic images of its two atoms. compute(system, *, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis. The time grows with the number of paths of up to half the largest ring from each atom: rings of up to 12 atoms of a thousand atoms of diamond take a tenth of a second.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A RingResult:

Attribute Type Meaning atoms (M, max_size) int64 the atoms of each ring in order around it, from its atom of the smallest index on toward the smaller of its two neighbors; -1 after the last shifts (M, max_size, 3) int32 the periodic image of each atom of a ring relative to its first atom, so that positions[atoms] + shifts @ box.matrix is the ring whole sizes (M,) int64 the number of atoms of each ring counts (max_size + 1,) int64 the number of rings of each size per_atom (N,) int64 the number of rings each atom is in; its column rings

The rings are in the order of their first atom, then of size, then of their atoms. polygons(system) gives a TriangleMesh of the rings, a fan of triangles about the center of each, and the ring of each triangle, for render(mesh=..., mesh_color=...).

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: RingStatistics raises InvalidParameter for sizes that are not integers with 3 ≤ min_size ≤ max_size ≤ 36, and for both cutoff and cutoffs; compute raises MissingProperty without a cutoff for a system with no bonds in its topology, and with cutoffs for a system without an element column.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A ring is a closed path of bonds through distinct atoms, its atoms told apart by their periodic images, so that a path around a periodic box is no ring however small the box. A ring of n atoms is a shortest-path ring when the number of bonds between any two of its atoms along the shortest path through the whole network equals the smaller number along the ring:

\[ d(i, j) = \min(|k_i - k_j|,\; n - |k_i - k_j|) \]

for atoms at places \(k_i\) and \(k_j\) of the ring. A ring with a shortcut, a shorter path between two of its atoms elsewhere in the network, is two smaller rings and is left out. Two atoms joined by several paths of the same length make every ring of two of them a shortest-path ring: the faces of a cube and the four hexagons about its body diagonals, three rings of six atoms where two atoms are joined by three paths of three bonds. Other definitions differ in such cases: OVITO's find rings keeps some of them, and primitive or strong rings keep fewer.

Each ring is found from its atom of the smallest index: a breadth-first search of the network from it, each atom in each periodic image a node of its own, gives every shortest path out to half the largest ring; a ring of 2k atoms is two such paths to an atom k bonds away that share no other atom, a ring of 2k + 1 atoms two paths to the two ends of a bond k bonds away, and each is kept when no two of its atoms have a shortcut.

Franzblau (1991).

docs.title: Smoothed trajectories
docs.text:
smooth_trajectory averages the positions of each frame over a window of frames about it, the atoms followed through the periodic boundaries, as OVITO's smooth trajectory. The thermal vibrations average out and the slow motion stays; velocities, forces and other columns of real numbers are averaged too.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.transform import smooth_trajectory

# an atom that drifts slowly along x through a periodic box of 10 Å,
# vibrating by 0.3 Å in each of 100 frames
box = mp.Box(10.0)
rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
t = np.arange(100)
x = 0.12 * t + rng.normal(0, 0.3, 100)
frames = [
    mp.System(box.wrap([[x[k], 5.0, 5.0]])[0], box, elements="Ar").with_columns(id=[1])
    for k in t
]

smoothed = smooth_trajectory(frames, 9)  # the frames, each computed when used
smoothed[50]["positions"]  # the mean of frames 46 to 54 about the atom

The path of the atom unwrapped, frame by frame and smoothed:

from mdapy.analysis import trajectory_lines
from mdapy.visualization import plot

with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    ax.plot(
        t, trajectory_lines(frames)[0, :, 0], ".", color="#bbbbbb", label="each frame"
    )
    ax.plot(t, trajectory_lines(smoothed)[0, :, 0], label="smoothed over 9 frames")
    ax.set_xlabel("Frame")
    ax.set_ylabel("x (Å), unwrapped")
    ax.legend(frameon=False)
    plot.save(fig, "images/smooth-trajectory", formats=("png",))

The atom crosses the box about once every 80 frames; the smoothed path follows the drift through the boundary without the jumps.

docs.text:
smooth_trajectory(frames, window)

Name Type Meaning frames sequence of System the same atoms in every frame, such as a Trajectory, matched by the id column where the frames have one, else in the same order; without an image column, atoms must move less than half the box between frames window int32 the number of frames averaged: the frame, (window - 1) // 2 frames before it and window // 2 after it, the first and last frames repeated beyond the ends; 1 leaves the positions as they are

docs.title: Results
docs.text: A sequence of systems, one per frame, each computed when it is used: the mean positions placed about the atoms where they are in that frame, the mean of every other column of real numbers matched by atom, and the columns of integers or text, such as ids and elements, as they are.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: InvalidParameter for a window that is not a positive integer, no frames, or frames that do not hold the same atoms; IndexError for a frame beyond the end.

docs.title: Space group
docs.text:
SpaceGroup finds the space group of a crystal with spglib: its number and symbol, its symmetry operations, and the atoms they make equivalent. The same operations let phonons and elastic constants skip the displacements and strains that symmetry relates to others.

from mdapy.analysis import SpaceGroup
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

cell = build_crystal("l1_2", 3.75, elements=("Cu", "Au"))
result = SpaceGroup().compute(cell)
result.number, result.symbol  # 221, 'Pm-3m'
len(result.rotations)  # 48 operations
result.equivalent  # the Au corner on its own, the three Cu face centers together

spglib is an optional dependency: pip install spglib, or the extra symmetry of MDAPY.

docs.title: The point group
docs.text:
The rotations of the operations, without their translations, form the point group of the crystal: the rotations about axes, mirrors, the inversion and their products that leave the directions of the crystal as they were. A rotation of order \(n\) turns by \(360°/n\), and its trace is \(1 + 2\cos(360°/n)\); a mirror has the determinant \(-1\) and the trace 1. Each axis and the normal of each mirror is the eigenvector of the eigenvalue 1 or \(-1\):

import numpy as np


def symmetry_elements(result):
    """The axes of the rotations with their largest order, and the mirrors."""
    axes, mirrors = {}, set()
    for rotation in result.rotations:
        values, vectors = np.linalg.eig(rotation)
        proper = np.linalg.det(rotation) > 0
        if proper and not np.allclose(rotation, np.eye(3)):
            vector = vectors[:, np.argmin(np.abs(values - 1))]
            cosine = np.clip((np.trace(rotation) - 1) / 2, -1, 1)
            order = round(2 * np.pi / np.arccos(cosine))
        elif not proper and np.isclose(np.trace(rotation), 1):
            vector, order = vectors[:, np.argmin(np.abs(values + 1))], 0
        else:
            continue  # the identity, the inversion and the rotoinversions
        vector = np.real(vector) / np.linalg.norm(vector)
        vector *= np.sign(vector[np.flatnonzero(np.abs(vector) > 1e-6)[0]])
        key = tuple(np.round(vector, 6))
        if order:
            axes[key] = max(axes.get(key, 0), order)
        else:
            mirrors.add(key)
    return axes, mirrors


axes, mirrors = symmetry_elements(result)
sorted(axes.values())  # 6 two-fold, 4 three-fold and 3 four-fold axes
len(mirrors)  # 9 mirrors: the point group m-3m

The axes drawn through an Au atom of the crystal, in its middle:

from mdapy.transform import replicate
from mdapy.visualization import element_colors, render

ORDERS = {6: "#9467bd", 4: "#d62728", 3: "#1f77b4", 2: "#2ca02c"}
crystal = replicate(cell, (2, 2, 2))
middle = crystal.box.matrix.sum(axis=0) / 2  # an Au atom
reach = 0.6 * np.linalg.norm(crystal.box.matrix.sum(axis=0))
legend = dict(zip(["Au", "Cu"], element_colors(["Au", "Cu"])))
render(
    crystal,
    "images/space-group-axes.png",
    radius=0.6,
    lines=[np.array([middle - reach * np.array(a), middle + reach * np.array(a)]) for a in axes],
    line_color=[ORDERS[order] for order in axes.values()],
    line_radius=0.05,
    view=[1, 0.6, 0.45],
    legend=legend | {f"{n}-fold axes": ORDERS[n] for n in (4, 3, 2)},
    width=760,
    height=600,
)  # fmt: skip

Cu3Au, 2 × 2 × 2 cubic cells: the three four-fold axes along the edges of the cube, the four three-fold axes along its diagonals and the six two-fold axes along the diagonals of its faces.

The usual picture of a point group is its stereogram: each axis and each mirror cut with a sphere about the crystal, and the upper half of the sphere projected onto its equator from its south pole. A mirror becomes a line or an arc, an axis a point in the symbol of its order. That of Cu3Au, and that of hcp magnesium, whose operations include the screw axis 63:

from mdapy.visualization import plot

SYMBOLS = {6: "h", 4: "s", 3: "^", 2: "o"}


def stereogram(ax, axes, mirrors):
    turn = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 361)
    ax.plot(np.cos(turn), np.sin(turn), color="black", lw=0.8)
    for normal in map(np.array, mirrors):
        u = np.cross(normal, [0, 0, 1.0] if abs(normal[2]) < 0.9 else [1.0, 0, 0])
        u /= np.linalg.norm(u)
        circle = np.outer(np.cos(turn), u) + np.outer(np.sin(turn), np.cross(normal, u))
        circle[circle[:, 2] < -1e-9] = np.nan  # the upper half only
        ax.plot(*(circle[:, :2].T / (1 + circle[:, 2])), color="0.4", lw=0.8)
    for axis, order in axes.items():
        for end in (np.array(axis), -np.array(axis)):
            if end[2] > -1e-9:
                ax.plot(
                    *(end[:2] / (1 + end[2])),
                    SYMBOLS[order],
                    color=ORDERS[order],
                    ms=7 if order > 2 else 4.5,
                    zorder=3,
                )
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_axis_off()


magnesium = build_crystal("hcp", 3.21, c=5.21, elements="Mg")
with plot.style():
    fig, panels = plot.figure("double", 82, ncols=2)
    for ax, crystal, title in zip(
        panels, (cell, magnesium), ("Cu$_3$Au, Pm-3m: m-3m", "Mg, P6$_3$/mmc: 6/mmm")
    ):
        stereogram(ax, *symmetry_elements(SpaceGroup().compute(crystal)))
        ax.set_title(title)
    for n in (6, 4, 3, 2):
        ax.plot([], [], SYMBOLS[n], color=ORDERS[n], label=f"{n}-fold axis")
    ax.plot([], [], color="0.4", label="mirror")
    fig.legend(loc="outside right center")
    plot.save(fig, "images/space-group", formats=("png",))

Left: m-3m, the point group of Cu3Au and of every cubic metal, 48 operations: nine mirrors, three normal to the edges of the cube, one of them the equator, and six normal to the diagonals of its faces. Right: 6/mmm, that of hcp, 24 operations: a six-fold axis along c, the equator a mirror, and six mirrors and six two-fold axes about it.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning tolerance float64 1e-5 Å atoms closer than it count as images of each other

compute(system) takes the cell of a crystal, periodic in every direction, of at most 2000 atoms: spglib searches its translations pair by pair, which takes minutes for 100,000 atoms where a unit cell takes milliseconds. Atoms of different elements are different; without an element column, atoms of different types; without either, all atoms are alike. Relaxed crystals keep their symmetry to well below the default tolerance; a structure whose atoms have moved more, such as a crystal at a temperature, needs a larger one to show the symmetry of its lattice.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A SpaceGroupResult:

Attribute Type Meaning number int32 the number of the space group in the International Tables, 1 to 230 symbol str its Hermann–Mauguin symbol, such as "Fm-3m" rotations (K, 3, 3) float64 the rotations of the K symmetry operations, on Cartesian column vectors translations (K, 3) float64 their translations in Å: operation k moves the point r to rotations[k] @ r + translations[k] equivalent (N,) int64 the first atom that symmetry makes each atom equivalent to

The operations of a supercell include the translations of its lattice that are not translations of the supercell: a cubic cell of fcc has 192, four times the 48 of its primitive cell.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for a tolerance that is not positive; compute raises it for a box that is not periodic, a system without atoms or of more than 2000, and without spglib.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The space group is the group of the rotations, reflections and translations that map the crystal onto itself, each atom onto an atom of its kind. spglib (Togo et al. 2024) finds it from the lattice and the positions, within the tolerance.

docs.title: Spatial binning
docs.text:
SpatialBinning divides the box into bins of equal size along one, two or three of its vectors and reduces a property of the atoms in each: its mean, sum, sum per volume, minimum or maximum. Profiles across interfaces and surfaces, and maps over a plane, are made this way.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import SpatialBinning, SteinhardtParameters
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

# copper whose upper half is disordered like a liquid
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
melt = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(8, 8, 12))
shaking = np.where(melt["positions.z"] > 22.0, 0.6, 0.1)[:, None]
melt = melt.with_columns(
    positions=melt["positions"] + rng.normal(0, shaking, (len(melt), 3))
)
melt = melt.with_columns(SteinhardtParameters(solid=True).compute(melt))

# the fraction of solid-like atoms in 24 slabs along z
profile = SpatialBinning("solid", 24, axes="z").compute(melt)
profile.centers[0]  # Å along c, the middle of each slab
profile.values  # 1 in the crystal, near 0 above 22 Å
profile.counts  # atoms in each slab

# a map over x and z of the mean number of solid-like bonds
bonds = SpatialBinning("solid_bonds", (16, 24), axes=("x", "z")).compute(melt)
bonds.values.shape  # (16, 24)

# the solid-like atoms per Å³ in each slab
density = SpatialBinning("solid", 24, reduction="density").compute(melt)

from mdapy.visualization import plot

with plot.style():
    fig, (left, right) = plot.figure("double", 60, ncols=2)
    left.plot(profile.centers[0], profile.values, marker="o", markersize=3)
    left.set_xlabel("z (Å)")
    left.set_ylabel("Fraction of solid-like atoms")
    image = right.imshow(
        bonds.values.T,
        origin="lower",
        extent=(0, melt.box.matrix[0, 0], 0, melt.box.matrix[2, 2]),
        aspect="auto",
        vmin=0,
        vmax=12,
    )
    right.set_xlabel("x (Å)")
    right.set_ylabel("z (Å)")
    fig.colorbar(image, ax=right, label="Solid-like bonds")
    plot.save(fig, "images/spatial-binning", formats=("png",))

Left: the fraction of solid-like atoms falls from 1 to 0 across the interface at 22 Å, and rises again at the top, where the crystal below the periodic boundary orders the first layer. Right: the mean number of solid-like bonds over x and z.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning column str a column, a component such as positions.z, or an expression over the columns, as system[...] takes bins int32 or sequence of int32 the number of bins along each axis, or one number for all axes int32, str or a sequence of them "z" the box vectors binned along, one to three of 0, 1, 2 or x, y, z reduction str "mean" one of REDUCTIONS: "mean", "sum", "density" (the sum per Å³), "min", "max"

compute(system) takes the system. Along periodic vectors the atoms are wrapped into the box first; along the others, those outside the box are left out.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A SpatialBinningResult:

Attribute Type Meaning values (n1[, n2[, n3]]) float64 the reduced property in each bin, with a last axis for its components when it has several; NaN for the mean, minimum or maximum of an empty bin counts (n1[, n2[, n3]]) int64 the number of atoms in each bin centers tuple of (n,) float64 for each axis, the centers of its bins in Å along its box vector, from the origin of the box

The bins are numbered as the axes are given: values[i, j] for the bin i along the first axis and j along the second.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for no axis or more than three, an unknown or repeated axis, a number of bins that is not a positive integer or not one per axis, and an unknown reduction; compute raises it for a property the system does not have.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The bin of an atom along a box vector is \(\lfloor n s \rfloor\), with \(s\) its fractional coordinate along that vector, from 0 to below 1, and \(n\) the number of bins. The density is the sum divided by the volume of a bin, \(V / (n_1 n_2 n_3)\).

docs.title: See also
docs.text: • OVITO Spatial binning, which gives 0 for the mean, minimum and maximum of an empty bin, where SpatialBinning gives NaN, as an empty bin has no value.

docs.title: Spatial correlation function
docs.text:
SpatialCorrelation gives how a property of the atoms at one place goes with a property, the same or another, at a distance r from it: the correlation function ⟨P₁(0) P₂(r)⟩, from fast Fourier transforms on a grid up to half the box, and on request by a direct sum over the pairs of neighbors at short range, as OVITO's spatial correlation function does.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import SpatialCorrelation
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.visualization import plot

# nickel with twelve spherical copper precipitates of radius 8 Å
nickel = build_crystal("fcc", 3.55, elements="Ni", repeat=(16, 16, 16))
box = nickel.box
centers = np.random.default_rng(3).random((12, 3))
step = box.to_fractional(nickel["positions"])[:, None, :] - centers
step -= np.round(step)
inside = (np.linalg.norm(step @ box.matrix, axis=-1) < 8).any(axis=1)
alloy = nickel.with_columns(
    element=np.where(inside, "Cu", "Ni"), copper=inside.astype(float)
)

result = SpatialCorrelation("copper", direct=True, cutoff=10.0, bins=40).compute(alloy)
result.r, result.correlation  # the grid, up to half the box
result.neighbor_r, result.neighbor_correlation  # the pairs closer than 10 Å

# normalized as OVITO's plot offers it: by the pair distribution, less the
# square of the mean, over the variance
mean = result.means[0]
variance = result.mean_squares[0] - mean**2
grid = (result.correlation / result.rdf - mean**2) / variance
shells = result.neighbor_rdf > 0  # the bins of the crystal's neighbor shells
pairs = result.neighbor_correlation[shells] / result.neighbor_rdf[shells]
pairs = (pairs - mean**2) / variance
with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    ax.plot(result.r, grid, "o-", label="grid of 3 Å")
    ax.plot(result.neighbor_r[shells], pairs, "s", label="neighbor shells")
    ax.axhline(0, color="0.6", lw=0.5)
    ax.set_xlabel("r (Å)")
    ax.set_ylabel("normalized correlation")
    ax.legend()
    plot.save(fig, "images/spatial-correlation", formats=("png",))

Copper atoms go with copper atoms within the size of the precipitates: the correlation of the copper fraction falls from 0.75 at the nearest neighbors, which the atoms at the surface of a precipitate share with nickel, to none over about 16 Å, their diameter. The grid, whose cells are some 3 Å wide, blurs the shortest distances, which the shells of neighbors of the direct sum resolve.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
SpatialCorrelation(first, second=None, *, grid_spacing=3.0, window=True, direct=False, cutoff=5.0, bins=50)

Name Type Default Unit Meaning first str a column of one value per atom, a component such as "velocities.x", or an expression over the columns second str first the other property; by default the autocorrelation of the first grid_spacing float64 3.0 Å the approximate size of the cells of the grid: each box vector is cut into as many cells of at least this length as fit window bool True weight the atoms by a Hann window along the box vectors that are not periodic, which takes away the ringing of the edges of the box direct bool False also sum the correlation over the pairs of neighbors closer than cutoff cutoff float64 5.0 Å the reach of the direct sum bins int32 50 the number of bins of the direct sum

compute(system) takes the atoms in their box; along the periodic box vectors atoms outside the box count in the cells they fold back into, along the others they are left out.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A SpatialCorrelationResult:

Attribute Type Unit Meaning r (bins,) float64 Å the centers of the distance bins of the grid, each as wide as half the shortest distance between opposite faces of the box over their number correlation (bins,) float64 the correlation function from the grid rdf (bins,) float64 the radial distribution function of the same grid q (wavevectors,) float64 1/Å the centers of the wavevector bins reciprocal (wavevectors,) float64 the correlation function in reciprocal space; of two properties equal to 1, the structure factor means (2,) float64 the mean of each property over the atoms mean_squares (2,) float64 the mean of the square of each property mean_product float64 the mean over the atoms of the product of the two properties neighbor_r (bins,) float64 or None Å the centers of the bins of the direct sum, with direct neighbor_correlation (bins,) float64 or None the correlation function summed over the pairs of neighbors, with direct neighbor_rdf (bins,) float64 or None the radial distribution function of the pairs of neighbors, with direct

These are OVITO's tables correlation-real-space, correlation-real-space-rdf, correlation-reciprocal-space, correlation-neighbor and correlation-neighbor-rdf, and its attributes mean1, mean2, variance1, variance2 and covariance, which are the means, the mean squares and the mean product. OVITO's plots offer three normalizations, each a line of NumPy as above: by the radial distribution function, correlation / rdf; by the covariance, (correlation - means.prod()) / (mean_product - means.prod()); and the difference correlation, (mean_squares.sum() / 2) - correlation. Atoms whose value is NaN are left out of the grid and make the means NaN.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: SpatialCorrelation raises InvalidParameter for a grid spacing or a cutoff that is not positive, and a number of bins that is not a positive integer; compute raises it for a property that is not one number per atom, a system of no atoms, and a grid spacing larger than a quarter of the shortest distance between opposite faces of the box.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Each property is summed over the atoms in the cells of a grid of \(n_a \times n_b \times n_c\) cells along the box vectors, \(n_a\) the length of \(\mathbf a\) over the grid spacing, rounded down; an atom falls in the cell its fractional coordinates times \(n\) give, rounded toward zero. With \(\hat P_1\), \(\hat P_2\) and \(\hat\rho\) the discrete Fourier transforms of the grids of the two properties and of the number of atoms,

\[ C(\mathbf q) = \frac{V}{N^2}\,\operatorname{Re}\,\hat P_1(\mathbf q)\,\hat P_2^*(\mathbf q), \qquad C(\mathbf r) = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{\mathbf q} \hat P_1(\mathbf q)\,\hat P_2^*(\mathbf q)\,e^{i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r}, \]

the second of which, with \(|\hat\rho|^2\), gives the radial distribution function of the grid. Both are averaged over the grid points in shells of \(|\mathbf q|\) or \(|\mathbf r|\), leaving out the origin. The direct sum adds \(P_1(i)\,P_2(j)\) over the ordered pairs closer than the cutoff in bins of its distance and divides by \(N^2 / V\) times the volume of the shell of each bin, as the radial distribution function does.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• OVITO Spatial correlation function.
  • Radial distribution function and structure factor.

docs.title: Chemical species
docs.text:
ChemicalSpecies finds the molecules of a system, the groups of atoms joined by bonds, and their chemical formulas, from the radii of the elements or bond lengths given by hand; and counts the molecules of each formula along a trajectory, as the products of reactions form.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.analysis import ChemicalSpecies

# two water molecules and a carbon dioxide in a 20 Å box
water = np.array([[0, 0, 0.119], [0, 0.763, -0.477], [0, -0.763, -0.477]])
co2 = np.array([[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1.16], [0, 0, -1.16]])
positions = np.vstack([water + 2, water + 8, co2 + 14])
system = mp.System(
    positions, mp.Box(20.0), elements=["O", "H", "H"] * 2 + ["C", "O", "O"]
)

result = ChemicalSpecies().compute(system)
result.formulas  # ['H2O', 'H2O', 'CO2']
result.counts()  # formula and count: H2O 2, CO2 1
system = system.with_columns(result)  # the column 'molecule', from 1

# by the van der Waals radii, as VMD and OVITO bond atoms
vdw = ChemicalSpecies("vdw").compute(system)

A box of 64 molecules of three kinds, each kind in its own color:

from mdapy.visualization import render

methane = np.array([[0, 0, 0], [0.629, 0.629, 0.629], [-0.629, -0.629, 0.629],
                    [-0.629, 0.629, -0.629], [0.629, -0.629, -0.629]])  # fmt: skip
kinds = [
    (water, ["O", "H", "H"]),
    (co2, ["C", "O", "O"]),
    (methane, ["C", "H", "H", "H", "H"]),
]
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
grid = (
    np.stack(np.meshgrid(*[np.arange(4)] * 3, indexing="ij"), -1).reshape(-1, 3) * 5.0
    + 2.5
)
positions, elements = [], []
for center in grid:  # a molecule of a random kind, turned at random, near each point
    shape, names = kinds[rng.integers(3)]
    turn = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(3, 3)))[0]
    positions.append(shape @ turn.T + center + rng.normal(0, 0.6, 3))
    elements += names
gas = mp.System(np.vstack(positions), mp.Box(20.0), elements=elements)

found = ChemicalSpecies().compute(gas)
found.counts()  # CH4 28, CO2 19, H2O 17
kind = np.asarray(found.formulas)[found.molecule - 1]
palette = {"H2O": [0.2, 0.5, 0.9], "CO2": [0.9, 0.4, 0.2], "CH4": [0.3, 0.75, 0.4]}
render(gas, "images/species.png", color=np.array([palette[k] for k in kind]),
       representation="ball_and_stick", width=800, height=700, legend=palette)  # fmt: skip

Water in blue, carbon dioxide in orange and methane in green: every atom takes the color of the formula of its molecule.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
ChemicalSpecies(radii="covalent", *, scale=None, tolerance=None, cutoffs=None)

Name Type Default Unit Meaning radii str or dict of str to float64 "covalent" Å the radius of each element: "covalent", the covalent radii, "vdw", the van der Waals radii, or radii by element such as {"H": 0.4, "O": 0.7} scale float64 0.6 with "vdw", else 1 factor on the sum of the radii of two atoms tolerance float64 0.45 with "covalent", else 0 Å length added to it cutoffs dict of (str, str) to float64 None Å bond lengths for pairs of elements (a, b), in either order, instead of the radii; 0 for pairs never bonded

Two atoms are bonded when they are closer than \(s(r_i + r_j) + t\), with \(r\) their radii, \(s\) the scale and \(t\) the tolerance, or than the cutoff of their pair of elements. Two rules come ready:

  • "covalent", the default: the covalent radii plus 0.45 Å, the rule of Jmol and OpenBabel, and of the bonds MDAPY draws in pictures;
  • "vdw": 0.6 of the van der Waals radii, without tolerance, and two hydrogen atoms never bonded, the rule of VMD and of OVITO's Create bonds in its van der Waals mode. VMD and OVITO have tables of radii of their own, so their bonds can differ from these. A cutoff for ("H", "H") bonds hydrogen atoms again, as in the H2 molecule.

Hydrogen bonds and other contacts are left out by both. Radii by element default to a scale of 1 and no tolerance: atoms closer than the sum of their radii.

compute(system, *, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis; neighbors must reach the longest bond. bond_lengths(elements) gives the bond length of each pair of elements.

count(frames) computes each frame and gives a table of the number of molecules of each formula in each frame: a frame column and a column for each formula, the most common first.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A SpeciesResult:

Attribute or method Type Meaning molecule (N,) int64 the molecule of each atom, numbered from 1 by decreasing size, ties by their first atom formulas (M,) str the chemical formula of each molecule sizes (M,) int64 the number of atoms of each molecule counts() polars DataFrame formula and count, the most common first

The column is molecule, the molecule ID of LAMMPS data files. Formulas are in Hill order: carbon, then hydrogen, then the other elements alphabetically, or all alphabetically without carbon, so that ammonia is H3N and sodium chloride ClNa; isomers have the same formula.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for unknown radii, elements or pairs, radii that are not positive, a scale that is not positive, a negative tolerance or cutoff; compute raises MissingProperty without an element column and InvalidParameter for an element without a radius, such as "X", unless cutoffs cover its pairs.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Molecules are the clusters of atoms joined by bonds, across periodic boundaries too. The covalent radii are those of Cordero et al. (2008), the van der Waals radii those of Alvarez (2013), both in mdapy.elements.

docs.title: Steinhardt parameters
docs.text:
SteinhardtParameters gives the bond-orientational order parameters \(q_l\) of each atom, which tell crystals, liquids and glasses apart, plain or averaged over the neighbors, with neighbors by number, by distance or by Voronoi cell, optionally weighted by the areas of the Voronoi faces; with solid, it also tells the solid-like atoms from the liquid-like ones by the order their bonds share.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import SteinhardtParameters
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

# fcc copper of 3 x 3 x 3 cubic cells
system = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(3, 3, 3))

result = SteinhardtParameters(degrees=(4, 6), num_neighbors=12).compute(system)
result[6]  # q6 of each atom: 0.574524 in fcc
averaged = SteinhardtParameters(cutoff=3.0, average=True).compute(system)
weighted = SteinhardtParameters(voronoi=True, weighted=True).compute(system)
system = system.with_columns(result)  # columns q4 and q6

The averaged parameters tell the structures apart even when the atoms are shaken by 0.15 Å:

from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.visualization import plot

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
crystals = {
    "fcc": build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(5, 5, 5)),
    "hcp": build_crystal("hcp", 3.21, elements="Mg", repeat=(6, 6, 4)),
    "bcc": build_crystal("bcc", 2.87, elements="Fe", repeat=(6, 6, 6)),
}
with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    for name, crystal in crystals.items():
        shaken = crystal.with_columns(
            positions=crystal["positions"] + rng.normal(0, 0.15, (len(crystal), 3))
        )
        neighbors = 14 if name == "bcc" else 12  # bcc: the first two shells
        q = SteinhardtParameters(
            degrees=(4, 6), num_neighbors=neighbors, average=True
        ).compute(shaken)
        ax.scatter(q[4], q[6], s=2, alpha=0.6, label=name)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$\bar q_4$")
    ax.set_ylabel(r"$\bar q_6$")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, markerscale=4)
    plot.save(fig, "images/steinhardt", formats=("png",))

Each atom of the three crystals as a point: fcc, hcp and bcc fall in separate clouds, as in Lechner and Dellago (2008).

With solid, each atom gets its number of solid-like bonds, those to neighbors whose harmonics of degree 6 are nearly parallel to its own, and is solid-like with at least 7: copper whose upper half is disordered like a liquid, the lower half shaken as at a high temperature:

from mdapy.visualization import render

melt = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(8, 8, 12))
upper = melt["positions"][:, 2] > 22.0
shake = (
    rng.normal(0, 0.1, (len(melt), 3))
    + rng.normal(0, 0.6, (len(melt), 3)) * upper[:, None]
)
melt = melt.with_columns(positions=melt["positions"] + shake)

phases = SteinhardtParameters(solid=True).compute(melt)
phases.solid  # True for the solid-like atoms
phases.solid_bonds  # their solid-like bonds, of 12
melt = melt.with_columns(phases)  # columns q4, q6, solid and solid_bonds

side = [0, -1, 0.15]
render(
    melt,
    "images/steinhardt-solid.png",
    color=phases.solid_bonds,
    value_range=(0, 12),
    view=side,
    legend="solid bonds",
)

The solid-like bonds of each atom, from 0 (dark) to 12 (yellow): all 12 in the crystal, few in the disordered half, a few layers in between at the interfaces, the lower one across the periodic boundary.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning degrees sequence of int32 (4, 6) the degrees \(l\), from 0 to 20 num_neighbors int32 None the number of nearest neighbors; 12 when neither it, cutoff nor voronoi is given cutoff float64 None Å instead, the neighbors are closer than it voronoi bool False instead, the neighbors share a face of the Voronoi cell weighted bool False with voronoi, weight each neighbor by the area of its face average bool False average the \(q_{lm}\) over the atom and its neighbors solid bool False also count the solid-like bonds of each atom and tell the solid-like atoms solid_degree int32 6 with solid, the degree \(l\) of the harmonics of the bonds bond_threshold float64 0.7 with solid, a bond is solid-like when the normalized product of the harmonics of its atoms exceeds it min_solid_bonds int32 7 with solid, an atom is solid-like with at least so many solid-like bonds

compute(system, *, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis. A given neighbor list must reach the cutoff, hold the num_neighbors nearest neighbors of every atom, or, with voronoi, be a list of Voronoi neighbors, whose thresholds then choose the faces; without one, every face of a cell counts. The walls of a box that is not periodic are not neighbors.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A SteinhardtResult:

Attribute or method Type Meaning degrees tuple of int32 the degrees q (N, degrees) float64 \(q_l\) of each atom, one column per degree; 0 for an atom without neighbors average bool whether the parameters are averaged result[l] (N,) float64 the parameter of degree \(l\) solid_bonds (N,) int32 with solid, the number of solid-like bonds of each atom; else None solid (N,) bool with solid, whether each atom is solid-like; else None

Its columns are q4, q6, …, with the options in their names, in this order: q6_average, q6_voronoi, q6_average_voronoi, q6_voronoi_weighted, and with solid also solid and solid_bonds.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for a degree outside 0 to 20, more than one of num_neighbors, cutoff and voronoi, either number not positive, weighted without voronoi, a solid_degree that is not an integer from 0 to 20, a bond_threshold outside −1 to 1, or a min_solid_bonds that is not an integer of at least 0; compute raises it for a neighbor list that does not fit or, with voronoi, two atoms at the same position, and result[l] for a degree not computed.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For the \(N_b(i)\) neighbors \(j\) of atom \(i\), with \(\hat{\mathbf r}_{ij}\) the direction to \(j\) and \(Y_{lm}\) the spherical harmonics,

\[ q_{lm}(i) = \frac{1}{N_b(i)} \sum_{j} Y_{lm}(\hat{\mathbf r}_{ij}), \qquad q_l(i) = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{2l + 1} \sum_{m=-l}^{l} \lvert q_{lm}(i) \rvert^2 } . \]

With weighted, each neighbor counts by the area \(A_{ij}\) of the face it shares with atom \(i\), so that a small face, which a tiny displacement can create or remove, adds little:

\[ q_{lm}(i) = \frac{1}{\sum_j A_{ij}} \sum_{j} A_{ij}\, Y_{lm}(\hat{\mathbf r}_{ij}) . \]

With average, the \(q_{lm}\) of each atom are first averaged over the atom and its neighbors, which separates crystal structures more sharply:

\[ \bar q_{lm}(i) = \frac{1}{N_b(i) + 1} \Big( q_{lm}(i) + \sum_{j} q_{lm}(j) \Big), \]

and \(\bar q_l\) is formed from them as \(q_l\), the average itself unweighted. Values for perfect lattices:

Lattice Neighbors \(q_4\) \(q_6\) fcc 12, or Voronoi 0.190941 0.574524 hcp 12, or Voronoi 0.097222 0.484762 bcc 8 0.509175 0.628539 bcc 14, or Voronoi 0.036369 0.510688 bcc Voronoi, weighted 0.224025 0.566940 icosahedron 12 0 0.663325

With solid, the bond between atom \(i\) and its neighbor \(j\) is solid-like when the harmonics of the two atoms, of degree \(l\) = solid_degree, point alike:

\[ d_l(i, j) = \frac{\operatorname{Re} \sum_{m=-l}^{l} q_{lm}(i)\, q_{lm}(j)^*} {\sqrt{\sum_m \lvert q_{lm}(i) \rvert^2} \sqrt{\sum_m \lvert q_{lm}(j) \rvert^2}} > d_c , \]

\(d_c\) = bond_threshold, from the plain \(q_{lm}\) (not averaged), with the neighbors and weights above; an atom with at least min_solid_bonds such bonds is solid-like (ten Wolde et al. 1996). For \(l = 6\), \(d_c = 0.7\) and 6 to 8 bonds suit fcc and bcc crystals (Filion et al. 2010); in a perfect crystal every bond is solid-like, \(d_6 = 1\). An atom without neighbors has no bonds.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• OVITO Steinhardt parameters.
  • LAMMPS compute orientorder/atom.
  • freud SolidLiquid, the same solid-like bonds and atoms.

Please cite

Steinhardt et al. (1983); with average, also Lechner and Dellago (2008); with weighted, also Mickel et al. (2013); with solid, also ten Wolde et al. (1996).

docs.title: Structure factor
docs.text:
StructureFactor gives the static structure factor S(q) of a periodic system and its partial factors for each pair of elements, by the exact sum over wave vectors or, for large systems, from the radial distribution function.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import StructureFactor
from mdapy.build import build_crystal, random_alloy

# a random Cu-Ni alloy on a disordered fcc lattice of 4 x 4 x 4 cubic cells
crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.6, elements="Cu", repeat=(4, 4, 4))
shake = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(0, 0.1, (len(crystal), 3))
disordered = crystal.with_columns(positions=crystal["positions"] + shake)
system = random_alloy(disordered, {"Cu": 0.5, "Ni": 0.5}, seed=0)

direct = StructureFactor(q_max=6.0, bins=60).compute(system)
direct.q, direct.s  # bin centers in 1/Å and S(q)
direct.faber_ziman["Ni", "Cu"]  # a Faber-Ziman partial factor
debye = StructureFactor(q_max=6.0, bins=60, method="debye", cutoff=7.2).compute(system)

from mdapy.visualization import plot

with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    plot.structure_factor(direct, ax=ax)
    plot.save(fig, "images/structure-factor", formats=("png",))

The disordered alloy scatters at the (111), (200), (220) and (311) reflections of fcc, \(q = 2\pi\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2}/a\) = 3.02, 3.49, 4.94 and 5.79 Å⁻¹; between them \(S(q)\) stays near zero.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning q_max float64 1/Å largest \(\lvert \mathbf q \rvert\) bins int32 200 number of bins of equal width from 0 to q_max method str "direct" "direct", the sum over the wave vectors that fit the box, or "debye", the transform of the radial distribution function cutoff float64 None Å with the Debye method, the largest distance of the radial distribution function; default half the length of the longest lattice vector

compute(system, *, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis; the box must be periodic in every direction. With the Debye method, a given neighbor list must reach cutoff. Partial factors need an element column.

The direct method costs the number of wave vectors, about \(q_\text{max}^3 V / (12\pi^2)\) for a box of volume \(V\), times the number of atoms. The Debye method costs a radial distribution function up to cutoff, which can be chosen well below half the box for large systems.

A StructureFactorResult:

Attribute or method Type Meaning q (bins,) float64 bin centers in 1/Å edges (bins + 1,) float64 bin edges in 1/Å s (bins,) float64 S(q); with the direct method NaN in bins without wave vectors vectors (bins,) int64 or None with the direct method, the number of wave vectors in each bin, one of each pair \(\pm\mathbf q\) partial dict of (str, str) to (bins,) float64 \(S_{ab}(q)\) of each pair of elements (a, b), a not after b by atomic number faber_ziman dict of (str, str) to (bins,) float64 \(A_{ab}(q)\), keyed as partial method str "direct" or "debye" pair(a, b) (bins,) float64 \(S_{ab}(q)\), with a and b in either order

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for a q_max that is not positive, fewer than one bin, an unknown method, or a cutoff that is not positive or given to the direct method; compute raises it for a box that is not periodic in every direction, a neighbor list given to the direct method or one that does not fit, more than 108 wave vectors for the direct method, which would take 1.6 GB, and pair for a pair of elements without a factor.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
With \(\rho_a(\mathbf q) = \sum_{j \in a} e^{i\mathbf q \cdot \mathbf r_j}\) the density of element \(a\) at wave vector \(\mathbf q\) and \(N\) the number of atoms,

\[ S(\mathbf q) = \frac{1}{N} \Big| \sum_j e^{i\mathbf q \cdot \mathbf r_j} \Big|^2, \qquad S_{ab}(\mathbf q) = \frac{1}{N} \operatorname{Re}\big[\rho_a(\mathbf q)\, \rho_b(\mathbf q)^*\big], \]

so that \(S = \sum_a S_{aa} + 2 \sum_{a < b} S_{ab}\). The direct method averages these over the wave vectors \(\mathbf q = h\mathbf b_1 + k\mathbf b_2 + l\mathbf b_3\) of the box, \(\mathbf b\) its reciprocal vectors, in each bin of \(0 < |\mathbf q| \le q_\text{max}\). A perfect crystal gives \(N\) at its Bragg reflections and 0 elsewhere; an ideal gas gives 1.

The Debye method transforms the radial distribution function \(g\) and its partial functions \(g_{ab}\), computed up to the cutoff \(r_c\) in bins of 0.01 Å, with a window \(w(r) = \sin(\pi r / r_c) / (\pi r / r_c)\) against the ripples of the cutoff, at the number density \(\rho = N / V\):

\[ S(q) = 1 + \frac{4\pi\rho}{q} \int_0^{r_c} r\, \big[g(r) - 1\big] \sin(qr)\, w(r)\, \mathrm dr , \]

and \(A_{ab}(q)\) the same with \(g_{ab}\). The integral is the sum over the bins at their centers.

The Faber–Ziman partial factors, which tend to 1 at large \(q\), and the partial factors are related by

\[ A_{ab}(q) = \frac{S_{ab}(q) - x_a \delta_{ab}}{x_a x_b} + 1 , \]

with the fractions \(x_a = N_a / N\); these are the conventions of OVITO.

docs.title: Why the results differ from OVITO
docs.text:
MDAPY follows the definitions above. OVITO's structure factor modifier (3.17.1) makes two other choices, so that its curves differ from those of MDAPY although the sums are the same: computed with OVITO's choices, MDAPY gives OVITO's numbers.

  • Direct method: OVITO averages over the wave vectors with \(h, k, l \ge 0\) only, an eighth of them. As \(\mathbf q\) and \(-\mathbf q\) give the same value, this leaves out the vectors of mixed signs, such as \((1, -1, 0)\). In a cubic crystal these are equivalent to vectors kept, but a family of equivalent vectors then counts by how many of its members have zero components; in a crystal of lower symmetry, a strained or textured one, or a small disordered system, they carry other values that OVITO's average misses. MDAPY averages over every wave vector, one of each pair \(\pm\mathbf q\).
  • Debye method: OVITO transforms \(g(r)\) rather than \(g(r) - 1\). The difference, \(\frac{4\pi\rho}{q} \int_0^{r_c} r \sin(qr)\, w(r)\, \mathrm dr\), is the transform of a uniform density inside \(r_c\): it holds nothing of the structure, grows without bound as \(q \to 0\) and decays with ripples at large \(q\). MDAPY leaves it out, so that \(S(q)\) tends to 1 at large \(q\) and stays finite at small \(q\).

The alloy above with both integrands:

cutoff = 7.2
r = (np.arange(720) + 0.5) * 0.01  # the bins of the radial distribution function
window = np.sinc(r / cutoff)  # sin(πr/cutoff) / (πr/cutoff)
density = len(system) / system.box.volume
uniform = (
    4
    * np.pi
    * density
    / debye.q
    * (r * np.sin(np.outer(debye.q, r)) * window).sum(axis=1)
    * 0.01
)

with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    ax.plot(debye.q, debye.s + uniform, label="with g(r), as OVITO")
    ax.plot(debye.q, debye.s, label="with g(r) − 1, mdapy")
    ax.set_xlabel("q (1/Å)")
    ax.set_ylabel("S(q)")
    ax.set_ylim(-2, 8)
    ax.legend()
    plot.save(fig, "images/structure-factor-ovito", formats=("png",))

The Debye structure factor of the alloy from \(g(r)\), as OVITO computes it, and from \(g(r) - 1\): the transform of the uniform density that sets them apart dominates below 2 Å⁻¹; above, the two nearly agree.

docs.title: Surface mesh
docs.text:
SurfaceMesh finds the surface of the solid the atoms make: the outside of a particle, the two faces of a slab, the walls of the voids and pores in a crystal. The surface is a mesh of triangles through the outer atoms, found by the alpha-shape method: the space a probe sphere cannot enter is solid. With regions=True the solid and the empty space are also split into connected regions, among them the voids, with the volume and the area of each.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import SurfaceMesh
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(14, 14, 14))
box = crystal.box
keep = np.ones(len(crystal), dtype=bool)
# voids of radius 7, 5 and 6 Å, the last around a corner of the box
for center, radius in [
    ((0.3, 0.3, 0.5), 7.0),
    ((0.7, 0.65, 0.4), 5.0),
    ((0, 0, 0), 6.0),
]:
    away = box.minimum_image(crystal["positions"] - np.array(center) @ box.matrix)
    keep &= np.linalg.norm(away, axis=1) > radius
system = crystal.filter(keep)

result = SurfaceMesh(radius=4.0, regions=True, surface=True).compute(system)
result.area  # Å², 1504: the walls of the voids
result.solid_volume  # Å³, 126360 of the 129631 of the box
regions = result.regions
voids = regions.voids  # the empty regions closed on every side: [1, 2, 3]
regions.volume[voids]  # Å³, [1181, 598, 1492]
regions.area[voids]  # Å², [536, 319, 649]
result.mesh  # TriangleMesh(166 vertices, 320 triangles, periodic)
system = system.with_columns(result)  # surface: the 166 atoms on it

A particle in a box that is not periodic is surrounded by the exterior, an empty region without end:

from mdapy import Box

block = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(10, 10, 10))
middle = block.box.matrix.sum(axis=0) / 2
ball = block.filter(np.linalg.norm(block["positions"] - middle, axis=1) < 15)
particle = ball.with_box(Box(block.box.matrix, pbc=False))

outside = SurfaceMesh(regions=True).compute(particle)
outside.regions.exterior  # [True, False]: the space around, then the particle
outside.regions.volume  # Å³, [inf, 12062]
outside.area  # Å², 2570, through the centers of the outer atoms

The voids, each in its own color, the particle as it is and smoothed, drawn by the renderer:

from mdapy.visualization import render, write_png

colors = np.array([(0.84, 0.37, 0.0), (0.0, 0.45, 0.7), (0.0, 0.62, 0.45)])
empty = regions.faces[:, 1]  # the empty region on the outer side of each triangle
pictures = [
    render(
        system,
        atoms=np.zeros(len(system), dtype=bool),
        mesh=result.mesh,
        mesh_color=colors[np.searchsorted(voids, empty)],
        width=500,
        height=500,
    )
]
for smoothing in (0, 8):
    mesh = SurfaceMesh(smoothing=smoothing).compute(particle).mesh
    pictures.append(
        render(particle, radius=0.5, mesh=mesh, box=False, width=500, height=500)
    )
write_png("images/surface-mesh.png", np.hstack(pictures))

Left: the three voids; the one around a corner of the box is cut by its faces and seen in all eight corners. Middle: the surface of a copper particle through the centers of its outer atoms, drawn small. Right: the same surface after 8 smoothing steps.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning radius float64 4 Å radius of the probe sphere; larger than the distance between neighbors and smaller than the voids looked for smoothing int32 8 the number of smoothing steps of the mesh, which round its shape and leave the volumes as they are regions bool False also split the solid and the empty space into regions, and find the voids surface bool False also mark the atoms on the surface

compute(system, *, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the progress and cancel of every analysis, but no neighbor list. No two atoms may be at the same position. Out of a box that is not periodic is empty space.

A smaller probe fits into smaller gaps: a probe smaller than the distance between neighbors sees the gaps between the atoms of a crystal as empty, one as large as a void fills it. The volumes and the areas of the regions do not depend on the smoothing; the area of the mesh does.

docs.text:
A SurfaceMeshResult:

Attribute Type Meaning mesh TriangleMesh the surface, its normals pointing out of the solid atoms (V,) int64 the atom at each vertex of the mesh area float64 the area of the surface in Å² solid_volume float64 the volume of the solid in Å³ regions SurfaceRegions or None the regions, with regions=True surface (N,) bool or None whether each atom lies on the surface, with surface=True; its column surface

A SurfaceRegions:

Attribute Type Meaning solid (R,) bool whether each region is solid volume (R,) float64 the volume of each region in Å³; infinite for the exterior area (R,) float64 the area of the surface around each region in Å² exterior (R,) bool whether the region is the empty space around the atoms, out of a box that is not periodic; the first region when there is one periodic (R,) bool whether the region runs across a periodic boundary into its own image, without end, as the vacuum over a slab faces (F, 2) int64 the solid and the empty region on the two sides of each triangle of the mesh voids (K,) int64 the empty regions that are neither exterior nor periodic: closed by the solid on every side

In a periodic box the volumes of the regions add up to that of the box. OVITO also calls the vacuum over a slab a void; here it is periodic and not among the voids.

docs.title: Triangle meshes
docs.text:
A TriangleMesh, also mdapy.analysis.TriangleMesh, holds any mesh of triangles, across periodic boundaries too:

Attribute or method Type Meaning vertices (V, 3) float64 the positions of the vertices in Å faces (F, 3) int64 the vertices of each triangle, counterclockwise seen from the side its normal points to shifts (F, 3, 3) int8 or None the periodic image of each corner: corner k of triangle f is at vertices[faces[f, k]] + shifts[f, k] @ box.matrix box Box or None the box of the periodic images corners() (F, 3, 3) float64 the corners of each triangle in Å, each triangle whole areas (F,) float64 the area of each triangle in Å² area float64 their sum normals (F, 3) float64 the unit normal of each triangle, zero for one without area pieces() (T, 3, 3) float64, (T,) int64 the triangles cut at the periodic faces of the box and moved into it, and the triangle of each piece

TriangleMesh(vertices, faces, shifts=None, box=None) makes one; like a Box it cannot be changed. render(system, mesh=...) draws it as its pieces(), with mesh_color one color or one per triangle and mesh_alpha its opacity.

mesh = result.mesh
corners = mesh.corners()  # (F, 3, 3) Å, each triangle whole
mesh.normals  # (F, 3) out of the solid: into the voids
pieces, triangle = mesh.pieces()  # in the box, for drawing elsewhere

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for a radius that is not positive and a smoothing that is not an integer of at least 0; compute raises it for a periodic box so short that an atom meets its own periodic image across a cell of the tessellation (replicate the system first). TriangleMesh raises it for arrays of the wrong shape, vertices that are not finite, faces of vertices that do not exist, and shifts without a box.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The atoms, periodic images included, are divided into the tetrahedra of their Delaunay tessellation: no atom lies inside the sphere through the four corners of a tetrahedron. A tetrahedron is solid when the radius \(R\) of that sphere is smaller than the probe radius \(r\),

\[ R < r , \]

the others and the space outside the tessellation empty: the alpha shape of the atoms. The surface is made of the faces between a solid and an empty tetrahedron, turned so that their normals point to the empty side; its vertices are the atoms on it, one for each sheet of the surface through the atom, as where two pores touch at an atom. The volume of the solid is that of its tetrahedra. Solid tetrahedra that share faces make a region, and so do empty ones; a region that meets itself in another periodic image runs without end. OVITO joins two empty regions also where their surfaces meet along an edge, so in a very porous solid it finds fewer and larger empty regions: in fcc with 30 % and 50 % of its atoms removed at random, 28 and 12 where MDAPY finds 38 and 79. Pores that touch only along a line are apart here, as no probe passes between them.

Smoothing moves every vertex \(\mathbf x\) toward the mean of its \(n\) neighbors along the edges of the mesh,

\[ \mathbf x \leftarrow \mathbf x + \frac{\lambda}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} (\mathbf x_k - \mathbf x) , \]

once with \(\lambda = 0.5\) and once with \(\mu = 1/(0.1 - 1/\lambda) \approx -0.53\) per step, which rounds the mesh without shrinking it (Taubin), with the factors OVITO takes.

The tessellation of a perfect crystal is not unique: four atoms of a square can be split into two triangles along either diagonal. The atoms are moved at random by up to \(10^{-4}\) Å first, always the same way, which settles each such choice. The area and the volumes are those of either choice; the smoothed mesh can differ from OVITO's where OVITO chose otherwise.

Please cite

Edelsbrunner and Mücke (1994) and Stukowski (2014); with smoothing Taubin (1995).

docs.title: Atomic temperature
docs.text:
AtomicTemperature gives each atom the temperature of the group formed by the atom and its neighbors, from their velocities relative to the group's center of mass; it shows hot spots, for example around a collision cascade or a moving crack.

import numpy as np
from mdapy import units
from mdapy.analysis import AtomicTemperature
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

# an fcc Cu crystal of 6 x 6 x 6 cubic cells with velocities at 300 K
a = 3.615
system = build_crystal("fcc", a, elements="Cu", repeat=(6, 6, 6))
mass = 63.546  # amu
spread = np.sqrt(units.BOLTZMANN * 300 / (mass * units.AMU_A2_PER_PS2_TO_EV))
velocities = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(scale=spread, size=(len(system), 3))
system = system.with_columns(velocities=velocities)  # Å/ps

result = AtomicTemperature(cutoff=3.0).compute(system)
result.temperature.mean()  # about 300 K
system = system.with_columns(result)  # the column 'temperature'

A thermal spike: atoms near the middle of a larger crystal move as if at 2300 K, the others at 300 K:

from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.visualization import render

crystal = build_crystal("fcc", a, elements="Cu", repeat=(14, 14, 14))
x = crystal["positions"] - crystal.box.matrix.diagonal() / 2
kelvin = 300 + 2000 * np.exp(-(x**2).sum(axis=1) / (2 * 8.0**2))
spread = np.sqrt(units.BOLTZMANN * kelvin / (mass * units.AMU_A2_PER_PS2_TO_EV))
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
spike = crystal.with_columns(velocities=rng.normal(size=x.shape) * spread[:, None])

local = AtomicTemperature(cutoff=5.0).compute(spike).temperature
render(spike, "images/temperature.png", atoms=x[:, 1] < 0, color=local, colormap="coolwarm",
       value_range=(0, 2400), width=800, height=700, legend="temperature (K)")  # fmt: skip

The crystal cut through the middle: the temperature averaged over the neighbors within 5 Å, from 300 K (blue) to about 2000 K in the core (red).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning cutoff float64 Å the neighbors closer than it form the group of an atom

compute(system, *, neighbors=None, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the arguments of every analysis. A given neighbor list must reach cutoff; without one, the neighbors are found and used at once, never stored. The system needs the velocities in Å/ps and the mass column in amu, else an element column for the standard atomic weights.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A TemperatureResult:

Attribute Type Meaning temperature (N,) float64 the temperature in K of each atom and its neighbors; NaN for an atom without neighbors; its column temperature

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for a cutoff that is not positive; compute raises it for a neighbor list that does not fit, and MissingProperty without velocities or without both mass and element.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For the group \(G_i\) of atom \(i\) and its neighbors closer than the cutoff, \(n_i\) atoms with masses \(m_j\) and velocities \(\mathbf v_j\),

\[ T_i = \frac{1}{3(n_i - 1)\, k_B} \sum_{j \in G_i} m_j \lvert \mathbf v_j - \bar{\mathbf v}_i \rvert^2 , \qquad \bar{\mathbf v}_i = \frac{\sum_{j \in G_i} m_j \mathbf v_j}{\sum_{j \in G_i} m_j} . \]

Removing the motion of the center of mass takes three of the \(3 n_i\) degrees of freedom, so that a group in equilibrium at a temperature \(T\) has \(T_i = T\) on average and a uniform drift of the atoms changes nothing. Periodic images of the atom itself are not counted.

docs.title: Time averages
docs.text:
TimeAverage gives the mean of a quantity over the frames of a trajectory: a column of the atoms, such as their positions, the box, or anything a function computes from a frame, such as a radial distribution function, as OVITO's time averaging does. Averaged positions take the thermal vibrations out of a crystal, so that its structure shows clearly.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import RadialDistributionFunction, TimeAverage
from mdapy.build import build_crystal
from mdapy.identify import CommonNeighborAnalysis

# copper whose atoms vibrate about their sites, 0.18 Å along each axis
copper = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(8, 8, 8))
copper = copper.with_columns(id=np.arange(1, len(copper) + 1))
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
frames = [
    copper.with_columns(
        positions=copper["positions"] + rng.normal(0, 0.18, (len(copper), 3))
    )
    for _ in range(20)
]

positions = TimeAverage("positions").compute(frames)  # (N, 3)
averaged = frames[0].with_columns(positions=positions.value)
rdf = TimeAverage(lambda f: RadialDistributionFunction(6.0).compute(f).g)
mean_g = rdf.compute(frames).value  # the mean g(r) over the frames

The common neighbor analysis of one frame and of the averaged positions:

from mdapy.visualization import render, write_png

cna = CommonNeighborAnalysis()
one, mean = cna.compute(frames[0]), cna.compute(averaged)
options = dict(view="iso", width=500, height=500)
write_png(
    "images/time-average.png",
    np.hstack(
        [
            render(frames[0], color=one, **options, legend=True),
            render(averaged, color=mean, **options, legend=True),
        ]
    ),
)

Left: one frame, in which the vibrations leave half of the atoms unrecognized (white) among the fcc atoms (green). Right: the positions averaged over 20 frames, all fcc.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
TimeAverage(quantity, *, unwrap=True)

Name Type Default Unit Meaning quantity str or callable a column of numbers of the atoms, such as "positions" or "csp"; "box" for the lattice vectors; or a function of a frame that gives a number, or an array of the same shape in every frame unwrap bool True for positions: follow the atoms through the periodic boundaries, or average the positions as they are

compute(frames) takes an iterable of systems, such as a Trajectory or a slice of one, read one at a time. For a column the atoms are matched by their ids, as for the mean squared displacement, and positions are unwrapped in the same way: by the image flags, or else through the nearest periodic image of each step. OVITO's time averaging instead takes the atoms in the order they come and needs the positions unwrapped beforehand.

docs.text:
A TimeAverageResult:

Attribute Type Meaning value float64 the mean: of each atom in the order of the first frame for a column, (3, 3) for the box, of the shape of the function otherwise num_frames int32 the number of frames name str or None the column; system.with_columns(result) adds name_average, a component such as positions.z written positions_z_average

docs.text: compute raises InvalidParameter when there are no frames, as the mean squared displacement does for frames of other atoms, for a column that is not numbers, and when a function gives another shape in a later frame; MissingProperty for a column a frame lacks. TimeAverage raises InvalidParameter for a quantity that is neither a name nor a function.

docs.title: Time series
docs.text:
TimeSeries gives a quantity in every frame of a trajectory, as OVITO's time series: a column of the atoms reduced to one number in each frame, as reduce does, or anything a function computes from a frame.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import TimeSeries
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

# copper heated from 300 K to 1200 K over 20 frames 1000 steps apart:
# velocities in Å/ps of the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of each temperature
copper = build_crystal("fcc", 3.615, elements="Cu", repeat=(8, 8, 8))
mass, kB, unit = 63.546, 8.617333e-5, 1.0364269e-4  # amu, eV/K, eV per amu Å²/ps²
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
frames = []
for k, T in enumerate(np.linspace(300, 1200, 20)):
    sigma = np.sqrt(kB * T / mass / unit)
    v = rng.normal(0, sigma, (len(copper), 3))
    frames.append(copper.with_columns(velocities=v).with_info(timestep=1000 * k))


def temperature(frame):
    """The kinetic temperature in K of a frame."""
    v2 = (frame["velocities"] ** 2).sum(axis=1).mean()
    return mass * unit * v2 / (3 * kB)


spread = TimeSeries("velocities.x", "std").compute(frames)
heated = TimeSeries(temperature).compute(frames)
heated.timestep, heated.values  # (20,) each

The temperature of each frame:

from mdapy.visualization import plot

with plot.style():
    fig, ax = plot.figure("single")
    ax.plot(heated.timestep, heated.values, "o-")
    ax.set_xlabel("Timestep")
    ax.set_ylabel("Temperature (K)")
    plot.save(fig, "images/time-series", formats=("png",))

The kinetic temperature of the 2048 atoms follows the ramp from 300 K to 1200 K, within the spread of a sample of that size.

docs.title: Trajectory lines
docs.text:
trajectory_lines gives the path of each atom over the frames of a trajectory, followed through the periodic boundaries, as OVITO's generate trajectory lines does; render(lines=...) draws the paths.

import numpy as np
import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.analysis import trajectory_lines
from mdapy.visualization import colormap, render

# twelve atoms that wander through a periodic box for 300 frames
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
box = mp.Box(20.0)
walk = rng.random((12, 3)) * 20 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.3, (300, 12, 3)), axis=0)
frames = [
    mp.System(box.wrap(x)[0], box, elements="Ar").with_columns(id=np.arange(1, 13))
    for x in walk
]

paths = trajectory_lines(frames)  # (12, 300, 3), unwrapped
some = trajectory_lines(frames, atoms=[0, 3, 5])  # (3, 300, 3)
colors = colormap(np.arange(12), "labels")  # one for each atom and its path
render(
    frames[-1],
    "images/trajectory-lines.png",
    color=colors,
    radius=0.8,
    lines=paths,
    line_radius=0.12,
    line_color=colors,
    wrap_lines=True,
    view=(-1.0, -0.7, -0.5),
    width=600,
    height=600,
)

The paths of twelve atoms over 300 frames, each in the color of its atom, cut at the faces of the periodic box and moved in through the opposite faces, and the atoms where they end.

docs.title: Parameters

trajectory_lines(frames, *, atoms=None, unwrap=True)

The atoms are matched by their ids and unwrapped as for the mean squared displacement: by the image flags, or else through the nearest periodic image of each step. OVITO follows the nearest image only, so that its lines of atoms that move more than half the box between frames differ.

render draws polylines with lines, line_radius (Å, 0.1 as OVITO's line width of 0.2), line_color, one or one for each line, and wrap_lines, which cuts the lines at the periodic faces of the box and moves the parts outside in through the opposite faces; see Rendering.

docs.title: Voronoi analysis
docs.text:
VoronoiAnalysis divides space into the Voronoi cells of the atoms, the regions closer to one atom than to any other, and gives the volume and the coordination of each cell, and, when asked for, its faces, its Voronoi index and its shape as a polyhedron.

import numpy as np
from mdapy.analysis import VoronoiAnalysis
from mdapy.build import build_crystal

# an fcc crystal of 5 x 5 x 5 cubic cells, atoms displaced by about 0.05 Å
crystal = build_crystal("fcc", 3.6, elements="Cu", repeat=(5, 5, 5))
shake = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(scale=0.05, size=(len(crystal), 3))
system = crystal.with_columns(positions=crystal["positions"] + shake)

voronoi = VoronoiAnalysis(relative_face_threshold=0.01, edge_threshold=0.5)
result = voronoi.compute(system)
result.volume  # Å³, a³/4 = 11.66 on average
result.coordination  # 12 for every atom
system = system.with_columns(result)  # voronoi_volume, ..., cavity_radius

# the faces too: the atom across each, its area and its edges
faces = VoronoiAnalysis(relative_face_threshold=0.01, edge_threshold=0.5, faces=True)
result = faces.compute(system)
result.index(6)  # faces with 3, 4, 5 and 6 edges: [0, 12, 0, 0]

shapes = VoronoiAnalysis(polyhedra=True).compute(system).polyhedra
shapes.vertices  # Å, the corners of every cell

The cell of an atom in fcc and in bcc, with the neighbors across its faces, and the cells of atoms packed at random, as voro++ draws them: each face a closed line through its corners, drawn as a tube by the renderer:

import mdapy as mp
from mdapy.build import add_interstitials
from mdapy.visualization import render, write_png


def faces(cells, i):
    """The faces of the cell of atom i, each a closed line through its corners."""
    lines = []
    for f in range(cells.face_offsets[i], cells.face_offsets[i + 1]):
        corners = cells.corners[cells.corner_offsets[f] : cells.corner_offsets[f + 1]]
        lines.append(cells.vertices[np.append(corners, corners[0])])
    return lines


blue, yellow, gray = (0.36, 0.62, 0.82), (0.95, 0.88, 0.52), (0.82, 0.82, 0.82)
look = dict(line_color=blue, box=False, style="shiny", width=600, height=600)
pictures = []
for crystal, reach in (
    (build_crystal("fcc", 3.6, elements="Cu", repeat=(3, 3, 3)), 2.6),
    (build_crystal("bcc", 2.87, elements="Fe", repeat=(4, 4, 4)), 2.9),
):
    cells = VoronoiAnalysis(polyhedra=True).compute(crystal).polyhedra
    middle = crystal.box.matrix.diagonal() / 2
    i = int(np.argmin(np.linalg.norm(crystal["positions"] - middle, axis=1)))
    apart = crystal.box.minimum_image(crystal["positions"] - crystal["positions"][i])
    distance = np.linalg.norm(apart, axis=1)
    pictures.append(
        render(
            crystal,
            atoms=distance < reach,
            color=np.where((distance < 0.1)[:, None], yellow, gray),
            radius=np.where(distance < 0.1, 0.5, 0.3),
            lines=faces(cells, i),
            line_radius=0.07,
            view=[1, 0.6, 0.45],
            **look,
        )
    )

# 320 atoms at random, none closer than 2.3 Å, in a box that is not periodic
empty = mp.System(np.zeros((0, 3)), mp.Box(18.0, pbc=False), elements=[])
packed = add_interstitials(empty, "Ar", 320, min_distance=2.3, seed=3)
cells = VoronoiAnalysis(polyhedra=True).compute(packed).polyhedra
edges = [face for i in range(len(packed)) for face in faces(cells, i)]
pictures.append(
    render(packed, color=yellow, radius=0.9, lines=edges, line_radius=0.14, **look)
)
write_png("images/voronoi.png", np.hstack(pictures))

Left: the cell of an atom of fcc, a rhombic dodecahedron, each of its 12 faces halfway to one of its 12 nearest neighbors (gray). Middle: in bcc a truncated octahedron, 8 hexagons toward the first neighbors and 6 squares toward the second. Right: 320 atoms packed at random in a box that is not periodic, whose faces close the outer cells.

render(system, polyhedra=cells) draws the cells of all the atoms shown as solids instead, their faces in the color of their atom or by their number of edges; see Rendering.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Default Unit Meaning face_threshold float64 0 Å² faces of this area or less do not count relative_face_threshold float64 0 faces of this fraction of the surface of their cell or less do not count; from 0 to below 1 edge_threshold float64 0 Å edges shorter than this do not count, and faces with fewer than three edges that count do not count faces bool False also give the faces of each cell that count, with the atom across each, its area and its edges polyhedra bool False also give the shape of each cell

Without faces, the faces of each cell are counted and let go as soon as its volume and coordination are known, so that the memory a computation takes does not grow with the faces: some 14 per atom, which take as much as the rest of the result several times over.

compute(system, *, progress=None, cancel=None) takes the progress and cancel of every analysis, but no neighbor list: the neighbors of each cell are searched as far as the cell needs. No two atoms may be at the same position. Directions that are not periodic are closed by the faces of the box, moved out as far as needed to include every atom.

The thresholds remove the small faces and short edges that thermal motion creates where a perfect crystal has a vertex shared by more than four cells, as in fcc; they do not change the volume, the radius or the shapes. The atoms across the faces are also a kind of neighbor list, built with NeighborList.build(system, voronoi=True) and the same thresholds.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A VoronoiResult:

Attribute or method Type Meaning volume (N,) float64 the volume of each cell in Å³; its column voronoi_volume coordination (N,) int64 the number of faces that count shared with other atoms; its column voronoi_coordination radius (N,) float64 the distance from each atom to the farthest vertex of its cell in Å; its column cavity_radius offsets (N + 1,) int64 the faces that count of atom i are offsets[i]:offsets[i + 1]; with faces, else None j (F,) mdapy.index_dtype the atom across each face, −1 for a wall of the box; with faces shifts (F, 3) int8 the periodic image of that atom; with faces areas (F,) float64 the area of each face in Å²; with faces edges (F,) int32 the number of edges of each face that count; with faces index(largest=8) (N, largest − 2) int64 the Voronoi index: the number of faces with 3, 4, ..., largest edges shared with other atoms; with faces polyhedra VoronoiPolyhedra or None the shapes of the cells, with polyhedra=True

The faces are listed like the pairs of a neighbor list: the vector from atom i to the atom across a face is x[j] - x[i] + shifts @ box.matrix.

The walls of the box are faces of the cells of the atoms next to them, in the faces with j = −1, but they are not neighbors: coordination, index and the Voronoi neighbors count only the faces shared with atoms. OVITO and LAMMPS count the walls in the coordination and the Voronoi index as well, so their values are larger for atoms next to a wall.

A VoronoiPolyhedra holds every face of every cell, those that do not count included, so that each cell is a closed polyhedron, for example to draw it:

Attribute Type Meaning vertices (V, 3) float64 the corners of the cells in Å, each cell with its own; a cell may reach out of the box vertex_offsets (N + 1,) int64 the vertices of the cell of atom i are vertex_offsets[i]:vertex_offsets[i + 1] face_offsets (N + 1,) int64 the faces of the cell of atom i are face_offsets[i]:face_offsets[i + 1] corner_offsets (F + 1,) int64 the corners of face f are corners[corner_offsets[f]:corner_offsets[f + 1]] corners (C,) int64 the vertex of each corner, counterclockwise seen from outside the cell j (F,) mdapy.index_dtype the atom across each face, −1 for a wall of the box areas (F,) float64 the area of each face in Å² 
f = shapes.face_offsets[0]  # the first face of the cell of atom 0
loop = shapes.corners[shapes.corner_offsets[f] : shapes.corner_offsets[f + 1]]
polygon = shapes.vertices[loop]  # its corners in order

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The constructor raises InvalidParameter for a negative threshold or a relative_face_threshold of 1 or more; compute raises it for two atoms at the same position, and index for a largest below 3.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Voronoi cell of atom \(i\) at \(\mathbf r_i\) is the set of points closer to it than to any other atom or periodic image,

\[ V_i = \{\, \mathbf x : \lvert \mathbf x - \mathbf r_i \rvert \le \lvert \mathbf x - \mathbf r_j - \mathbf s H \rvert \text{ for every } (j, \mathbf s) \ne (i, \mathbf 0) \,\}, \]

with \(H\) the matrix of the lattice vectors as rows. It is a convex polyhedron whose faces lie on the planes halfway to its neighbors, or on a wall of the box in a direction that is not periodic. A face counts when its area \(A\) and its edges satisfy

\[ A > \max(A_\text{min},\; f\, S_i) \quad\text{and}\quad \#\{\text{edges of length} \ge \ell_\text{min}\} \ge 3 , \]

with \(A_\text{min}\) the face_threshold, \(f\) the relative_face_threshold, \(\ell_\text{min}\) the edge_threshold and \(S_i\) the surface of the cell, walls included. The coordination is the number of faces that count shared with atoms, and the Voronoi index \(\langle n_3, n_4, n_5, \dots \rangle\) the number of these faces with 3, 4, 5, ... edges that count. The radius, the distance to the farthest vertex of the cell, is that of the largest sphere centered on a vertex of the cell with no atom inside.

Crystal Cell Faces Volume fcc rhombic dodecahedron 12 rhombi \(a^3/4\) bcc truncated octahedron 6 squares, 8 hexagons \(a^3/2\) hcp trapezo-rhombic dodecahedron 12 quadrilaterals \(\sqrt 2\, a^3 / 2\) cubic diamond 12 triangles, 4 hexagons \(a^3/8\)

Please cite

Voronoi (1908).
